MY JOHN. wish we still were little, John, The world was then so wide! • - When on the stone by neighbour's bourn We rested side by side. ' We saw the moon in silver veiled Sail silent through the sky, Our thoughts were deeper than the bourn, And as the heavens high. You know how still it was then, John; All nature seemed at rest; So is it now no longer, John, Or in our dreams at best! Think when the shepherd boy then sang Alone o'er all the plain, Ave, John, you know, that was a sound We ne'er shall hear again. Sometimes now, John, the eventides The self-same feelings bring, My pulses beat as loud and strong As then beside the spring. And then I turn affrighted round, some stranger to descry— But nothing can I see, my John-- I am alone and cry. —Groth, a Schlestoig-Holsteix Poet.

"ON GREAT WATERS." The ship has orossed the harbour bar, And leaving home and friends afar, Sails forth beneath the evening star. With prayer of watchers left behind, - It sails before the springing wind: Strong is the bark. and God in kind. 0 baby-souls, sent forth from heaven, To you the sea is also given— A weary struggle to be striven! Ye too have left the light of home For warring winds and waves—to roam Across a dreary waste of foam; And what shall be the end for ye? Dark shipwreck in the midmost sea? Or triumph to eternity? Fear not; for if ye brave the blast With God's own colours at the mast, •"""""' The haven will be sure at last.
—Arthur L. Salmon.

The second son of George IL, it was said, had a very cold and ungenial manner. Lamb stammered out in his defence that "This was very natural in the Duke of Cu-Cum-ber-land." Whatever you may be sure of, be sure at least of this, that you are dreadfully like other people. Human natttre has a much greater genius for sameness than for One rogue can easily overmatch a dozen honest men. The rogue has a definite motive—his own interest. The Meet man has a very vague one—the interests of morality.--erulian Hawthorne. °Nature," said some one to Jerrold, speaking of a person for whom he had no great esteem, "Nature has written honesty on his face." " Humph," replied the wit, "the pen must have been a very bad one." , It is said that a baby can wear out a pair of kid shoes' In 24 hours. This is pretty fast work, but an ordinary baby can do much better. It can wear out the patience of an average bachelor in about seven minutes. "So you've got married, old man, while I have been away?" "Yes." Well, I congratulate you on having Shaken off that she-dragon of a housekeeper of yours at last." The late Mr. Bush, of Aberdeen, used to tell :this story of a brother barrister. As the coach was about starting before breakfast, the modest limb of the law approached the landlady, a pretty Quakeress, who was near the fire, and said he could not think of going without giving her a kiss. "Friend." said she, "thee must not ,do it." "Oh, by heavens. I will," replied the barrister. "Well, my friend, as thou hast sworn, thee may do it, but thee must not make a practice of it." NOBLESSE OBLIGE.—When Mr. Toole was playing "Uncle Dick's Darling" at Birmingham some years ago, in the rush for gallery seats a man broke his leg, and his chief distress was, not that he had broken his leg, but that the accident had happened in the gallery. "I have never," he said. "been in the gallery before. The pit was so crowded I couldn't !rot a seat. I am a commercial traveller, and I shouldn't like my firm to know that I was in the gallery. It would lower me in their esti- mation." FIGURATIVE SPERCH.—As an example of the error of talking figuredirely to those who do not appreciate, and who are apt to take everything literally, this story is worth reading. The respected superintendent of a Sun- day school had told his boys that they should endeavour to bring their neighbours to the school, saving that they should be like a train, the scholar being the engine and his converts the carriages. Judge of his surprise when, next Sunday, the door opened during lessons, and a little boy, making a noise like an engine, ran in. followed by kW a dozen others in single file at his back! He came to a halt before the superintendent, who asked the meaning of it all. The naïve reply was:—" Please, sir, I'm the engine, and them's the carriages." The best anecdote of Dr. Johnson, not to he fopnd in Boswell, was related by Dr. Chalmers. "Dr. Johnson," be said, "on his arrival at St. Andrews, was taken by. the College authorities to see the ruins. He afterwards dined with them in the College Hall; but he had not got over his ineljgnation at the vandalism which had wan- tonly destroyed some of the oldest and finest remains of ecclesiastical architecture in Scotland. He was so rude and overbearing that at last the coinversation dropped. After a pause, one of the younger and more adventurous professors addressed him—" Dr. Johnson, I hope that you have not been disapnointed in your visit to Scotland ?" "Sir," replied the Doctor, "I came here to see savage men and savage manners, and I have not been dis- appointed." MATTHEW ARNOLD'S LITERARY COURAGE.—Mr. Arnold had courage. Indeed he carried one kind of courage to an heroic pitch. I mean the courage of repeating your- self over and over again. It is a sound forensic maxim: Tell a judge twice whatever you want him to hear. Tell a special jury thrice, and a common jury half-a-dozen times the view of a case you wish them to entertain. Mr. Arnold treated the middle class as a common jury, and hammered away at them remorselessly :tad with the most unblushing iteration. They groaned under him. they snorted, and they sniffed—but they listened. and, 'what was more to the purpose, their children listened, and with filial frankness told their heavy sires that Mr. Arnold was quite right, and that their lives were dull, and hkqeous, and arid, even as he described them as being.—Scrtbner's for November. FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR. W. FELL.

On Saturday afternoon the lemains of the late Mr. William Fell, at one time a member of the firm of Messrs. G. and W. Fell, grocers, Sankey-street, Warrington, were interred in the Friends', Burial Ground, Penketh. Mr. Fell left Warrington some two or three years ago, and, after living with a friend, at lluyton had within the last three or four weeks removed into a house of his own at Roby,and it was fore that his death took place,the deceased gentle man was of a modest and retiring disposition, and, although a decided Liberal in politics, to ~k little active part in political or municipal affairs. In other and less prominent ways he, however, use- fully coutributed to the public life of the com- munity. In early days he'Nvas a student at the School of Art, and was the winner of the first medal gained by that institution. In later days he took a lively interest of the School, and was a member of the School Council for many years. Some of his best and most enduring work. was done in connection with our Meal museum, of which for a long period he was an honorary curator, and for many years a member of the Committee of the Corporation having charge of that , department. A contribution of great value which he made to the Museum was a series of about forty plaster casts of fishes, painted in oil with his own hand. Mr. Fell was also an enthusiastic amateur photographer, and attnirld no mean proficiency in the art. In reference to the deceased gentleman's connection with the Museum it will be seen from our report that his services were suit- ably acknowledged at the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening. On Saturday the body was brought : by rail from Roby to Bank Quay Station, and thence taken to the burial ground at Penketh. A number of beautiful wreaths were laid on the coffin, having been sent by Miss Fell, Mrs. Walter Milner, Mrs. George H. Bolton (Penketh), and other relatives and friends. The principaimonrners were Alderman King (Manchester) and Mr. William King (Rollington), brothers-in-law ; Mr. Edward Milner (Hartford), Mr. Walter Milner (Warrington), Mr. G. King (Manchester), and Mr H. King (Manchester), nephews; Mr. George King Harrison (Stourbridge) and Mr. John Harrison (Warrington),, cousins ; and Mr. Storrs Sutton (Liverpool). Around' the grave were, amongst others, Alderman Holmes, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, Mr. Charles Cherloy, Mr. Robert Garnett, Mr. William Sharp, Mr. George H. Bolton, Mr. James Bolton, Mr. G. Y. llolton, Mr. J. T. Gomersal, Mr. William Long (Thelwail), Mr. J. IT. W. Todhunter, , Mr. William Darbyshire (Morris Brook), Mr. Edward Bolton, Mr. W. B. Houghton, Mr. Charles Twiss. Mr. T. Birtles, and Mr. W. D. Jeans. The body was enclosed in a shell, which VMS placed in an outer coffin of fumed oak. The breastplate bore- the simple inscription : " William Fell, died October 25th, .1888, aged 65 years." Messrs. Holmes and Powell, Bridge-st., and R. Garnett and Sons, Sankey-st., were entrusted with the funeral arrangements', and carried them out in an efficient manner.

div.head: DEATH OF WARRINGTON VETERANS.
div.p: DEATH OF WARRINGTON VETERANS.

The death occurred early on Sunday morning of Mr. Thomas Davies, a local veteran in the cause of Liberalism, who passed away at his residence in Bewsey-street at the age of 78 years. The decased gentleman, who was well-known and highly respected, had for fifty years been an enthusiastic Liberal, and had rendered yeomen service to the cause. Of late yews, however, owing to his advanced age, he did not take an active part in political matters. In his earlier days he carried on business as a coppersmith, but for the last 25 years he had been retired from business. He was a member Of the Liberal Club up to the time of his death. For many years he did good work for the political cause that lie had espoused almost from boyhood by visiting the country districts and attending to the county register of voters. He also for many years officiated as one of the overseers of the parish of Warrington. The deceased gentleman was unmarried. His remains were interred in the Cairo. street burial ground on Tuesday afternoon, the ceremony being strictly of a private character. The late Mr. Davies was a brother of Mr. W. Davies, who at present carries on business as a tin-plate worker, &cy, in King- street and Lyme-street, and who has himself-reached a ripe old age and enjoys the respect of his townsmen. Mr. William Hartley, of 48, Church-street, a well- known and much respected resitlent of Warrington, died at his residence on Monday afternoon at the age of 80 years. The deceased took a great interest in the work of restoring the Parish Church. He had for a longtime been an invalid. The remains of the deceased gentle- man, who leaves a widow and five children, were interred in the Cemetery on Thursday afternoon.

div.head: *AN WHO STOLE A PUBLIC
div.p: THE *AN WHO STOLE A PUBLIC
ROAD. BY INIC-SLINGER.

There are no burglars or murderers in our village. Poets were not encouraged among people who looked i upon work as an essential of life. Statesmen were regaided as beings of quite another sphere, and, in fact, distinction was never an object of competition in our village. And so the man who stole the public highway from Willowbrook to the top of the hill remained a celebrity ut.til the day of his death. Daniel Winfell owned the land he tilled, and nobody begrudged it him. The well-to-do farmers would strip, and toil, and sweat with their labourers before they , asked a helping hand from Winfell, and the poor must ' be poor indeed who relied on his bounty for obtaining , the necessaries of life. As Daniel went along the road - with his cart and horse, none of the village boys ever asked him to let them ride, or even begged the privilege of swinging behind the cumbrous vehicle. Winfell's dog never made the acquaintance of other dogs, but ran along by the side of the cart, keeping the children at a respectful distance on either side or trotting in a dignified manner before the head of the tall, bony steed. Winfell was a screw, and it was only when he meddled with matters that he didn't understand that he occa- sionally over-reached himself. People said that on one occasion—none would hazard his reputation for veracity by mentioning the year—Winfell had an additional barn erected the crop of hay was so heavy, and that the con- tents of this barn were sold to a hay dealer, and for a while the latter stood indebted to Mr. Winfell to the amount of purchase money. Knowing that Daniel was to be allured with money at any time, the dealer called casually upon the farmer, and in the course of conversa- tion remarked—

" Well, iv aw pay yo' thad bit o' th' brass, yo'll tek mo five per cent. off ?" "Now! now!! There's to be no disceawnt—we agreed upo' thad.7 "Aye, bud then yo'll hey to wait for yo'r brass a bit longer, an' iv aw were to dee, wed then? Yo'd be twelve peawnd fifteen th' lovser." "Well," said Daniel. alarmed at the prospect, "a bargain's a bargain, an' tha shouldn'd run off id, tha knows!"

"Well, then. shall we say four per cent, off, an' aw'll pay tha neaw 2" said the dealer, diving jut) his pocket. "Now, now. Aw corn'd affooard no four per cent." "Well, then, good afternoon," said the other, turning

away. " Howd on a bit. Aw corn'd affooard four per cent. Tha doesn'd want to tek booath th' hay an' th' money on mo, does tha? Aw'll tell tha wed aw'll do. Aw'll tek tha th' odd fifteen shillin' off, iv thad'll suit tha." The dealer pretended to demur, but at last gave in, and when he had got the receipt safely in his pocket he asked Daniel—

" Wod does tin think neaw, four per cent. disceawnt on twelve peawnd fifteen would hey bin ?" "Aw dorn'd know. There wor no per cents. invented when aw were at skoo.'' "Well, id would hey bin abeawt five shillin' less then th' fifteen tha's alleawed mo, soa thou'rt rfboan rich a bad sooart, after o." But the victim of this sharp practice was by no means a very simple man, or he would not have earned his present farm. During his earliest years he displayed a remarkable ingenuity in the various means of acquiring and retaining property, and as such he was the delight of his father, the latter being described by his detractors as a miserable old skinflint, who lived to the age of eighty to gain the interest on the amount of his funeral expenses, but took care that nobody else lived for a day at his expense if he could help it. The careful Daniel was, as I have said, his father's pride and the increasing joy of his declining years. One day, some time previous to the old man's death, he called all his children together round his bed, and informed them that as he felt be should not long be spared to watch over them, he had given directions for his will to be prepared by a certain cheap lawyer in the neighbouring town. In this he had made due provision for them all, haying in mind their several habits and dispositions, and he warned them to look out after his death and see if Daniel did not soon, outstrip them all in the race for wealth. The next day Daniel was despatched to town for the will, for the father was not going to pay a lawyer to come down and see him sign it. An instinctive curiosity Prompted the messenger to open the packet and peruse the bold handwriting, when to his horror he discovered that his father had mentioned him as possessing vihkues that were better than gold,and had divided the prop&ty amongst the other children, leaving Daniel to subsist by the exercise of those talents which the testator had so highly. commended.
-Daniel exercised his talents. and he didn't wait until his father's death before he commenced to do so, either:

In fact, he took the document right away to a friend of his who had a little experience. This obliging gentle- man drafted another will, giving the farm and thetongue of land by the breok to Daniel. This was sealed up and taken to the old gentlemdm. The latter couldn't tell an R from a ram's horn, but he had unlimited faith in his legal adviser. So begot the schoolmaster and the parish clerk o witness the signing of the document, and went to rest confident tilt he had done his best to provide for the future of his family. Of course there was an uproar when he was dead, but the will was there, good and sound, and couldn't be got over, and so out the brothers went, and Daniel entered into full possession otthe property. The road we have spoken of had been a road ever since the hill was a hill. At least, all the old inhabitants said so, and the younger ones could not bring proof to the contrary. It was a zigzag, grassy, shaded, flower- decked, badly fenced, and uneven road, and never a stranger went up it from. one year's end to another. So . .

it occurred to Daniel that if tile natives could be pre- vented going along the road to it would be a great convenience as it was just the place to pasture cattle while the fields were under crops. Accordingly the prospective owner begah to discourage travellers by turning a fierce hull to graze on the road, and the drivers of vehicles found themselves opposed by carts, barrows, sand such like implements, which had been left out in
the lane in such ;), position that they virtually blocked the road. e •

In six months' time one point was gained. The whole populace avoided the road by night. That was half the object accomplished. But by day the travellers were defensive of their rights—and occasionally aggressive also. On one occasion a few farmers of the neighbour- hood agreed to take their carts down in procession. Daniel got to hear ot this, and so he yoked up his carts and horses, and placed them in the narrow road in front of his barn, where they completely blocked the way. When the waiting drivers of the opposition procession angrily threatened him for blocking the road, he had only to move the carts one by one round the barn and back into the road below again, in the manner in which a march of the graad army is contrived at minor theatres, to be quit(' within his legal rights and still keep possession of the disputed road. Eventually the farmers turned back, and while they were still unde- cided what course to pursue in order to maintain the right of way, an incident happened which, small in it- self, led to very great results. The gamekeeper to Sir Brutus Bulfeld—Sir Brutus owned all the surrounding property—happened to pass up the disputed lane one evening after dark, when he came in contact with a mowing machine, by which he was deftly overturned into the ditch. The keeper vowed vengeance; Daniel reciprocated the kindly senti- ment. The keeper, backed by his neighbours, sum- moned Daniel for obstruction, and in a few days Daniel's lawyer subpamed Mr. Snivin, the steward of the estate, as a witness on his behalf. As the steward invariably spent all his spare moments in thirSting for Mr: Winfell's blood, the, reception of the document alluded to above was a surprise, if not a pleasure. With the object of seeking a reason for this unexpected favour, Mr. Snivin paid a visit to Daniel's home, and demanded to be informed that it was a mistake that Mr. Winfell's lawyer had made and must apologise for. "Now, now, id's no mistake; yo'll find eawt as id's no mistake." said Daniel, most emphatically. " Yo'r th' best witness we hey." "How the cm you make that out 2" roared the agent. "Well, yo' see, idT be a gret help to eawr case iv we con prove as th' rooad were bein' used for an un-legal porpose, id'll be a gret help to us, yo' know. An' we want yo' to prove id." "Me, me ?i What do I know about the purpose it was used for 2" - "Well, this keeper dropped this letter when he fell into the dyke," said'Daniel, producing a letter from his pocket; "an iv yo' hevn'd written id, there's beawn to be a forgery case on th' jist." Let me see it." snouted the steward, jumping up and tying to seize it. "If its my letter, I'll have it." Daniel replaced the letter in his pocket as the steward said this, afterwards facetiously imitating the action of the person of Ingoldsby celebrity, who "said no word to indicate a doubt, but put his thumb unto his nose and spread his fingers out.'

"Aw con ell yo' wod id seys," remarked Daniel pleasantly," Id says as yo' want a lot o game for some friends, an' as th' keeper Iles to ged o' as he con within a day oF two. Id tells him to set a net across th' top o' Winfells Lane, an' aw believe he'd a net wi' him thad fleet beconas aw've getten pieces on't as hes cotched onto th' machine—at least th' lawyer bes 'ern new—" The steward considered moment, and then went on with a forced attempt to pray the agreeable. " Ah, well, we'll say no more about it. I'll tell the keeper to withdraw the summons, and we'll not quarrel." "Oh, wern'd we quarrel. Ah, bud aw'm not satisfied yet, aw'm nod thad. Iv yo' tek thad summons deawn aw shall hey this letter sent to Sir Brutus, soa just yo' be lookin' eawt for another shop." "What will you take and say nothing about it ?" " Aw'll tek nowt. Aw'll keep id o' quate an' never mention id no moor iv yell keep yo'r tenants eawt o' my looan. Sir Brutus keers nowt abeawt rooads yo' known, bud game----7' " Mr. Snivin protested that he couldn't stop the road, upon which Mr. Winfell declared that be couldn't stop the letter going to Sir Brutus. In the end, however, it happened that Mr. Snivin protested against the very unseemly and unneighbourly behaviour of certain of his tenants in annoying Mr. Winfell, and declared that any-

one guilty of such conduct in future would be con- sidered unworthy ts remain on the estate. As this affected everybody but Daniel Winfell for miles around, the road was soon deserted. Now it is enclosed by rails and stoops and a notice put up warning trespassers away. Daniel has gained his point—and the people's property. He laugh.; at the " village Hampdens" whom he has defeated, and three generations know him as the man who stole a Public Road.
ANOTHER AMERICAN LETTER FROM MR. H. WHITHAM.
Our townsman in America is still carrying the war into the enemy's camp on behalf of his country, as will be seen from the annexed letter, which we take from "The San Francisco Morning Call :"

"ITS ENGLISH, IiYOU KNOW I" • Sir,—l seem to have cut rather deep in my letter under the above heading. As the Immortal Bard says, and he was 'English, ye know": "Conscience makes cowards of us all." Hence, lam not at all surprised at "Imogene" in withholding her real name. No; I did not get out of the wrong side of the bed, not by any means. As a matter of fact, I was so much on the right side of the question that "Imogene " found it necessary to use language for the mere o,oncealment of her thoughts. _ _ _

Like a previous writer ("America ") on a kindred subject, " Imolene " seems to be eaten up with an overweening amount of conceit; hence the opaque- ness of her second and third paragraphs. Does "Imogene" deny my statement as to the studied insults which some true Americans seem so intent upon casting at everything that is "Eng- lish, ye know ?" If so, I can only conclude that she neither reads the papers, nor yet takes her part in the political demonstrations which do so much toward keeping the city lively. No Englishman would try "to ape the airs of a San Francisco hoodlum or a New Y ork Bowery boy." Their acquaintance with such is of the faintest kind. There may be, as she states, "a class of Americans with little brains who try to be Eng- lish in manners, speech, dress, and style," but I 'rather doubt it. I have not met with them.

I am rather of the opinion that the true American is so intent in his search after the almighty dollar that he neither cares for one nationality nor another. Now as to the British Lion—" Did not England fight a hundred years ago to make us her subjects?" I must confess my disbelief of this assertion. Who does "Imogene" mean by "us ?" If she is of English descent her ancestors, as well as the present writer's, were parties to the great wrong intended to be done to the early settlers on this continent. Perhaps "Imogene" cannot boast of ever having a grandfather, hence her Eden-like innocence. She, having nothing to repent of, need not cover herself with sackcloth and ashes for her forefathers' mis- deeds. But now, why all this childish wrangling about either one nation or another? Here you have a great nation, America, proud of her lineage, whose greatest men, from the days of Washington down to our own, take pride in pointing to the town or village in England from whence they have sprung. Minds such as "Imogene " and "America " carry about with them cannot possibly rise above the peculiar ideals they have before them. " Imogene " refers to my being "suited here." Well, I may say that I, like most other folks, am a crea- ture of circumstances, and in trying to mould these circumstances a little I, almost as soon as I landed, took out my papers. This I state to show that I did my duty to the land of my adoption. If "Imogene" was born in this sunny land, no thanks are due to her for her patriotic display. Her actions are simply the result of her parents' thoughts and actions. When I hear the utterances of such as "America" and "Imogene" about "It's English, ye know," I can always find a sure antidote in a walk through the city. I have but to keep my ears open and I find the English language all but universal; I suppose it's because "it's English, ye know." When I look for further evidence of the city's growth in civilization, I turn toward literature, and I find that 'book-store windows and shelves are crowded with the works of English authors. I leave out the piracy question in deference to the feelings of " Imogene. ' Take up any of the book- sellers' catalogues, and they beam with the results of English brains. Do I wish to study an American writer, such as Emerson, 0. W. Holmes or Walt Whitman, I can do so with a keen knowledge that these America's foremost writers, were proud of the ;tale village away in England, which they claimed as the home of their fathers. Leaving these, I have but to go into the dry-goods stores to find that the store-keeper and his assistants put their best goods forward as " English, ye know." Do I murmur at the high price charged, I am at once told that "English goods are so much superior to) native manufacture," and numerous cases have come under my observation in which attempts have been made to pass off superior native-manu- factured goods for "English, ye know." You cannot pass along any of the main streets without seeing sign-boards bristling everywhere, "English goods imported direct." You do not see German, French or Italian goods so advertised. Oh, no, "It's English, ye know"— for does not civilization tend westward? and why should not the Golden Gate feel its good effects, in spite of all the Imogenes that evolution has failed to stamp out? - H. Wurrmaat, 13, Valparaiso-street, San Francisco.

div.head: WARRINGTON INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARY. •
div.p: WARRINGTON INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARY. •

The annual concert promoted by the Working- men's Committee of this Institution was held on , Saturday evening, in the Public Hall, mosich was crowded. The chair was occupied by the Maybr ( Alderman T. H. Sutton), who, before the concert was commenced, said that he could not resist the opportunity of saying a word or. two in reference to its object. As they were all aware, the object of the concert was to aid the funds of the Infirmary and Dispensary—a noble institution, perhaps he might go so far as to say'the most valuable institu- tion in the town. (Applause.) He was lery glad to see that the working-men and their wives appre- ciated the 'concert, and supported it in the way that their presence indicated .they were doing that night. As the institution was essentiallya working- • men's_institution, and was intended principally for, the benefit of the working-men, -it was of course only natural that they should take an interest in it. Only a few years ago, before the had the Infir- mary established, when a man unfortunately met with an accident he had to be taken either to Man- chester or Liverpool, a course which was attended with great risk, even so far as the risk of the patient's life. Therefore, as they had public bene- factors in Warrington to provide such a noble building as thepresent Infirmary, he thought that they should be very thankful indeed. He noticed in looking over the report for last year that the Working-men subscribed, including about £4O, the profit on last year's concert, the large sum of £368 odd. (Applause.) That was a very good sum ler the working-men to raise, and it ' spoke well for them. For their informs- mation ~he had had placed in his hand an epitome of the subscriftions of the workinemen which read as follows :-1880, £165; 1881, £.339 1882:X363 ; -1883. £422; 1884, £397; 1885; £478; 1886. £367; and 1887, £368. This gave a total of £2,002, being an average of £362. He hoped that they would continue to support the institution to the best of their ability. The concerts commenced in 1881 with a profit .4 £29.65:8d., and last year the amount realised was £4O us. 7d. Great credit was due to the Workingmen's Committee, and to Mr. John Roberts the Chairmar, for the interest that they had taken in the concerts. Mr. Roberta had worked hard, and was deserving of their best thanks. He hoped that they would never be in want of funds with which to ptovide aseistance fQr working people who were so unfortunate as to meet with an accident. (Applause.) An enjoyable pro- gramme was then proceeded with. A very pleasant feature was the admirable playing of Mr. T. J. Down's orchestral band, which gave several selec- tions that delighted the audience. Mr. Alfred Cavanagh was very successful in his songs, and Miss Ashworth and Mr. Sheargold, who also gave songs, were well received. Mr. Harry Collins sustainell the hutnourous element. Mr. George -Riley acted as accompanist. At the close of the proceedings a very cordial vote of thanks to Mr. Down was passed on the motion of Mr. T. Morris, seconded by the Mayor. Mr. Down having made an acknowledgment, a similar compliment was paid to the Chairman, on themotion of Mr. John Roberts, seconded by Mr.. John Griffiths.

div.head: HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
div.p: HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
By Mu. J. K. SPENDrit,
Author Qf "Mr. Nobody," "Parted Lives," "Both in the Wrong," "Recollections of a Country Doctor," "Trust Me," Sze.
CHAPTER XVII. "WHO COULD REFUSE HER?"

She was a creature of impulses, and after many such conversations,she suddenly remembered that she hated herself for doing nothing—abhorred all this standing about and sitting with her hands before her. Dancing might be all very well, but she could not dance always, could not be always declining offers of marriage, and wearing the scalps of her victims. She gained more admiration than she cared for, partly on atcount of her naive speeches, the daring things which she ventured to say, andpthich made her so unlike the majority of women, and partly, no doubt, on account of the repute of her fortune.

In vain she blamed herself when two or three men made her offers, and when they went abotit, as she said, "looking sea sick.". She could not help their mistaken hopes, nor could she help refusing them. But their disappointment left her brooding all the more on the thoughts which she kept close in her heart, and which made her spirits droop. Wilfrid Fielding never flattered her. He was young like herself. He was safe and not likely to have any thoughts about marriage. In fact, he was only one of the many " comrades ' who in the old days had treated her as if they were he brothers. She had not known him long. But, putting Raymond out of the question- as her, dear brother after the flesh, there were days when she accused herself of feeling too quickly about this new comer, as if he were " The one - , Brother, and that one only, who had evello Made her heart leap," Those were the days when she felt as if her whole soul rose up against the enforced inactivity of her life. She had felt so before at S. Agatha's, but never to this extent, as if she would rather have scrubbed the floor, rather have eaten bread and dripping than be any longer satiated with luxuries in this land flowing with milk and honey! She had inquired into things for herself, and found that Fielding's words were true, and the enormous expenditure of untold thousands on feasts of art for the rich when the poor were starving, the grotesque disproportion between human pain and pleasure, began to fill her passionate soul with indignation. She cared no more for her drives in the park when she thought of those tombs for living people who are buried in miserable holes, only alive to the struggle for the mere necessaries of life. It is difficult to analyse human sentiments, which are often as complicated as human motives, and we , will not inquire how much her sympathy just then I for other women who weie suffering from physical hunger was quickened by the heart hunger which she herself was experiencing for the first thee in her life. At any rate, she thought much of that cruel physical hunger with its hideous nausea diffi- cult to be borne, and hated to think how it might be tearing at the vitals pf some poor sisters not endowed as well as herself.

If it was Fielding's dream, as some people said it was, that the differences of the race might be re- duced, special traits obliterated, and that' the great leveller, democracy, might wake .the majority of mankind from the torpor of uniformity, she felt that she hgtl no right to 'blame him for it. • He himself had never spoken te her about it, so she had no right to convict him of such theories. And if others had told her sneeringly that it was a pet scheme of his, of other young men, and of older en- thusiasts than himself to transport a bit of msthetic Oxford into the heart of the East End of London, just as the devil was said to have carried a church and dropped it in the centre of a wood where—as the sneerer said—it could not possibly be wanted, she equally felt 'she had. no business to inquire into the matter. _
She had a greater excuse for a show of interest when he told her, after xnefting her two or three times, that he was not rich enough to be wasting his tlme in London.

"I am looking out for some tutoring during the Long. I was tutoring before when I met you at Abbeyford. 1 don't know that I have any special faculty for teaching, but ,just for the present I must try and do my best at it." A wild thought came to her. It was a rare thing for her to be nervous, but for a minute or two she was nervous, with her heart .beating rapidly, and sat in a•rigid attitude with her head cast down. But the nervous diffidence was utterly incongruous with her character:

There was a sudden light leaping to her brown eyes, and biinging out the Olden 11,,rlits in them, as she sat bolt upright, and looked at him with a sort of challenge in her expression. He knew her sufficiently well already to be used to her changes of.mood, and yet was rather taken aback when she asked him, almost as if she were out of breath, " Will you tutor my brother ? " He happened to have heard a good deal about the brother.
"I—l---- "he began falteringly. But she took the words out of his mouth.

" There are difficulties—l know you are young yourself; but Ton are a man to cope with difficulties, the very man to influence a younger one as my brother should be influenced. Oh, no, don't misunderstand lit me; I know you are not a prig; u , undervalue your own influence; you do good, as vere, by stealth, and no one knows that you do i , and here is an opportanity. Oh, if you knew all about it, my .brother is to be pitied. He has had no one to help him forward, and I, who was so confident hi myself , —I know there were reports--perhaps you heard them at Abbeyford ? It is all the more necessar.y he should not return at once to S. Agatha's, and the clergyman who wa ;With him is obliged to come back to 'England." He had risen as if to screen her from observation. The blood had mounted to his biAv. He could not say , to her, "People will be wondering and suspecting something. No, Ido not think that would exactly do." He could not enter into all the reasons why he feared it would not do, and why it would 'be wise for him not to encumber himself with a tutorship for her brothor. Unconventional himself, he could understand her unconventionality. And yet it was a relief when her quick perception of something amiss in his face led her to lower her voice and break off in in her urgent speech. "Mrs. Wilson is quite close to us, and I—l am not so hampered by rules of etitrette as many girls,". she said with a little sigh. "You must re- eollpet that I was brought up abroad— always with My father and brother, and always accuitorned to 'manage, even in things of this sort. I lictd no mother, and no relations to lecture me on the pro- prieties." He did not lel] her that he liked •her a thousand times better without what she called the " proprie- ties," that it was no such absolute concession for him p undertake to help her brother, rather a thiug which he considered it his duty to guard against, for reasons best known to himself. He was not a man of many words. But an expression, which trans- figured the irregularity of a iace which was al- ways grand came into it as he. sat 'down again, still in an attitude in which. it would be possible for him to shield her from cynical remarks: _.. .._ .

The precaution Was not unnecessary. • For, as she said, "You will not refuse me then, when I have stooped to ask a favour of you," the way in which she leant towards.hinl Was enough to confuse and turn anyone's brain. "Refuse ! who could refuse you anything? though I think you make a fool of me,"miirmure(Ltim young rn.an,listening to the musical vibrations which at certain times when she was moved came into her voice. ,

div.head: CHAPTER XVIII. "I TELL THEM THEY NEEDNA COME WOOING TO ME."
div.p: CHAPTER XVIII. "I TELL THEM THEY NEEDNA COME WOOING TO ME."

She had her heart's desire,a.nd for once accepted Dr. Havard's advice to remain quietly where She was for a week or two longer, while a letter, was sent to Ray- mund to tell him to wait at Heidelberg, and Field- ing made his arrangements for travelling on the Continent.

_ "By what faculty of successful natural selection did you hit upon the very young fallow fora tutor towhom Raymond would be likely to take?" the good doctor wrote in high spirits from S. Agatha's, We are all of us,charmed with Fielding. He is good all round, and being a bit of an artist himself • can sympathise most thoroughly with Ray's favourite fads. A. man of the world in the best sense, he is yet opposed to those habits of luxury and excessive display, that senseless and vulgar extravagance which bids fair to be the devil's trap for your brother. No one could be more calculated to counteract by his own high tone those habits which our 'poor lad has been ready to contract, and which we know to be as ridiculous as they are foolish. What I like is that there is no /foolish parade about Fielding. He is not one of your canting and drawling soft, with a bit of blue ribbon pinned to his buttonhole, but he does not go in for expensive wines, and he has a hand stivang enough to 'protect the feeble knees of another."
Meanwhile Ursnli had to wait in town whilst it was emptying fast of its fashionable crowd.

The first week of August was wet and parties were few. Hove'desolate it was, with leaves turning already and beginning to drop in the London squares! Mrs. Wilson could take her siestas, blit whilst her cap was nodding (Ursula longed to tear it off, and wondered why Englishwomen of a certain age would wear those hideous stiff erections on their respectable heads) it was difficult for the girl to be as happy as she had expected. Wilfred Fielding was to take care of Ray through thu long "vac.,' and to accompany him to Oxford as soon as he was forward enough to go in for his matric. Even then there would be two more terms before he passed his own final examination, so that he would be with Ray at the first settling in to the un- accustomed life. What could Ursula wish for more? Why should she be panting for a new sensation— watching the wet flags or the sooty trees of London which Cad been so novel to her at first, and were already so dismally familiar? Others who were L'ondoners to the core would have found plenty to amuse them still at the West End, but it struck Ursula that few of her fashionable friends really cared when they bid her adieu. She had made no successful match like other débutantes, ,and had not troubled herself to entertain.

- They protested to have a sincere regard for her, but it seemed to her they protested too much. Such warm susceptibilities as they might once have had seemed to the girl to have been worn off by a quiet unnoticed slow process, like that of water upon stones, produced by constant association with the world. _ _

No, the West-End was decidedly triste. She longed to see the golden corn alp the mellowing harvest fields, and thought with regret of the scythe of the mower, which had but lately gathered in the second crop of hay with the incense-breath- ing flowers. If she were to stay in London at all she felt she would rather have staid where Mr. Fieldinn had told her some artists had chosen to pitch their bachelor tents, near the river, which flowed through the huge city pulsating with the beats of its „areat heart—played upon by sunlight and crisped by the wind, olive-tinged and brown, with groups of sails, boats and bridges, like those which the dying eyes of Turner looked at, and surmounted by hurrying clouds such as Keats so boldly compared to "herded elephants," and Wordsworth to Innocent sheep. There, at least, she might have gratified her love of the pictvesque, and she chafed and fretted as many women are apt to do in this transitional age because she had not quite the same independence as men, and could not live the same life as these men lived.

Theoretically Louis Grandet could have chosen no more favourable time to make his debut on the scenes. He had inquired for Ursula at S. Agatha's, and had come on by the next train to London, having travelled rapidly from Paris with the glad news that a small picture of his that had been hung for the first time, in the salon had actually found a purchaser, and that the whole secret of his private understanding with "Ursula" had at last been divulged to ins fond parents, who,— understanding that the lady had money—had given their instant consent, garnished with various pretty speeches and blessings invoked on her head. "'here was a sort of stupid constancy about the poor fellow : which he had by nature, and, to do him itistice, he had abstained from urging his claims on the English , girl till he had made a widi success for himself in life. Ursula ought to have been ready for any ' distraction as Mrs. Wilson's cap had nodded that ,day a good deal more than usual, and the girti herself had been prevented by the heat from exertidg herself.

She was lying on a sofa. gomewhat in deshabille yawning over a romance—bored even by its be- ginning—and longing for something to happen, when Grandet , was announced, spruce- and neat, as if he had never been on a. dusty journey, with hair cropped closely to his well-shaped head, moustache skilfully trimmed, and tears in the eyes, which were otherwise dark and bright. Why will Frenchmen be lachrymose when they mean to-be impressive? The whole get-up was so unexceptionable, from the crown of his head to the tips of his shiny boots, and the .manner so artificially- adapted for the occasion, that somehow it jarred on -Ursula, and she lost het usual amiability* She instinctively thought of Fielding, whose clothes were loosely fitted, and often none of the newest, and whose boots were rarely polished; arid when Louis bent elegantly on one knee and touched hfr hand with his lips, she could not help wincing, and saying with a laugh— Is this a fall-dress rehearsal? We are not on the boards." Grandet straightened himself, the colour rose to Ids. forehead. He was not devoid of sensitiveness, and the shaft went home at once. The white morning which had come to him with the good news that his picture hail sold was white- no longer' to him from that moment. Be tried his bast to be practical and not melo- dramatic, and succeeded with a violent effort in so altering his manner, that she who had been accusing hinaap, minute before of strutting and mistaking gewgaws for realities, now only thought how tiresome it was to have a friend who would have done very well as a friend, but who wished to be more than a friend, and would not be content with a reasonalle position. "Why did you not write and let me know you were coating? It takes away one's breath to have you burst upon-me in this sudden way, and the old lady, who is asleep upstairs, will think it so odd," she said, a little ashamed of the coldness of her reception. "I had asked You so often to fix the time of our marriage—and had received no answer," ha faltered, dismayed: "Time cool way which men have of assuming they have only to ask and have," she said, with a little toss of her head. Her. indifference was more than he could bear. Ho burst into urgent appeal and then into passionate entreaty. In his excitement he possessed himself again of her hand. "I never said,"—she began to explain,and drew it softly away. Now that she perceived how terribly he was in earnest, she looked at him with a kindly com- miserating look, and tried gently to explain to him, as she had explained to othare before, how any such plan for her future life might be a fatal experiment. "1 never said I would marry you yet. It was to be some day—a very long way off—how do we,know that day may ever come? You seem to have different views about marriage than mine. Half the misery in the world conies from ill-assorted mar- riages I" And'then when he took in a little of her meaning and seemed to be half distraught, she meant 'to be gracious as she explained, " You are my friefid— does not that content you? Why should I think of you in any other light? No ; it , is not the money that nzed stand between us, though the money is not mine, and I do net mean to give it to the man I marry—l did not want the money—l never thought of its coming to me, but new that I have got it I mean to use it, for tI benefit of others, for may brother, for instance. But wewere so young (you and I) when we thought of this, and to be tied together —to be perhaps offending each other, and not -be able to get away, like convicts chained together,why even a poor lobster can hide itself sometimes, for the shell which has disappeared to grow again. Would it not. be too dreadful for you as well, as me !" He could scarcely be complimented. She anticipated immense pleasure from making other people happy a—himself no doubt , amongst .the rest ! "We shall he so much more free and unfettered as we are. Now, if many a man is anxious to secure his full, unmutilated life, why not women the same? Why should it be supposed that women are obliged to marry?" she continued in her usual fashion, not noticing that she was making him nearly beside himself. • "Oh, no, you need not be afraid. I shall keep my promise to you "—with a little sigh—" I never broke a promise in all my life, yet, and I am not going to begin now. Till you set me free from it I shall never dream of marrying anyone else. But you must ge away, and, not come again for a whole year," she said, with a beaming smile, and an attempt at lightness id her unwillingness to give distress to anything that breathed. "You do not know Oar English way of looking. at things —that is all--it is impossible to make you understane, Most women are slaves. I should demand equality. You would pretend to give it to me; and then, because our English ways are different from yours, you would get put out with me and then—when it suited "you —you would turn round and want to be master." It was useless for him to protest. She meant to be yerectly kind. But when he pressed his arm lovingly close to her side, she drew herself away with a gesture of annoyance, and rang the bell for the servant to summon Mrs. Wilson. This pre- tence of affection—this piofanation of the higkest —was utterly impossible for her to carry out. It strengthened her in her resolution of insisting on the separation for at least a year. . She vouchsafed no sort of explanation to her dupirca, and that good lady was at her wit's end, tearful and desperate, when she wrote to Margaret Havard a lamentable account of the audacious

stripling wno naa arnYea rroni ruts and presumed to visit Ursula, taking up his abode in the neighbour- hood of her lodgings, and coming in to see her at all hours of the day. "Well," said the doctor, laughing, "this heat?, all. It is taking French leave with a vengeance! And both of them decided it would be best to per suade the Aung lady to come home to S. Agatus:B as soon as she could. '

The new Rugby rules came into force on ThursdaT3 and it is anticipated by competent judges that they we' be the means of encouraging a faster and more scientific playing of this popular game. Under these rules a free kick may be claimed fora knock on from touch. Players should always have it in mind, too, that the referee 113,e power to award a free kick for :-1. Intentionally We° ling the ball in the scrummage. 2. Intentionally falling down in the scummage. 3. For notimmediately putting the ball down on its being fairly tackled, or, if on the ground, for not getting up at once and playing the bail- 4. For wilfully touching the ball when off-side. 5. For off-side tackling. The referee, without being appeal to, and without any caution being necessary, may order a man off the field for rough or foul play, and thl offending player will, in addition, stand a very geeu chance of being suspended by the Rugby Union Oole" mittee who will also deal very severely with anrne reported to them for disputing the decision of tbs referee.

There have been few pleasanter and more interesting games than that between Warrington and Coventry nri, Saturday. The only thing that was to be regrette“ about it was the mishap to Gooderick, a smart player in the visiting team who had to retire owing to an injury l'e the muscles of one of his arms. As this took place the first half Coventry were, of course, for the rest e` the game put at a disadvantage, but to the finish the played a plucky and fast game, and although thel, retired defeated they were by no means disgraced. was clear that this midland team is formed of • the he material and will give a good account of itself where're' it goes. The principal match in St. Helens on Saturday aft,el: noon was that between the St. Helens Recs. and Log' r—twb old cup tie opponents—and considerable excite* ment was manifested in the contest. Rather rinfortn- nately the visitors arrived very late, and the play restricted to two 30's. Even then, much of the gain`• was played in semi-darkness, and the 1,200 spectal who accompanied the Leigh team would not feel vl repaid for their trouble and expense. As was generaq anticipated the game was very fast and fairly even through. As an exhibition of first class play too linicr excitement and eagerness was shown by the contes„"; ants ; and at times the play was far too rough. I'd 'home eleven secured a popular victory of one goal ne„, three minors to one try and one minor, and a large Btha `of money changed hands over tha result. The secnn 5 • teams of the two clubs met at Leigh, and the St. Helen contingent won by two tries and ten minors to nil. Owing to the attraction at Boundary-road, on Salo; day the Denton's Green ground had a somewhat desert,,. appearance on the occasion of the meeting of the t Helens and Manchester Free Wanderers. The visitor' were no match for their opponents, who played sPlef, didly from the commencement and ultimately won two goals, two tries and six minors to one goal. • fll4 St. Helens Association and Golborne played their , match on the ground of the latter. The visitors ban weak eleven, and the home team were short of Case,,,„Y" The play was in favour of the Golborne contingent, won an interesting game by two goals to one. The meeting of Earlestown and Haydock in fern years was pkoductive of widespread excitement ne, interest, buc last Saturday's encounter at Earlestni. did not give rise to the keen anticipation and conversno, tion of former times. The brilliant form of Earlestnying and the unlucky play of the Llaydock "boys" dur,.116, the present season, presaged an easy victory for ground eleven. Though Earlestown Neon by six g 0515.170 two, the score does not fairly represent the state of game, as the Havdock men showed up well on severe occasions. There is no doubt the Haydock team, et improving as the season advances, and they vril' make some of their opponents "sit up."

div.head: NARROW 'ESCAPE OF THE CZAR.
div.p: NARROW 'ESCAPE OF THE CZAR.

- S. PETERSBURG, SUNDAY NTGHT.—It appears from telegram mshiclie Minis; er of the Interior has received from the Mini.. of the Imperial Court that the Czar has had a very-narrow escape from assassination. It 'occurred during his Ma c..st y's pre.sence at Ku tais, a small city of 13,000 inhabitants., in Transcaucasia, on the toute•from Tiflis to the coast of the Black Sea. About. eie minutes sbefore the advent of the Emperor, for 'Whom a dense crowd was waiting in the Rue Tiflis, a Rouban Cossack was arrfisted, having upon him several explosives in.a handy form, as well as some Poison in gelatine • capsules. The man who haii; beep deputed-to make an attempt on the life of the Czar -came from Tarquirot, •where his movements had been 'atched by the police, and was disguised as a Cossack officer. In this attire he had mixed freely with the crowd, and his capture was made in the very nick 0"! time. It was :accomplished so quietly as to attract no attention, and tho matter wts immediately hushed up. The prisoner .roade. no re4,4,,nnen, but directly after his seizure he attempted. tlmugh unsueeessfullY, to take Poison. The wOuld-be assassin is known. Some years ago he. was expelled from one of the Universities for some imaginary political offence, and his career being thus ruined, he became one of the founders of the Solidi Russian Revolutionary Society. No papers were found upon him except a proclamation emanating from that aociety. He will be sent to St- Petersburg, to be detained in the fortress of St. Peter and St. Paul, and dealt with administratively

The defendants Matthews and Press, who were in- dicted for frand in ,connection with the Equitable Assurance Company at Belfast, were on lliaturday at Wicklow Assizes found guilty and sentenced each to nine months' imprisonment. A proposed meeting, at Barraduff, which Mr. Sheehan, M.P., should have addressed, was attempted to be held on Sunday afternoon. The police and military from Kil- larney, however. interfered. and on Mr. O'Brien atternp- Mg to speak ha was removed from the platform. The Proceedings were .i mmediately stopped. At Kilrush on Monday,, Thomas Conte, a young Nationalist. who has served three months' imprison- ment for assisting to barricade tenants' houses on the Vandelour estate, was sent to prison for another fort- night, the charge against him being that on the night of the Home Rule victory in the Ayr Burghs be assaulted a Constable at Kilrush during a police charge among the People who were rejoicing at Mr. Sinclair's election. Stephen Howard and Martin Nevin Were charged at Kilrusb, on Monday, with intimidating Daniel Grogan. The man's house was tarred ens night, and though the evidence was contradictory, the resident magistrates (Captain Welch and Mr. Irwin) considered the case Droved, and sentenced Howard to a month's and Nevin to a fortnight's imprisonment. Mr. .T. D. Sheehan. M. P, for Kerry, was arrested in Killarney on Saturday tunITT the Coercion Act, on the Charge of having advocated the adoption of tho Plan of Campaign among Lord Kenmare's tenants. Bail was refused, and he was escorted by a large force of police Tralee county prison. As the hon, member was being driven to gaol amid the,, cheers of the people several Ries hooted, but they fled on the approach of the pollee. The constables then bent. and otherwise molested a group Of men who had neither expressed dissent nor approba- tion of Mr. Sheehan's arrest. . .

-- Much indignation is felt in county Clare at the collec- tion of what is known as the " Wholehan Blood Tax " really a levy of £1,200 grarifed by the Clare Grand Jury !O the widow of Bead Constable Whelehan, who wry: killed near Lisdoonvarna a year ago while be was endea- vouring to arrest men wha were committing an outrage 'which had been planned, in concert with some police- !nen, by a notorious ex-convict and informer. The tax 13, collected as part of th.• county cess, and the National- St S have refused to pay. In each barony the cess col- 'ector has had-recourse to decrees, and there are likely to be some exciting scenes in the Clare Courts.

THE PARNELL COMMISSION. SIXTH DAY. THE LEAGUE'S BANKING TRANSACTIONS.

The special Commissioners appointed to investigate the charges made against Mr. Parnell and his party by The nines, sat again, on Tuesday, in the Probate Court, London. The court commenced to fill immediately the doors were opened. Counsel were also early in their places; and Mr. Biggar and Mr. Devitt again took their accustomed seats, near the solicitors' table. There was also the usual large complement of Pressmen, and iteveral gentlemen representing the illustrated papers. .Justices Thinner', Smith, and Day took their seats punc- tually at 10 30. The Attorney-General asked whether the bank docu- ments previously alluded to had been ploduced, and Sir Chart= Russell said, spetkinc for the National Bank of Dublin, that they were not.: end an affidavit was read from the secreta'ry of the Hibernian Bank (Mr. Alfred Collins), stating that they woald produce their books, but nevertheless objected to their inspection, because they declined to disclose the privacy of their customers' accouniie.

The Attorney-General *pitied that the order fekl. spection of the books be enforced. Sir :Walter Philircore, fortbe Hibernian Bank, opposed this • but the President heid that the books must be produced and inspected. An argument thee followed as to whether the accounts of certain persons not mentioned in the -charges should be inspected, the Attornev-Goneral maintaining that the powers of the COMMIS/4On ought not to circumscribed. It was essential, for instance, that they should sec Mr. Patrick Egan's. Accounts ought not, however, to be disclosed without revious consultation with the. banker's clients concerne•l
Mr. Wheeler followed in a similar strain, on behalf of the National Bank.

The rremdent ruled that the accounts must an te pro- duced. and made an order accordinViY• The Hibernian Bank simplified matters by withdraw- ing any objection, so far as they were concerned, and Ur. Cdline was sworn, and formally handed over the hooks to the Court, •

Sir Charles Russell comtilained that the Attorney- General had not given any deinite idea of the course of evidence he intended to call.—The President, however, said the Court was not in a position to give any direc- tionsin the matter.

MT. T. Healy, M.P., said he was willing to facilitate the business of the 'Court by admitting any speeches he had made that were reported in the Freeman's Journal, and was proud of it. Head Constable Bernard o'lr/filly was here called to give evideneeregarding speeches made at Land League meetings in-county Galway:- commencing July. 1880. The witness said he took notes in shorthand, and then proceeded in an almost inaudible tone, and with & strong Irish brogue, to (mote from a speech by Thos. Brennan, at Milltown. Nobody appeared to understand what O'bialley-was reading. The dlllieultv was, however, re- moved by Sir Henry James undertaking to read the ex- tracts to the Commissioners. The witness also produced the transcript of speeches by Patrick Gordon and Mr. Nally, from whicn it appeared violent language was usgd. Other speeches were put in evidence, and O'Malley 'commenced to read an address by Mr. Matthew Harris from his shorthand notes:. Although there were several stoppages, the witness read his notes very creditably. it was too Mew, however,' for the President, who, after listening for about twenty minutes, suddenly asked, "Is there muds more of this'?" On being told that such was the case, Mr. Harris's speech was banished until to- morrow, '*hen O'Malley promised to produced a tran- script Sir 'Henry James them.continued to read from manu- scripts in his possession of speeches by Mr. Nally. "'PHIS," meaning bullets, wern freely mentioned, and in ono :instance, where an Obscure provincial ekpression was used; Mr. Davitt rose and gave his services as in- terpreter to the Commissinners. Sir Henry James was reading from a speech by Mr. Richard Walsh, at Galway, in 1881,• in which the speaker anpfauded Allen, Larkin, and O'Brien. when thi? Court adjourned for luncheon. Alter luncheon-Sir Henry James renewed his exami- nation of O'Malley, as h the Galway speeches, commenc- ing with one by Mr.' Matthew Harris, at Ballinasloe. Mr. 'Parnell was still absent teem the court: but after luncheon a seat near the solicitors' table was occupied by Mr. John Parnell. brother of the hon. gentleman, who sat between Mr. Biggar and Mr. 'Healy.

The witness, having-concluded his evidence regarding sneeehes delivered in Galway. produced the manuscript of speeches that were given in county Kerry. • The first speech dealt with was one delivereg biefdr. Timothy Harrington, at Brosna. in 880, wlin he proposed a resolution pledging the people at the meeting to take no farm. from which an honest farmer had been evicted. "Depend upon it," he said. •• the people had the land question in I,lleir hands:" Next cam"prechee by ...Patrick Boyton and the Rev, Michael Mc.Mahon. The monotonous reading of the utterances of these gentlemen proved exceedingly dull work, add the sleepy aspect of the (hurt was only momentarily ruffled by an incident in Royton's speech. where he said that-" some illiterate people had even been seen 'tatting off their hats to a policeman." At three o'clock the monotony was relieved by the entrance of Mr. Parnell, • who joined du conversation with Mr. Geo. Lewis. _ _

SirHv. James eontn,dh,q reading. giving extracts from speeches at Knocknubull by a Mr. Curtin and the Rev. Fathers'Magillicuddy and Reardon. Mr.Flealy,.interruptine, said that the witness O'Malley was writing in the middle of his shorthand notes : but O'Malley denied this. Mr. Healy.: What were you doing then ? '•

The'President : 'This is not the time for questions. 1 can see what is being done with my own eyes. The witness explained that he was merely following Sir Hy. 'James, and the incident terminated. Sir Henry James had not proceeded much further, when Mr. Lockwood said his learned friend was not reading the whole of the speeches, and the extracts would give rise to misapprehension. Sir Henry 'James replied that their lordships would have the whole of the speeches laid before them. The President remarked that this would satisfy them. It was his.ovra•suggestion that only extracts ebould read.

Later •on, manuscripts of speeches delivered M Galway were put in by Head Constable Murphy, who also said he was •a shorthand writ/T. The first was by a Mr. Martin O'Halloran at Tynagli. and a speech by :qr. O'Halloran at Craighw.ll was being read, when the Court adjourned for the day. SEVENTH DAY. The evidencegiven before the Parnell Commission on Wednesday wasotif deep interest. Captain W. H. O'Shea, ex-M.P. for Clara and Galway, was examined by the Attorney-General. He said that he was on friendly terms with Mr. Parnell from 1880 to May or June. 1886, and in June, 1881, at Mr. Parnell's request, he communi- cated with Mr. Gladstone. He recommenced negotiations with the Government in the early part of 1882 without Mr. Parnell's authority, Mr. Parnell being then in Eilmainhare Gaol. After Mr. Parnell's release on parole witness acted as an intermediary between Mr. Parnell and the Government with reference to a settlement of the arrears question. Mr. Parnell 'always referred to the Arrears Bill as a measure that would help to tranquilise the country and put down outrage. Mr. Parnell was anitious for Mr. Davitt's release. but thought it would be inexpedient at that time to release certain other prisoners. On one occasion he gave a number of names, which -witness was to mention to Mr. Chamberlain, of persons not to be released, but neither Mr. Chamberlain nor witness approved Of this. Mr. Parnell authorised witness in his negotiations with the Government on the question of arrears to say that he would do his utmost to put down outrages. In witness's opinion no more severe blow could have been struck at Mr. Parnell's policy than the Phcesix Park murders. He had never associated Mr. Parnell's name with the com- mission of outrage, and did not know that Mr. Parnell had been in communication with Sheridan until a few months ago. The alleged forged letter was produced in court, and witness said that to the best of his belief the signature was that of Mr. Parnell. In cross- examination the witnesses embhatically denied that he procured the letters of which the Times had obtained possession, and disclaimed all knowledge of the source from which the letters were conveyed to the Times. lie was questioned at length with a view of showing that he had transactions with Patrick Casey, a dynamiter, but he denied that such was the case; although it was, he said, possible that Casey might have had money from him through a third person. On being asked to pro- duce letters received from Mr. Chamberlain and others during the arrears negotiations, witness said he des- troyed them all in 188.1 on the advice of Sir William Harcourt. On the conclusion of Captain O'Shea's examination, Head Constable Irwin again went into the witness-box and aave evidence as to speeches 'delivered in Galway and Kerry. He was still being examined when the Court adjourned. EIGHTH DAY.

At the sitting of the Parnell Commission on Thursday Head Constable Irwin produced further manuscript reports of speeches. In the course of cross-exa-hination he said that for about a week he had been at the Inns of Court Hotel, London, taking down evidence of Irish witnesses supcenaed by the "Times." He denied, how- ever, that he was engaged by the "Times." several resident magistrates sat in the room while he took this evidence. In reply to Mr. Davitt, the witness said he had heard Mr. Devitt denounce crime and outrage. The witness further stated that in many places the Land League was opposed by secret societies, and that the most disturbed places were those where these societies had the strongest hold. eir Henry James said they pro- posed next to go into the question of outrages, but if they must submit the evidence in sequence his clients would not be ready until Tuesday. With the acquies- cence of the Commissioners and Sir Charles Russell, the Court adjourned to Tuesday neat.

It is stated that the Porno—it Commission will be occupied on Mondays and Saturdays with the cmsidera- tion Of the evidence adduced, so that there may be no delay at the conclusion of the trial in the drawing tip ut their report. RTPERIENCE OF A LONDON HOSPITAL PATIENT. . [East London Advertiser, Odder 6th.] " Ranour to whom honour," is an injunction ven on high authority, although not one always served as it should be. It is therefore refreshing find a working man in East London throwing off reticence of his class and telling in simple, tffected language, but withal accompanied by an luence all his own, the story of his wonderful Atoration to health. That he should "honour" te means which has worked so marvellous a cure hi im is not surprising. When a working man finds life despaired of by the faculty in 'high places is informed by his own doctor that nOthing more e,_an be *done for him, the 'outlook is truly without nepe so Tar as this life isconcerned. But the truth ,Of the old adage that "whilst there is life there is woPe "was exemplified in the case under notice. In the extremity of despair he resorted to a remedy, the Nlects of which upon his shattered and almost lifeless SYStEM was little short of miraculous. He relates the history of his case in 'words that will Tarry conviction to the most incredulous. We freely confess that we should very likely have been amongst 'the number of the doubters had we not known the patient whilst suffering and hopeless and the same man withthealth restored and , going again to his every-day labour This so tar is our testimony, and we give it as "Honour to whom honour.' It only ,r7rmains now for the public to read tAie plain unvarnished tale of the man himself. . At 13, Plimsoll-street, East India-road, E., lives Mr. Alfred Foy, a maxi who has had a most wonderful per- , atonal experience. In the early part of last year he was 'taken with a mysterious illness. He kept growing *thinner and thinner from some unknown. cause which Vuzzled the doctors. He was obliged to give up work, ktod upon the advice, finally, of his doctor, went to the kLondon Hospital. Here he was put under the care of the leading physicians who made a most careful and 'aearchbigexantmation. Says Mr. Foy : "At that time I • "Vas so weak that I could scarcely go through the ordeal, y strength had run down so much that it was with ‘difficulty I could stand; and when the physician said he Inust have a %ample of my blood for microscopical, amination, it took a long time before they could get • stay for there was scarcely a drop of blood in my veins. At • last he said he would consult my own doctor, and • 'recommended my entering the hospital. On the advice, however, of my own doctor I stayed at home, because he said I should get better attention at my 'Wife's hands, although he added he could do no inore for me with medicine, and, unknown to me, Said to my wife that she must be prepared for a Change .as the case was hopeleas,and my death to be expected at any time. .To all appearances this seemed so, for I could not walk down the street 'Without holding on to the railings and gasping for breath. My friends with whom I had worked intimately for years passed me in the street without recognising In% and from a hale and hearty man, never having any- thing the matter with him, I had gone to a skeleton • scarcely able to walk. I then determined to try Warner's SAFE Cure, of which I had heard so much, and the result was simply marvellous. From the first I began to b. gain strength, the second bottle mUle an appreciable difference in me which all my friends noticed, and I had not completed the sixth bottle before I was thoroughly restored, and as well as ever I was in my life. There is no doubt about this being effected by Warner's Sane Cure, as my own doctor said the case was a hopeless one, and I could not recover, and he actually abandoned treatment altogether. It is impossible for me to be too grateful for what the medicine has done for me, and I am always only too glad to advise others to take it, and all these who have done so speak of the great benefits thy have already received.' the facts as narrated above are vouched for by the Iforoprietor of this paper, who knew Mr. Foy throughout Cs illness, and was one of those who certainly never expected to see him in the streets again after he went te - the hospital.

A man was stabbed in the throat by an unknown assailant, in the East End of tendon on Saturday night. Afterwards they went to Saighton Towers as the guestc of Countess Grosvenor. On Saturday evening, David Wilson, residing at Elliot-street, Glasgow, was killed on the switchback railway at the Glasgow Exhibition. He had lost his hat, and, contrary to warnings, went along the line to recover it, when he was run over by a-oar and killed on the spot. MARVELLOI7I3 EsCAEZ AT iWIITTEHAVEN.—OD Saturday afternoon, an engine was Backing six waggons of iron ore round the curve near the harbour-master's office, at Whitehaveu, when two young., children attempted to cross the line. HANDS.— The White Star royal mail steamer Adriatic, which reached Liverpool on Saturday from New York, brought particulars of the wreck of st,stertmer and the loss of all hands, a singular feature of . the disaster being that a large timber raft which was being towed by the steamer was fastened to the sunken vessel, and held as-if- it were at anchor. The finding of the raft led to the discovery of the loss of the steamer. It appears that on the-llth inst. some fishermen ,found a raft at anchor off Old Plantation Creek in Oresapeake Bay. The forward part of the raft was down under the water. The raft, it was believed. WaiS being -towed, and the steamer towing was believed to have foundered two days previous to the raft being discovered. On the 13th inst., two bodies were washed ashore. but -these did not lead to the identification of the ill-fated -vessel, which had, no doubt, gone sown with alt on board. Just after the bodies were found, the steamer commenced to break up, and portions of it, as well as some of elatetags, were being carried ashore by the current. THE CANONNI7RY MORDER.—TRIAL AND 'VERDICT.— At the Central Criminal Court, on Monslay, Glenny was indicted for the wilful murder of Mrs. -Wright, at Canonbury, in May last. The murdered woman was 71 years old, and two or three men, of whom theiprisoner was alleged to be one, knocked at her house door. The deceased opened it; the men rushed in; she screamed, and was knocked down. Her heart was weak, and the excitement and blow together cause immediate death. The men's object was clearly plunder: and they escaped. No clue was discovered as to their identity until recently, when a woman with whom Glenny had co- habited said he confessed the crime to her, and lie was then apprehended. If the deceasid had not suffered from heart disease her injueies would probably not have proved fatal, aud Mr. relived suggested that the jury might return a verdict of manslaughter. Mary Horning, a charwoman, and Phoebe Field, a girl with whom prisoner had been living, were the chief witnesses against him, but a satisfactorz alibi vows established, and the jury returned a verdict of acquittal. MR. GLADSTONE ON THE CHULICif OF- ENGLAND. —The forthcoming number of the Nineteenth Century contains an article by Mr. Gladstone on " Queen Eliza- beth and the Church of England." In Mr. Gladstone's opening there is every presumptinn that the important stroke of policy involved in the changes effected by Elizabeth in the form of public worship, as set forth in the Common Prayer Book, was duo not to clerical but to Royal influences. Had the divines had their way there might have been at once a conflict with the whole Roman Catholic party, a crisis in our foreign policy and in the country, and possibly war both civil and foreign. Apart from any ritualistic and theological leanings of the Queen, she did what the national safety and unity evidently required. The spirit of nationalism found in Elizabeth a restorer and champion. She admitted the Protestant claim in the cross, but admitted it with serious discounts, which were adjusal with extra- ordinary skin. Every ono of them lras an impor- tant concession to the -Roman Catholic party, with- the result that the mass of them conformed. The Queen pursued her work mainly in opposition to the Church's rulers, and without a party to support. her. Mr. Herbett 'Gladstone, MP., speaking at Chester on Monday, said there was now in the country one Liberal party, and one alone. The Liberals had tried to make, friends without compromising their principles. In this they had failed, and they said now that there was no room in the party for those who did not hold by its first principles. He asserted there, and should say it in the House of Commons, that Mr. Balfour had grossly neglected his duties in Ireland. Lord Armstrong, addressing a meeting at Newcastle, on Monday, on the subject of naval defence, said that whatever vessels were provided for the defence of our coasts and harbours they should be capable of engaging regular cruisers, and even regular mosquitos, for there was nothing to prevent a hostile cruiser making a dash at one of our harbours. Above all things the Govern- ment should not be encouraged to relieve itself from imperial obligations by throwing the burden on localities.

Mr. J. M. Maclean, MY.. addressed meetings of his constituents at Shaw and Oldham on Saturday evening. Speaking of the Merthyr Tydvil election, he said the re- quit showed the revolt of the people of Wales against the dictation of a caucus, and against that system which led people to the poll at the tolling of a chapel bell by the Nonconformist ministers. Those who knew South Wales well were all agreed in thinking that the revolt, of which the Merthyr Tydvil election was a sign, was likely to go on throughout the Principality, and was cal- culated to have a .vory great effect in changing the character of the representation of Wales in toe House ef Commons. • DEWSBURY ELECTION.—CHARGE OF ASSAULT.
