He is the strongest ‘candidate the Unionists could possibly secure. The meeting was attended by the loading Liberal Unionists in the borough. SIR GEORGE TREVELYAN ON IRELAND..

On Saturday night, Sir George Trevelyan addressed a meeting at the Masonic Hall, Morpeth. He said though the Government and its supporters alleged the state of Ireland to beeritical, the Chief Secretary from time to time simply issued from a Scotch retreat to make a par- ticular speech, and to offer nothing but a miserable series of taunts. In Parliament the gravest improprieties were being cenelonEsl in order that a Govemmentef re- action might be kept in office. He denied that thdlrish members were oarrupt. They. were always to the •front when it was a question of attacking jobs and abuse. The docbrinethat the root of the Irish Nationalist move- ment was agrarian he could not for one mcitnent endorse. He believed the desire for Home Rule had a different origin. Be admitted that what remained of disorderwas agrarian, but the Government were responsible 'for it. The people were being turned out of their own'hmnes because they eould not pay the arrears which the Gov- ernment, supported by the Dissentient Liberals, had by their legislation pronounced to be unjust rents. 'lrish- men, too, were denied positions of honotir, and they felt that our Parliament was out of sympathy with thefeel- ins of their-nation.

div.head: LORD 11ARTINGTON AT HUEMERSVIELD.
div.p: LORD 11ARTINGTON AT HUEMERSVIELD.

Lord Hartington attended a Liberal Unionist meeting at Huddersfield on Monday, and delivered an address in the Irish question. Admission was by ticket-and about 2,000 persons were present Lord Derby wrote that the subject under discussion was not the conduct of this or that Irish magistrate, but the continued, supremacy of the Imperial Parliament, and thereforeef -the Imperial Government, over Ireland. If nothing more was asked for than a legiskitive assem- nly in which Home Rulers might deal with Irish affairs subject to control, a committee formed of the present Irish memberswould be sufficient for the purpose, and from a proposal of that kind very few people would dis- sent. Ilut.itwas idle to suppose that any such ,partial concession would satisfy the demand for nationality. the land question was at the bottom of the trouble. Mr. Chamberlain wrote that "Mr.- Gladstonti's bill would have /node sAparation possible and even probable, and that no-Alternative proposal has yet been made by bins. Until he .condescends to show his hand emd•to take the people,into his confidence, I hope that those who love theincountry will refuse to give a blind assent to a policy whichapparently will not bear the light of day."

Lord HAR•rnormx, who wait recAived with remehesn- thutdasm, said that the Unioniqs remained masters of the situation. Their opponents would hear of nothing but the Irish ,question, and he asked how long the electors of this ,country would be content to have all their affairs postponed. It WAS true that the last had not been altogether an Irish session, but they all knew the ansialsie,motive,which allowed this to be the case. It was Thought , dna the discussion over the 'Local Government Bill ‘evould cause a disruptima; but happily the vesuit had been at least the laying of the foundation fora perfect superstructure °ma ques- tion of omit importance; and if any Liberals thought. that such Questions. could be better dealt with by a, Liberal -Government, the responsibility rested on the shoulders of those who had not adhered to the pro- gramme butecetho.leader of 1885. No doubt weber': not arrived At perfection in Irish land legislation. and no. doubt something might be done in developing Irish in- dustries and resources, and in, extending local govern- ment ; but be .denied -that any great grievance remained in Ireland. Mr. Gladstone had proposed changes t' which, without ussiikg, the word offeasively, meant' revolution. He denied that there was any restraint put upon political 'freedom in Ireland, and contended that what was being agitated for was not political liberty :but a .thantre in the system of government which the majority, if,they believed it would be preju- dicial to the .00ot:try:le interests, were justified in oppoe- ing. The contingency of local and separate legislatures for England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales was one the Gladstonians had not ventured to face; but it was one which ought to he lacethbefore taking the first step in a process likely to lead to 4asch a result. The people of Ulster, he declared., would rnover assist in carrying out Home Rule, and any attempt to coerce them would re- salt in fanning the dames of civil war. He asked whether this Ulster question had received even decent considera- tion at the hands of tbe Gladstonians, and concluded by urgibg the people to aet in this matter of Ireland as if they were jurors empanelled to try a question of life and death.

The mail steamer ?gra arrived at Plymouth on Satur- day frem the West Indies. and handed 18 of the .crew of the Arden Caple, GI I ow. and 11 survivors of the crew of the Earl Wenty Glasgow, which collided at sea. t The Arden Caple was mid out, and the Earl Wemyss bound kern San Francisco ,to Queenstown. Early on the morning of the Bth Septerriberein fine, cleacxeather, the Arden Caple struck the Earl ,Wemyss onghe star- board side, between the main and mizen rigging, cut- ting her .down to the water's edge. The Earl Wemyss sank in three minutes, twelve of the crow, with the captain's wife and three children, goinir down in her. The remainder were rescued by the Arden Caple, which had her bows smashed in, and was making a quantity of water. Fortunately the weather held fine. and the combined efforts of the crew succeeded in keep- ing her afloat. On the following day, the Norwegian vessel Creedmoor. bound to INew York hove in sight. andi bore down on the distressed vessel. The captain, howevec. refused to take elf the crew until the captain of the Arden Caple had given him per- mission. The captain and first mate of the Arden Caple refused to leave the vessel, and were left on board. having a good boat swinging on the vessel's quarter in case of emergency. Nothing more has been seen of the captain and mate, and it is learcd that they are lost. Toe Creedmoor, being short of provisions, ran into Bar- badoes, and transferred the crows rescued to the Fern.

FURTHER NOTES AND QUERIES ON SOME OBJECTIONS TO HOME RULE.

lll.—The third objection with which we shall deal, is that whereinit is maintained that the Irish are not fit for self-government, to which it might be replied in the first place that if this be the case, if they are not capable of choosing the right men, or if there are no men fit to be chosen to sit in a Parliament at Dublin, it was hardly reasonable to extend their voting power in 1884, thereby affirming and confirming their right to be represented and capacity to select suitable men tfor the Parliament at Westminster. Without, however, dwelling upon the dilemma in which, at the outset, our opponents thus find themselves placed, let us 'try to go a little deeper into the matter. In doing so, we shall be under the necessity of verifying our arguments by quotations, for the unusual length of which, we need scarcelvApologise either to reader or editor. Forming as these do, a most essential part of Irish history, they have a bearing of vital importance, not only upon the objection we are about to consider, but upon the national aspirations of the people : in short, upon the whole question. The Irish, as a rule, are ignorant and idle, and partly on this account, partly because of the large barren tracts in the country, to some extent also, it is true, owing to the unjust exaction of landlords), are poor, so poor as to live in hovels and cabins, a life that, to the aver- ageEnglishpeasant, wouldise one of abject and unendur- able misery. The original contrast between him and his Irish neighbour, is shewn by the satisfaction which the latter, to a certain extent, appears to feel in his wretched and squalid existence. Yet, he does not seem to be altogether contented with his lot, either. He does at times, display a wild 'disordered state of mind in which he is not very tractable nor easily to be kept quiet: Still as aturbulent ruffian or rebel,we must by no means give in to him, butowith a firm hand, keep him in subjection. Such it will betallowed, is a fairly accurate statement of the considerations which lead to the Irish- man being pronounced unfit foranything but strong cen- tralised non-representative Government,and which have procured for him the epithets, "rebel," " hottentot " etc. He is looked upon asadically depraved, his depravity directly shewing itself in his habit of living on a mud floor, with pigs and poultry sharing the cbmmon family lodging. It is perfectly true that Pat lives in this style, but that he would prefer it to a comfortable English homestead we decline to bileve. He values his one room dwelling with its damp mud floor, very much; we fancy, as the Esquimaux value blubber fat or tallow candle,— they both keep: out the &Ad. Where they are the only means of keeping out the cold it is not surprising that there should be a certain Amount of store set by them. Nature, after all, adapts 'man, like other animals' to his environment, and Pat becomes, in time, accustomed to a , state of dirt and discomfort. Had there not been some such sort of adaptation his life would, long since, have become utterly insupportable. His frequent cheerfulness under such circumstances remains not because, but in spite of them; and the very considerable humour that is still to be met with in Ireland, after all the fearful tribu- lation through which the country has passed, we hold to i be certain proof of the innate and unquenchable buoy- ancy and natural kindliness of the race. For warm- heartedness and good `humour do yet survive in the country :—which seemingly it were a pity to drive out or attempt to eradicate and replace by sourness and despair. But Pat is poor, no-body. Tory or Bad, having had eyes to read, ears be hear, and a mind to listen, will dis- pute that. Pat and poverty: the words are almost synonymous! But we are not all equally agreed as to the causes of that poverty. The question we would put is this :—Has Ireland had atchance of becoming rich? Mr. Lecky shall answer it. 'He says:— In the early Stuart reigns, comparative repose and good government 'were followed ,by a sudden rush of prosperity. The land was chiefly pasture, for which it was admirably adapted; the export of livacattle to England was carried on upon a large scale, and It became a chief source of Irish wealth. The English landowners, however, took the alarm. They complained that Irish rivalry in the cattle market was reducing English rents; and accordingly, by an Act which was first passed in 1663. andwas made perpetual in 1666, the importation of cattle into England was forbidden. The effect of a measure of this kind, levelled at the principal article of the commerce of the nation, was necessarily most disastrous. . . . . . . In 1696 it was enacted that no goods of any sort could be imported directly from the Colonies to Ireland. It will be remembered that at this time, the chief British colonies were those of America, and that Ireland, by her geographical position, was naturally of all countries Most fitted for the American trade. As far, then, as the colonial trade was concerned. Ireland at this time gained nothing whatever by her connection with England. To other coun- tries, however, her ports were still open, and in time of peace, a foreign commerce was unrestricted. When forbidden to -export their cattle to England, the Irish turned their land chiefly into sheep walks, and proceeded energetically to 'manufacture the wool. Some taint traces of this manufacture may be detected from an early period, and Lord Strafford, •when governing Ireland, had mentioned it with a character- fistic comment. Speaking of the Irish, he says "There was 'little or no manufactures amongst them, but some small beginnings towards a "cloth trade, which 'I had and so should still discourage all I could,' unless otherwise directed by His majesty and their Lordships. It Might be feared that they wonld best us out of the trade itself, by underselling us, which' they were able to do." With the 'exception, however, of an abortive effort by this governor she Irish wool mannfacture was du no degree impeded and was' indeed mentioned with special favour in many acts of Parliament. And it was in a great degree on the faith of this 'long-continued legislatins sanction that it was so greatly expanded. The poverty of Ireland, the low state of civiliza- tion,af a large proportion of its inhabitants, the effects of the civil Aram which had so recently convulsed it, and the exclu- sion of Its products from the English Colonies, were doubtless greet obstacles to manufacturing enterprise; but on the other hand'lrishiwool was very goocylving was cheaper, taxes were nghtertban in England, a spirit of real industrial energy began .to pervade the country, and a considerable number of English manufacturers came ever to colonize it. There appeared for a time, every probability that the Irish would become an industrial nation, and, had manufactures arisen, their whole social, political and economical condition would have been changed. But English jealousy again interposed. By an act of crushing and unprecedented severity, which was introduced in 1698 and carried in 1699. the export of the Irish woollen manufactures not only to England, but also to all other Countries, was absolutely forbidden. The effects of this measure were terrible, almost beyond conception. he main industry of the country wa3, at a blow completely and irretrievably annihilated. A vast population was thrown into a condition of utter destitution. Several thousands of manufacturers left the country and carried their skill and enterprise to Germany, France, and Spain. The Western and Southern districts of Ireland are said to have been nearly depopulated. Emigration to America began on a large scale, and the blow was so severe that long after a kind of chronic famine prevailed." It is, if Mr. Leeky is to be believed, a mistake to think that Irish poverty is, to any considerable extent, due to exceptional ignorance of the people. He says "The Irish people have always' even in the darkest period of the penal laws, been greedy for knowledge, and few races chew more quickness In acquiring it. The admirable system of national education, established in the present century. is beginning to bear abundant fruit, and, among the younger 'generation at least, the level of knowledge is quite as high as bc England." This opinion will be endorsed by those who have had opportunities of oblerring the manner and intelligence of the Irish peasantry. On the average—excepting, perhaps, the old, who generally have the appearance of being worn out and withered by the" hard times " that "come again too oft "—it is certainly not less than that of the same class in England. Nevertheless, there would not have been reason for much suprise if they had been intellectually inferior to the English. For if they are not so, or if there is little difference between the mental development of the two peoples, that has not been the result of any lack of any endeavour on the part of bigotted Protestant governors to reduce the Catholic Irishry to a state of brutal and depraved ignorance. In proof of which assertion' and as further examples of the fearful extent to which Irish Catholics have been handicapped, and Irish industries ruined. We give the following extracts from Mr. Lecky's account of the Penal laws. We should bear in mind that this famous code of the 18th followed closely, without giving the ufortunate Irishmen, so to speak, a moments breathing time, upon the legislation of the latter part of the 17th century * the effect of which, has been indicated in the last quotation but one.
* The system was, indeed, commenced in the reign of William 111., but many years elapsed before it reached the stage of full development finally attained.

Mr. Lecky writes. By this code, the Roman Catholics were absolutely excluded Irons the Pathanlent, from the magistracy, from the corpora- tions, from the bench and from the bar. They could not vote at Parliamentory elections, or at vestries; they could not act as constables, or sheriffs, or jurymen, or serve in the army or navy, or become solicitors, or even hold the position of game. keeper or watchman. Schools were established to bring up their children as Protestants ; and if they refused to avail themselves of these, they were deliberately assigned to hopeless ignorance, being excluded from the university and debarred, under crush- ing penalties, from acting as schoolmastars, as ushers, or as private tutors, or from sending their children abroad to obtain the instruction they were refused at home. They could not marry Protestants, and if such a marriage were celebrated it was annulled by law, and the priest who officiated might be hung.

An annuity of from twenty to forty pounds was provided as a bribe for every priest who would become a Protestant, to convert a Protestant to Catholicism was a capital offence. In every walk of life the Catholic was pursued by persecution or restriction. Except in the linen trade, he could not have more than twoapprentices. He could notpossess ahors.t. of the value of more than £5, and any Protestant, on giving him five pounds, could take his horse.

..... • . . ..... The Legislature, it is true, did not venture absolutely to fffppress their worship, but it existed only by a doubtful con- nivance, stignmtized as if it were a species of licensed prosti- tution, and subject to conditions which, if they had been enforced, would have rendered its continuance impossible. An old law which prohibited it, and another which enjoined attendance at the Anglican worship, remained unrepealed and might, at any time be revived : and the former was, in fact, enforced during the Scotch rebellion of 1715. The parish priests who alone were allowed to officiate, were compelled to be registered and were forbidden to keep curates or to officiate anywhere, except in their own parishes. The chapels might not have bells or steeples. The crosses might be publicly erected A graduated scale of rewards was offered for the discovery of Catholic bishops' priests and schoolmasters; and a resolution of the House of Commons pronounced 'the prosecuting and informing against Papists' an honourable service to the Government. Such were the principal articles of this famous code—a code which Burke truly described as "well digested and well dis- posed in all its parts ; a machine of wise and elaborate contri- vance, and as well fitted for the oppression, impoverishment and degradation of a people, and the debasement in them of human nature itself, as ever proceeded from the perverted ingenuity of man." Mr. Lecky describes the moral and economical effect, as "profoundly disastrous." But what of idleness ? Has that anything to do wi,h the Irishman's poverty! It must be admitted that it has: though, apathetic indifference and reck- lessness with regard to the future are expres- sions which apply to jlis case with greater accur- acy than idleness, if, bf the latter word, is implied an original and inveterate laziness and indolence. But again, there comes the question have their circumstances been such as to develop habit; of industry? Mr. Goldwin Smith has told us that "There seems no good reason for believing that the Irish Belts are averse to labor, provided they be placed,as people of all races require to be placed, for two or three generations, in circumstances favourable to industry." Previously,in the same .paragraph, he says : " I have myself sought and found in the study of Irish history the explanation of the paradox, that a people with so many gifts, so amiable, naturally so submissive to rulers, and everywhere but in their own country industrious, are in their own country bywords of idleness, lawlessness, disaffection and agrarian crime." He explains the paradox thus: But it is difficult to distinguish the faults of the Irish from their misfortunes. It has been well said of their past industrial character and history: "We were reckless. ignorant, improvi- dent, drunken and idle. We were idle, for we had nothing to do; we were reckless, for we had no hope; we were ignorant, for learning was denied us; we were improvident, for we had no future; we were drunken, for we sought to forget our misery." We have seen how Ireland's prospects of becoming an industrial commercial nation, were crushed by a relent- less, remorseless Government and heard of the fearful poverty which followed. The country was forced to remain dependent on agriculture ; in pursuing which, we would ask whether it has had a fair opportunity; not of growing as rich as England which was impossible, but of emerging from a state of extreme poverty which was not impossible? Have the tenants had any inducement to enddavour by industry, to emern from that condition. As touching this point, the follOwihg passages are of no small interest. They teach us that " rack-renting " is not a thing of to-day or yesterday, but that itis a system which has had its commencement and worked injuries upon the habits and lives of Irishmen centuries ago. We may derive from them some idea of the enormous evil of which this system, greatest amongst the disastrous agencies that have cursed Ireland, has been the cause. In his "New Views on Ireland," published in 1880, Sir Charles Russell writes upon the subject of the original land confiscations in Ireland as follows :—" It is enough to say that" (before the reign of Elizabeth) "The Superior lord or head of the clan or tribe, filled a repre- sentative character. He was, in a sense, trustee for his clan, and, though his powers were, great, the tribesmen or clansmen were looked upon as having special rights laths land." From Elizabeth's reign, Acts were passed by which surrenders to the Crown from the heads or chiefs of the clans were brought about, such chiefs taking re-grants from the Crown, but commonly without provision for the protection of the sub-rights of the cultivators, who were the clansmen or tribesmen." Inthisway, the cupidity of the chief was gratified at the cost of the members of the clan whose rights were thus sacrificed. These re-grants made, it was easy in troublous times to get up accusations against grantees, and the work of procuring confiscations was a business of profit. Here the English undertakers soon learned to turn their power to account. Sir William Herbert, writing from Kerry to Burghley (or Burleigh) in 1588 safg Our pretext in the enterprise of plantation was to estab- lish in these parts piety, justice, inhabitation, and civility, with eomfort and good example to the parts adjacent. Our drift now is being here possessed of land, to extort and make the state of things turbulent, and to live by prey and by •Pain another place, in the same year, he speaks of the undertakers as men who measure their conscience with their commodity. They searched into the titles of men's lands for the purpose of confiscation. They had pro- bably bribed heavily to get re-grants to themselves, and they felt justified in making the most of their bargains. Therights of the cultivators of the soil were disregarded, and when the people, feeling the yoke, loudly uttered their complaints of insecurity and of uncertain exac- tions; failing redress they broke into outrage and lawlessness. Sir Edward Denny, writing from Kerry in 1589, says The inhabitants of Irish birth and nation should not be left populous, wealthy or weaponed till they are ffret brought ton knowledge of God and obedience to the laws. As no person will ever bring the Irish to God or his Majesty, justice without mercy must first tame and command them. Are quotations of such events as these designated and disparaged as being past and done with? Unfortunately the results are not, by any means "past And done with." These events have a very real and practical effect upon the affairs of to-day. Or is our Conservative friend unable to conceive that this kind of tyranny can possibly have existed for 300 years under his glorious constitu- tion? We can only reply that it nevertheless has existed, and that this statement might, limit of time and space permitting, be abundantly verified. Time and space, however (of mortals and newspapers), are by no means unlimited, so we must be satisfied with simply stating—without, in any wise, setting up as an authority upon the Land question but as a fact which, in the main, cannot be refuted, and which those who have tried have failed to refute—that the usual and almost invariable order of things in Ireland has been this: The tenant first reclaims the land; he it is who clears the bog of stones, drains it, carrys manure and lime to it, and turns it from a mere waste into property of a certain value. Ile it is, and not the landlord, who puts up the fences, and in many, if not in most cases (in the south- west of Ireland, at any rate, and probably elsewhere) who builds the house. All the wealthy landlord has done, has been to assist ; perhaps at most, to bear one half the expense. The rent is fixed; but as the tenant reclaims more land, and improves his holding, is raised. That has been the regular proceeding up to quite recent times. Even in these latter days, the tenants as we all know, have been burdened with rents, the payment of which has been impossible, so that now the eviction of some 10,000 families has been started in Ireland, and seems, under this resolute government, in a fair way of being completed, unless for the salutary dread which even these mighty men occasionally show of popular feeling. But that is not the question before us: which is the effect of land- lordism upon industry The rents have, as above stated, been raised in proportion to the improvements of the tenant, who has left to him, aftcr payment, a margin of profit which, as a rule suffices only to keep him and his family alive. If he has been able to save something yearly, it is therefore—and now comes our point—to his interest not to avail himself of it for the purpose of increasing his operations and his industry, but to hoard it or to put it into the Savings Bank. You, in fact tell the Irishman not to use his talent but to bury it. You actually put a premium upon idleness and then blame or ridicule him for poverty, purely—or as you would argue incorrectly, but still, increasing the absurdity—chiefly caused by it. It is, as Mill well said, "a bitter satire to impute the backwardness of Irish people in improving their condition to a pecular indol- ence and recklessness in the Celtic race. It is indeed, the most vulgar mode of escaping from the consideration of the effect of moral and social influences on the human mind to attribute the diversities of conduct and charac- ter to inherent natural differences. "What race" he exclaims, "would not be indolent and insouciant when things are so arranged that they derive no advantage from forethought or from exertion." So much for the causes of Irish poverty, and for that partial cause of it, viz., the indolence, the want of heart and energy in their work, displayed by Irishmen in their own country. IV. But, it is urged, you surely do not fleah to say that rebels are fit for self Government? The Irish, it is true, are in a sense rebels--against English administra- tion of English law. So were we, such " rebels " 250 years since, but we did not therefore consider ourselves unfit for government according to our own ideas. On the contrary, to secure the right to so govern ourselves was the object of the "great rebellion." The question resolves itself into-this: Is it right to resist oppression? Will anyone reply to that broad proposition with a broad negative. Will any stout-hearted Tory have the courage to deny that the first maxim of English liberty was formulated by Blackstone when he wrote "it is right to

resist oppression." What the lawyer laid down Brad- shaw, the regicide, affirmed when he accompanied dip decree for the execution of Charles Stuart by the famous aphorism "Never forget that rebellion to tyrants is obedience to God."

Substitute the protracted despotism or, as far as the Irish have been concerned, a practically irresponsible government for the short lived, and much less irritating and oppressive despotism by which a fickle and unreliable monarch threatened English liberty : Would rebellion have been any the less justifiable ? Rather, in which case would the evil and aggravation of which it is the result, have been the less tolerable. It is impossible to defend all the means and methods which have been adop thd in successive struggles in Ireland. The atrocities some- times perpretrated there, every honest man must abhor- and while approving of combination, where entreaty ha; failed, and while unable to condemn such degree of severity, as is required to prevent the weaker minded from breaking it down, and which is supplied by exclu- sive dealing.—we nevertheless consider that the extremes of boycotting are bosh impolitic and wrong. Upon the terrible crimes that have occurred during Irish disturbances we pass no needless comment. They are admirably and justly criticised in the following pain- graph from the pen of Mr. Goldwin Smith The atrocities perpetrated by the Whiteboy's, especially in the early period of agrarianism (for they afterwards grew some- what less inhuman) are such as to make the flesh creep. No language can be too strong in speaking of the horrors of such a state of society. But it would be unjust to confound these agrarian conspiracies with ordinary hrime, or to suppose that they imply a propensity to ordinary crime either on the part of those who e,ommit them or on the part of the people who connive at and favour their commission. In the districts where agrarian conspiracy and outrage we's most rife, the number of ordinary crimes was very small. In Munster in 1833, out of 973 crimes, 627 were White.. boy or agrarian, and even of the remainder, many, being crimes of violence, were probably committed from the same motive. In plain truth, the secret tribunals which ad- ministered the Whiteboy code, were to the people, the organs of a wild law of social morality by which, on the whole, the interest of the peasant was protected. They were not regular tribunals; neither were the secret tribunals of Germany in the middle ages, the existence of which and the submission of the people to their jurisdiction, implied the presence of much violence, but not of much depravity, considering the wildness of the times. The Whiteboys found in their favour already existing a general and settled hatred of the law among the great body of the peasantry. We have seen how much the law, and the ministers of the law, had done to deserve the peasant's love. We have seen, too, in what successive guises property had presented itself to his mind, first as open. rapine; then as robbery carried on through the roguish technicalities of an alien code; finally as legalized and systematic oppression. Was it possible that he should have formed so affectionate a reverence either for law or property as would be proof against the pressure of starvation. A people cannot be expected toslove and reverence oppression because it is consigned to the statute-book and called law." These writings of Mr. Lecky and Mr. Goldwin Smith, two of the ablest members of the Uniqnist party, are worth pondering over, and surely deserve the attention of their party. Especially are they to be commended to those who, ascribing the poverty and. degraded life (the • material not the moral portion of their existence, though many people would include the latter as well) led by Irishmen, to inherent failings or vices of the race, ho that their debased condition is a result of a nature, depravity, rendering it impossible to treat them other- wise than as savages. Some could not fail to be struck with the =wisdom of thus confusing fact with cause, of continuing to deal with the Irish in the old style ; and with the impolicy (to put it on the lowest grounds) of treating them as unreasonable incorrigibles, and of intensifying by such treatment the feelings of bitter anime4ity for which there has already been only too severe provocation. Finding that these remarks are extending themselves to unexpected lengths we are once more obliged to deier for another week or so their completion.

150 PERSONS KILLED AND EATEN, REVOLTING BARBARITIES IN AFRICA. \ A despatch received in Liverpool on Monday by the West African mailTives particulars of a shocking native outbreak at Okrika, an island on the Bonny river, which resulted in the most horrible butcheries, about the 18th September. The occasion was a feud arose between the Okrikans and the Ogonis, a portion of the latter joining with the former after a tribal quarrel. Under the pre- text of an invitation to a friendly palaver, the Ogonis, accompanied by 80 of their chiefs, were treacherousty lured into a trap, captured, and taken to Okrika, where they were barbarously butchered and eaten, including women and children. The Okrikans compelled their chil- dren to drink the blood of their victims out of calabashes. Mangled remains and remnants of human beings were strewn in all directions, and others, mutulated, were observed floating down the Bonny river. Afterwards a raid was made upon the virtually undefended villages whence they came. The number of killed and eaten reports put at the lowest at 150. By the exertions of Consul Hewett, 10 of the survivors, in a deplorable state, were surrendered to the British authorities. In the end a tine of 100 puncheons of palm oil was imporxl upon the Okrikans. The Rev. C. E. Carew, who is in charge of the mission established by the Church Mis- sionary Society, used his utmost endeavours tos avert this holocaust.

div.head: CHANNEL FLEET AT LIVERPOOL
div.p: THE CHANNEL FLEET AT LIVERPOOL

On Saturday the Channel Fleet arrived in the Mersey. The vessels are five in number—viz., the Northumberland, Agincourt, Iron Duke, Monarch, and Curlew, the latter being a despatch vessel. The vessels took up an anchor- age in the centre of the river, for the most part exactly abreast of the landing stage. Admiral Baird is in com- mand of the Fleet, and it is the intention to remain at Liverpool until to-morrow, the vessels being open tor inspection during the 'reater part of each day. The Admiral and his officers have been enter- tained to a ball in the Town Ball by the Mayor, and a dinner VMS given to the sailors in St. George's Ball, for which latter purpose a subscription list was opened. The steamers on Saturday afternoon were wel- comed by immense crowds of people, who lined the dock walls and stores on both sides of the river. All the ves- sels have visited Liverpool before. 601110 of them during the recent naval manceuvres. On Sunday morning, a river boat on emerging from. Queen's Dock, Liverpool, for a trip on the Mersey to the. Channel Squadron, was overtaken by a squall, which caused the sail to jih, and the boat capsized. Three of the persons in the boat were rescued by the men be- longing to the Customs steam launch, which at once put off; but the fourth maw was drowned. A coxswain belonging to the Monarch, one of the Channel Fleet, lying in the Mersey, attempted to jump on to a tender which was plying with passengers to the fleet on Mcnday afternoon. Ile fell into the river, and was (=Tied away by the tide and drowned. It is computed that on Wednesday not less than 12,000 persons visited the vesselsmf the Channel Fleet lying in the Mersey. •It was intended that the fleet should leave on Thursday morning, but owing to a dense fog it was unable to get out of the port.

SIR WILFRID LAWSOI7.—Sir Wilfred Lawson was the principal speaker at a meeting in Carlisle on Saturday evening. In 1886. he said, the question before the country was whether they would have a Union of hearts or handcuffs. North Cumberland had decided for hearts —they hadsaid, "Hearts are trumps," and returned Mr. Allison. (Cheers and laughter.) He urged the electors to exert themselves as missionaries of Liberal principles. The omens were good up and down the country. The Liberal Unionists, it wad true, with their usual pluck held on and said "Never say die !" They addressed meetings and said they were convinced the country was coming over to the policy of coercion; and they gave banquets—he never saw such fellows as the Liberal Unionists were for banquets—(laughter),—in fact, the motto of the party seemed to be, "Let us eat and drink, for to-morrow we die." (Much laughter.) Yes; one by-election was worth a dozen banquets. (Cheers.) —On Monday, a meeting of the constituents of Sir W. Lawson was held in the Jubilee Hall Workington. Sir Wilfred Lawson said Mr. Parnell, by instituting his system of Parliamentary agitation and carrying it on as he had done, had done more to put down outrage in Ireland than any man living at the present moment ; and now three Judges iwere trying him in London in con- nection with the " Times " newspaper, which Mr. Bright once said was the devil's advocate on earth. Well, they might find out something against him, for it would be a very curious man they could not find some- thing against. I —‘iE.I2IOIIS ACCIDENT TO CARDINAL NEWEAN.—A serious illness from which Cardinal Newman is suffering is the result of. an accident which occurred on Sunday. His Eminence was alone in his study, when he fell with his head against the wall. He was rendered insensible by the sudden shock, and the greatest alarm prevailed among the fathers at the Oratory. His Eminence showed slight signs of recovery during the night, but ois Wednesday he was not so well, and the last ntes of the Church were administered. Cardinal Newman passed Wednesday night quietly, and his general condition is reported to be somewhat better. THE Rev. 3. D. Tnomt,s, Congregationalies minister of Runcorn, delivered on Sunday last,' what some would call a sermonistic lecture on - observance, or rather the non-observance of the' Sabbath in that town. He thinks Runcorn i 0 deteriorating in its regard for Sunday, but bolo" the evidence he adduces we do not suppnee that it is any Norse than other places in this respect. The reverend gentleman is to be

mended for dealing with a difficult subject in * frank, common.-sense manner. But whilst 1/0 agree with some things that he says, we cannoS but think that he does not stfficiently the difficulties of the situation. Take the rein- ark that there is no profit in lying in bed of * Sunday morning. To the minister, la; and' commercial man whose hours are pl regular, and who are not at any rate upon to be at work at six in the morning, ther* is certainly no profit in lying in bed on Sunall but it is otherwise with the workman to whota the gunday rest is one of the luxuries of
Mr. THOMAS, WO suspect, has never known what is to start from sleep at 5.30 a.m. with the agreeable feeling that you must rise—a _

which instantly changes to one of dreamy sal- faction as, the still tired soul turns over foranotha nap at the recollection that it is Sunday. Sail a man can say with Sancho Panza—" Blessiflg. light on him who first invented sleep " ; and if be. does in consequence of indulgence miss hearill the morning sermon he may console himself wiT' the reflection of the poet who said:—

The hours that leave us the least cause to weeP Are those we've passed in childhood or—asleep' If it be true, as it ieaseerted, that the large irOg- factories of the Runcorn district are worked 131°re on Sunday than was formerly the case—and 111°r° than is necessary-Lthat is a trespass cal should be inquired into and stopped. It is evil which will have a tendency to grow; for
pressure of competition is such that wherd takes the leaa in turning a penny a score are r
ta follow. Workmen should see to this for own sakes; they ought in their own interests

be strong Sabbatarians in the sense that as little work as possible shall be done dila Sunday. 111, grind is hard enough on six days of the Wee... without having to take it up on the seventh. Wit° regard to the sale of papers on Sunday, it seemil us that religious bodies are reaping where haVe sown. A stall at the Sunday School wl goody-goody books and magazines were sold kit,- of the earliest recollections of the present writer. It is a recollection which we do not doubt is - mon to a great many people; and it appears tic° have been thought unobjectionable until nec• vendors bettered the instruction. It is for us to encourage the sale of Sunday papers; but man might do worse than purchase a "War ell or a "Sunday Chronicle." lie might go to otra shops that are licensed to ho open on Sunday; r drunk, for instance, and beat or murder his It is no use troubling about the motes in our 0)' until we have dealt with the beams. We qtlitsr agree with Mr. Thomas in urging that the ail should be "to make the Sabbath the liveliest 0" best day in the seven." But what are the - means to this end? We should be glad if some our readers will help us, by their contributions, t' an ans4r to the question.

The Volunteers of London have found a synil thiser and supporter in Alderman Wnirmr the Lord-Mayor-Elect. He has made a proj that "a fund should be raised to assist the of the Metropolitan Volunteers ;" and the pi has been accepted on behalf of the Government ; 4 "taking, the lead in a movement of na importance." We have not a word to say Mr. Alderman WHITEHEAD ; it is very good him, seeing the need of something being dong, show his willingness to do something. But - must protest against the Volunteers being put a level with crippled colliers or wrecked mario; in having a Mansion House Fund opened on the behalf. They are not the creatures of a day,- their needs are not of a day. Their work essentially national work, and if, as is now 00°141 ally admitted, they require pecuniary aid that 611, should be provided out of the national exchW; It is paltry, it is mean, for a Government is spending over thirty millions a year on 7;f, .4.rmy and Navy to begrudge a few hundredsv. thousands on behalf of the Volunteers. Lord •'; enuacum. has shown that there is the lopse, b' shameful waste and extravagance in the manag • oa, ment of the military departments,; and no doubts who has given an hour's study to question that, with the exercise of average and economy as much might be saved everY as would give the Volunteers all the they require. It will be observed that proposal, so far, is to assist !Jondon Volur only, the presumption being that the manta subscribing will spread through the But there is no likelihood of anything of the happening. The fact is the moneyed men have hitherto taken an interest in the Volun' force, and lightened their purses to make the shortcomings of the Government, are got, tired of a thankless and unprofitable occuPal There is more and more difficulty of officers from this class; and there is a real of both officers and men becoming so

with their position as to be tempted to retire from the service. To ask them to raise a special fund When funds are already low will be to add fuel to the fire of their discontent; and it is no use aPpealing to the general public, for they feel that, hi one way or another, they are already suffici- ently taxed. It is to be hoped that the Volun- teers themselves will enter a strong protest against kly begging on their behalf. They are entitled to Something better than that. The Volunteer Force a force to be proud of; there is no other coun- trY in the world which can boast of such a Powerful auxiliary. They have done and are doing their duty; let the 'War Office do its duty, and we shall hear no more of this miserable 'cadging for which should Come out of the National Purse.

The Liberal Unionists continue to stick to their wwn particular beverage, but, as yet they gat "no .." They forget nothing, it is true, but Wafortunately they learn nothing. Lord ATINOTON was at it, at Huddersfield, on Mon- 4y, and it was the same old game--stolid resist- kee to a revoltition which, it is said, will "cause a daruption." We wonder if it never occurrs to the Liberal Unionists how they are driven to ring the lbanges upon phrases which were once deemed the Particular mark of the Tory mind. Has there ever been a reform worth fighting for of which the Voyles have not said that it was a revolution, and Would cause a disruption? The nation has been " ruined" on account of reform a score of times since the first Reform Bill; but it is still in exist- e, and still stronger, and it will be stronger than ever when the reform has been effected which now call Home Rule. Mr. CHAMBEE.LAIN wrote said repeated his parrot-cry that Mr. GLADSTONE Should "show his hand." We do not suppose the Member for West Birmingham is in any real doubt; but, if he is, it may be as well to remind biro that Mr. GLADSTONE Will be in Birmingham neat week. He may then have an opportunity of Peeping over the shoulder of the Grand Old Man, and, if ho does, we venture to say that Mr. ClRANumment will see BB =My trump cards as Will bb likely to Make him ill. Mr.• Gomm= is, of course, in the Ring of Resistance. He always distrusted the people; but still it does seem odd that he, as Skeleton of the Feast, should, with his pirtner Rip Van Winkle, have taken aosepn, with the coat of many colours, into their deadly-lively Company. Mr. GOSCHEN was hammering away at Aberdeen on Tuesday night, and he went thump, thump, thump, to the tune of the phrase—" They must stand by the Consti- tution." "Stand 1" of course. Are we not all Willing to "stand?" As "Punch" suggested last Week, it is the question of the hour—" What are YOU going to stand ?" Some stand beer, some Whisky, some rum. GOSCHEN stands by the Con- stitution, and it is a rum stand altogether. But the Liberal Unionists ought to change their tipple; to borrow a Shakespearean phrase, it has become "stale, flat and unprofitable ;" and when that has been said, what more can be said?

THE Municipal Elections throughout the country, °T). Thursday, resulted in leaving parties pretty ranch as they were before the contests commenced; and Warringtonis a fair type of the rest in this .teellect. There have been contests in four wards "it of the five; there was a stern if , not an exei; • struggle; and the seats have been 80cured, for the most part, 1,1 the men who were exPected to win. Muth-West Ward is one of atnall beer so far as .the total number of voters is .aceined ; but, as it includes a large proportion of the " gigocracy," it is well organized and exclusive. It dealt with Mr. JONES as an °abider, and he was therefore beaten, but not badly beaten. M;. E. GREENALL, jun., was run Pretty close, and he has deservedly lost influence With many of his supporters by playing fast and loose with the constituency. The large number ,of tntes he received may be taken as a warning to those who a pooh-pooh " the complaints as to the ntlisance caused by the Intercepting Depots. In liorth East Ward, Mr. JOSEPH GARNER, who has been first favourite since he was adopted as one of the Liberal candidates, headed the poll, Mr. 4taililNs, who had the seat thrown at him through chrision amongst the Liberal candidates, coming 44coricl. " TOUCH AND GO." It has "come off." It was predicted, on Monday night, that the Liberals of North-west ward would have'a high tide which would cover the Pier-point, and enable them to go in on the Flood. And it was so.

"The "World" says :—"The Manchester Ship Canal Company have just appointed a chaplain for the navvies on thoit work and plant; the post has been accepted by Mr. Robert Grimston the third son of Lord Verulant, who has lately taken orders."

"What is this in the,papers about Mark Masonry in Cheshire ?" said the Warrington Mrs. Par- tington. "rye heard of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; but never before of Mark Masonry. Wonder who he is, and what he's doing in Cheshire.° (Left sitting and pondering.)

The Corporation of St. Helens are about to take steps for increasing the number of wards and the number of town councillors. This is a good Big" ; the town is moving. St. Helens is like a thriving boy, who requires a new suit, not so much because he has outworn his clothes as because he has out- grown them.

Yesterday Patrick Lane was examined at Bow- at. Police Court, London, as to an attempt to shoot him by a man who is a witness in the Parnell inquiry. Asked if he made "a judicious bob," when the revolver was presented at him, he replied: "Faith I did. It's better to be a coward five minutes than to be dead all your lifetime." Query: Was this a specimen of Irish wit, or was it an Irish blunder?

"The Story of the Great Struggle 3 or, the Home Rule Movement from 1885" is just pub- lished by Mr. John Heywood, Manchester, and may be liad for threepence. It is written by Mr. Andrew Reid, and is lively reading. As there are several good portraits and equally good cari- catures, the publication should command a large sale.

"Two correspondents of important English newspapers and a member of the British Embassy were placed under arrest at Baku recently, and prevented from witnessing the arrival of the Czar. When his Majesty and suite" had left the town they were liberated." Things are coming to a pretty pass in Russia; they are almost as bad as they are in Ireland.

At the last meeting of the Warrington Town Council,a sort of thanksgiving service is always held. I.is the day on which the aldermen arise as Chairman of Committees, and call each other blessed. Tuesday last was not an exception to the rule; it is important in these matters to observe the rule. Any departure from it might lead to "disruption of the empire," or, more serious still, a revolt amongst the aldermen.

Alderman Burgess scored one on Tuesday off Councillor Bolton's' complaint as to the particular individual who could not eat his dinner beLause of the smell from the Howie Intercepting Depot. Of course Councillor Boltdiu had been canvassing. He would probably have known nothing of either the voter or the smell, if it had not been for the canvass. But to go further back, it is Mr. Diggle who caused the canvass, and he has always been a deadly enemy of the nuisance. So, although he is beaten, Diggle has scored also.

It was just a little startling, on Wednesday,to take up a London pallor and see the head-line " Mr. Diggle's Reply." Naturally, the first thought was —Can it be that our friend William is setting the Thames as well as the Mersey on fire? Further observation showed that the particular Mr. Diggle referred to is the chairman of the London School Board. Ho, too, has a mission; the Diggles go to what is called "the basis" wherever they happen to be, and they always stir matters up.
Jiggle —Can

The reported Nihilistic attempt on the life of the Czar is denied; but denial in these matters is the order of the day in Russia. It is not, how- ever, denied that the Czar and Czarina have had a narrow escape from being killed on the railway. The train containing their Majesties, together with other members of the Imperial Family, ran off the lino on the Azoft Railway, but fortunately no one sustained any hurt. Their lot is like that of the policeman's,"when constabulary duty's to be done"; it is "not a happy one."

The Memoir of Principal TuHoch which M. Oliphant has just issued shows that the noted Scottish Churchman was keen of criticism. This is how he referred to two prominent politicians, in a letter to a friend ;—" I feel more and more a sort of moral loathing at men like Chamberlain on one side and Randolph Churchill on the other. If politics is to become the sort of game these men play I would rather be done with it altogether:: This must, be pleasant reading for the parents of the (still-born) Great National Party.

The Parnell Commission drags its slow length along, but it is not very damaging, as yet, to the Parnellites. Police-constable Irwin, a hostile witness admitted, under cross-examination, on Thursday, that "up to 1879 there had been peace in the land and comparative prosperity. Then came a period of elistress that threatened to recall the famine times. The people could not pay their rent. Falling, into arrears they were evicted, and close upon evictions followed outrages. The places where outrages were most common were those where the secret societies, always hostile to the Land League, had the strongest hold."

Last evening there was an unofficial meeting of the Warrington Town Council, to arrange Com- mittees with a view to their final appointment at the first formal meeting. With regard to the new members, it is proposed that Mr. Voisey should be placed on the Finance, and Sanitary Committees; Mr. Jenkins on the Cemetery,. and Markets; Mr. Flood upon the Fire, and Paving and Sewerage; and Mr. Garner upon Fire' and School Attendance Committees. If they would have a round peg in a round hole, Mr. Garner would be placed on the Markets Committee, as he has for half-a-century had to do with markets.

" But the most extraordinary proposal is that Clounaillor Bolton should have a seat on the Watch Ciommittee. He is a brewer, and knows how to serve himself and the publicans. The interests of the public are, of course, of no moment in the matter. Now, how would it be to set Warrington cats to watch WaiTington cream? Why not, whilst on the job, insist on Councillor Ashton (publican) and Councillor Taylor (pub- lican) having seats en the Committee, with Councillor Jenkins as legal adviser? There is nothing like going the whole hog—bristle % and all

Lord Sackville, as British Ambassador to the United States Government, has got himself into a mess by writing a private letter to a sham English- man in favour of re-electing President Cleveland. He has fallen into a trap laid for him by a Yankee reporter. It is, of course, an abominable thing, to publish a letter marked "private," but that does not do away with the fact that Lord Sackville was indiscreet in expressing an opinion. And indiscre- tion in an ambassador is worse than a crime. Party politicians in America are making a moun- tain of this molehill, and Lord Sackville is to be recalled.

The " Daily News "of yesterday, commenting on the reports of a debate of the Liverpool Diocesan Conference' says : "Liverpool appears to suffer frona a peculiar mani- festation of the disease known as CONNELLY'S tickets,' which are said to be sold in public-houses at a shilling each. According to the statement of the Rev. R. Cr. MAT- mew no fewer than twenty-four thousand of these tickets are disposed of weekly in that city. Thousands more are sold in Wigan and St. Helens. Certain of these tickets, he added, bring money prizes, while the holders of others are treated to twopennyworth of beer. How CONNOLLY'S ticke,ts 'contrive to escape the meshes of the criminal law is net explained. Canon TAYLOR did not hesitate to denounce ' bazaars, with their lotteries,' lucky bags, raffles, and drawings." Our London contemporary is in error as to how 'Connolly's tickets' are dealt with at St. Helens. As some of our _ readers will know, a number of people have, at various times, been heavily fined at St. Helens for selling them.

WESTON MISSION CHURCH.—The Rev. H. J. Hall has taken up his residence at Weston in the honed lately occupied by Mr. Claudet; and the rev, gentleman will pay special attention to that portion of the parish of Runcorn. POOR RATES FOR RUNCORN DisrmeT.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the Bench sanctioned the laying of the following poor rates.—Clifton, is. in the £1 to realize £2lO Bs. 6d.; and Stockham, 10d. in the £ to realize £35 10s. 11d. ST. Parrs Cnuneg Max-e.g.—Special services were conducted in this church on Sunday. In the morning the Rev. G. H. St. Patrick Garrett preached on the sub- ject of "Purity," and in the evening the Rev. J. Connell ' B.A. curate discoursed upon swearing. There were good attendances at each service. A WIDNES MAN'S DIVERSION AT ST. HELHNS.—Michael O'Connor, of Joseph-street, Widnes, went to St. Helens last Monday week, and created a diversion in Peasley Cross by throwing stones at Constable Littler, some of which struck and injured the officer. H 9 was summoned to appear at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Friday but as he did not answer to the summons he was fined £1 and 6s. 6d. costs. RATEPAYERS? MEETING AT FRODSHAX.—A meeting of the ratepayers of the District of the Frodsham and Ilelsby Drainage Boards had been, announced to take place in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Friday evening, for the purpose of receiving the accounts of the Board and for the appointment of an auditor, but only one gentleman (Mr. John Forster) put in an appearance, besides the Clerk and Surveyor, Mr. Charles E, Linaker. THE FATAL PARAFFIN LAMP iltgLosioN AT WIDNES.—Mr. W. T. Husband the deputy coroner, on Saturday held an inquest at Widnes Police Court on the body of Catherine Palle, 30 years of age a single woman who had resided at 41,Charlotte-st. About half-past one on the morning of the 13th Oct., the woman before retiring to rest turned down the wick of the paraffin lamp. The light was not extinguished as usual, and she attempted to blow it out. An explosion occurred, and her clothes being set on fire she was terribly burned about the upper part of the body, and succumbed to her injuries on Thursday the 25th ult. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned by the jury. PROPERTY SALE AT RuNeorisi.—On Tuesday evening at Wilsons Hotel, Mr. Luke Holmes, auctioneer offered five lots of property for sale. Only two were disposed of, the reserves not being reached in the ether instances. Two leasehold shops and residences in Church-street. occupied by Messrs. Savage and Broadhurst, and also three cottages at the rear, occupied by William Owen, Thomas Stanley, &c., were knocked down at £l,OOO. The lot was subject to an annual ground rent of £8 13s. 10d. The leasehold shop occupied by Messrs. Scales and Son in Church-street, which was subject to an annual ground rent of £2 19s. 4d., was sold for £7OO. Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., of Warrington, were the solictors in the matter. STABBED ON THE NOSE AT WIDNES.—LaWreIIa Mulroy, a labourer, was brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Monday, to answer a charge of having wounded Thomas McCann, with intent to do him some grievous bodily harm.—The men, it appeared, lodge at 4, Victoria-street, and occupy the same bedroom. About ten' o'clock on Sunday. night McCann went upstairs and he alleged that, without the slightest provocation, the prisoner stabbed him in the nose with a knife.—Dr. O'Keeffe said McCann was suffering from a dangerous punctured wound on the nose and he could not tell how it would turn out.—The prisoner stated that McCann struck the first blow, and he retorted by striking him on the face with his fist. He denied having used a knife.— The prisoner was remanded for a week. THE RENOWNED RUNCORN RELISH Is prepare' from the choicest herbs, roots, and spices, which rensler it of most valuable assistance In the digestion of food.--Prepared and sold wholesale by Isaac Stubbs. Lowlands-road. Runcorn.— Advt. ST. LUNE'S CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—In connection with this place of worship harvest thanks- giving services were conducted on Sunday last, and the sacred edifice was beautifully decorated for the occasion. In the afternoon the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. E. • Hall (Methodist Free Church), and in the evening by Mr. R. Peacock (Primitive Methodist). Collections were made in aid of the funds. During the week special religious services have been carried on in the chapel, and have proved highly successful. Thp building was crowded on Monday evening when Mr. Hill, of Bridge- street, directed the proceedings. On Tuesday evening Mr. Smith, the evangelist, who has been appointed by the Congregational County Union to labour amongst the navvies, conducted the service. Wednesday evening Mr. Hayes, and Thursday evening the Rev. .1.1 D. Thomas. The Congregational Hall in Mason-street has been converted into a resort for the navvies, and will be opened on Saturday evening. Tea and coffee will be provided at very cheap rates, and the navvies will have - the opportunity of reading newspapers and periodicals. This is an attempt to keep the men from the snares of the public-house. VOLUNTEER PARADE AT RUNCORN.—The Runcorn Volunteers on Sunday morning attended divine service at Holy Trinity Church. The men paraded at the Drill Hall and then marched to the church under the command of Captain Timmins. The Rev. W. Preston, the recently appointed chaplain to the companies, appeared in his regimentals and occupied a position in the procession Afterwards the chaplain preached an appropriate sermon . from Phillipians 14. Addressing the Volunteers he said he wished to be their chaplain in reality, not in name or as a kind of ornamental appendage. He trusted they would whilst he served with them, regard him as a friend,ready to be of service at all times in sspiritualmatters, and when religious ministration might be needed. He was proud to be once again connected with a force so patriotic and noble. His former zeal, love, and admiration since he was sworn in as a Volunteer had never departed, although he was not actively engaged. Now he was again in harness and rejoiced at it. He wished them to be soldiers of the best and noblest I type, steady in duty, bold in danger, fearless before the foe. At the conclusion of the service, the Volunteers returned to the Drill Hall, where they were dismissed. The Volunteer Brass Band took part in the procession A BATCH 6v YOUNG THIEVES AT nIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court,on Mcinday,Martha Lewis, (11) and Thomas Lewis, (9) of 25 Sankey-st., were charged with stealing coal belongingto the London and North Western Rail- way Company.—P.C. Murray caught the children taking the coal from the canal bank, near the crane. They had told him that their mothers had sent them to 'pick coal."—The mother denied this allegation, and Mr. Gaskell remarked that it this allegation could be proved, the women ought to be prosecuted. Each prisoner was fined ss.—Fanny Moss, (13) Of Water-st., was charged with stealing a number of pinafores belonging to Patrick Firanity, of Crossley-st., Warrington,who occupies a stall in the Widnes market. While Mrs. Finnity was drink- ing a gill of ale which the prisoner had fetched her, P.C. Worsfeld saw the piisoner steal the pinafores and place them under the breast of her frock.—The Bench discharged the prispner on her promising not to offend again.—Mary Godfrey, (15) of Dock-st., was convicted of having stolen from the Widnes market, on Saturday night, a cap worth is. belonging to Peter McKinley, of St. Helens, and a jacket and a scarf worth 25., the pro- perty of A. Walker, of Manchester.—The prisoner was ordered to pay 10s. or go to gaol for 14 days.—John Ford, (16) of Muspratt-st., was sentenced to 14. days hard labour for stealing three pocket knives from the shop of William Kershaw, of 22 Albert-road. ALLEGED ROI3I3ERY AT RUNCORN—At the Runcorn Police Court yesterday, Joseph Bradshaw, a boatman, was remanded on a charge of stealing a pair of trousers value 9s. 6d., belonging to William Wagstaff, a boatman inthe employ of Messrs. Verdin and CO. WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY.—The first rehearsal of the members of this society was held on Tuesday evening. The attendance was very satisfactory and a very pleasant and profitable evening was spent. Mr. J. Morrison conducted and Miss Cullen accompanied on the piano. • MOSS BANK WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—With the object of aiding the Trust Fund of this chapel a very interesting magic lantern entertainment entitled " The Jackdaw of Rheims," illustrated with continental scenery and comic sketches was given. Mr. C. .T. lon,of Lil;erpod, was the lecturer, and also performed the duties of operator.. There was a crowded audience. Mr. ' Francis J. Poole occupied the chair, and delivered a speech appropriate to the occasion. PROPOSED CHORAL SOCIETY AT RUNCORN.—FIORI an advertisement in another column it will be ga hered that an attempt is to be made td form a choral society ' for Rtincorn. Annceting of those interested is called for Tuesday evening, at tha -National Schools, Church. That there are in the town more than sufficient vocalists of ability to sustain such a society cannot be doubted, and with a little encouragement from the public, there would be no fears, if onceestablished,of its success. The society would be • entirely unsectarian and, it is rumored, would have at its head a gentleman of high musical attainment in the person of Mr. Wynne Humph- reys, solicitor. ALLEGED THEFT AT WESTON POINT. Before Major Haziehurst and Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, Margaret Gorman, hawker, who appeared with a delicate-looking child in her arms, was charged with stealing 21 yards of oilcloth, the property of Wm. Maddocks, of Weston Point. About three weeks ago Mrs. Maddocka purchased the oilcloth from the prisoner, and on Tuesday when the latter called again at the house, she complained that she did not like it. • The prisoner then pursuaded Mrs. Maddocks to pay 4s. foi another piece which she contended was a bargain. After the prisoner had left Mrs. Maddocks missed the first piece of cloth and she pursued and accused the prisoner of robbing her. The prisoner denied the charge and she was set at liberty. THEFTS I3Y A LODGER AT WIDNP.S.I--AliCe RiIIIMCE, of no fixed abode, was charged at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, with having stolen two sheets, valued at 25., the property of Joseph Mil's, 2, Oxford-st. rho evidence shqwed that the prisoner was lodging with the prosecu- tor, and on Saturday morning Mills missed the sheets from the bed where the prisoner had slept. Rimier was also Charged with havingstolen twoplates,valued at 2d.. the property of Patrick Duffy, 4,Suttons-lane. Mrs. Duffy stated that the prisoner had also lodged with them, and on Monday she had to turn her out in consequence of her drunkenness. About half an hour after the woman left the plates were missed. P.C. Messenger appre- hended-the prisoner at No. 6, Suttons-lane, and found the plates there.—Prisoner was sentto goal for amonth's hard labour in each case.

THE HALTON MEDICINE AGENT AND HIS CREDITORS.— At Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, before His Honor Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, William Garner, of Halton, medicine agent" wis summoned at the instance of Thomas Smith, of London, to show cause why an order for his committal should not be made. The balance due was £35 2.3. I.ld. Mr. Burton, solicitor, appeared for plaintiff and called John Stringer who spoke as to defen- dant's means stating he frequently drove about the town in a carriage. Mr. Wynne Humphreys, solicitor, who appeared for defendant submitted that his client was totally unable to pay the amount due. His business had gone down considerably of late, and at the present time the bailiffs were in possession at his house for rent. The whole of his effects were secured by bill of sale. Defen- dant confirmed this statement. His Honor made an order of £2 a month, first payment to be made in a month. DAUGHTERS OF TE3ITEHAIiCE, RUNCORN.—On Monday evening the Runcorn Branch of the Order of the Daughters a Temperance held a Conversazione in the Regent-street Schoolroom. There was a good atten- dance. Mr. J. W. *Woodland presided, and in an admirable address, spoke of the good work the ladies were doing on behalf of temperance all through the country, and of the great influence they had on the rising generation. He hoped their influence would be used on the side of right. An excelleut programme was then gone tlgough consisting of songs, readings, Ike., Miss TempetieV &ding Siataottpallistt. Mr. T. J., Holt gave an excellent report on the progress the Daughters of Temperance were making both financially and numeri- cally, and pressed upon the laidies present who were not already associated with them to become so at once. A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the first part of the programme to a close, after which refreshments and fruit of various kinds, were handed round. The rest of the evening was spent in a sociable and enjoyable manner.

-THE INFIXENCE OF THE MOON AT WEvrox.—Yestert day at Runcorn Police Court before Mr. Jas. Handler and Dr. Steele, John Caskin, 12 years of age, was charge4l with hating an Monday la:st aiolen Ave caps from the, Wesleyan School, Weston. Inspector O'Donnell said the boy was irretrievable in his habits; and he was utterly beyond the control of his parents. He had been in court on several occasions and it was intended to send him to an industrial school, but he was physically unfit, and Superintendent Hollingworth desired him to be sent to a reformatory school.—The theft was p:oved by two boys named Thomas Hazlehurst and Albert Brown. The father said he did not think thebov was altogether right in his head. At every change of the moon he wandered away and slept away from home at nights. He had a step-mother, but there was no step between him and her, and he had a comfortable home. He promised that if the Bench would forgive the boy he would take better care of him:—The prisoner was discharged on, his father entering his own recognizanms‘ of LIO to bring the boy up for judgment when called upon. THE VICARAGE OF HALTON.—The Rev. J. Lockwood preached his farewell sermon to a large and sympathetic congregation on Sunday evening last. The rev, gentle- man thanked the congregation for the many kindnesses he had received at their hands, for their sympathy, brotherly and sisterly love, and kind forbearance. Those who had been unfriendly he forgave, and should try to forget for the sake of him who said "Bless them which persecute you, do good to those whc hate you and pray for them which despitefully use you Rnd persecute I you." To all, whether friends or fees," farewell, God bless you." If they never met again on•arth, might they all meet in Heaven. Mr. LoCkwood, who has endeared himself to the Hearts of numerous parishioners in Halton by his genial demeanour and self-sacrificing ' labours, was the recipient of a handsome testimonial to his personal worth in the shape of an illuminated address, and a purse of gold. The presentation took place at the residence of Mr. Joseph Stokes, of Rock savage, one of the churchwardens. The address, which was tormented by Mr. Wright, was signed on behalf of the parishioners, members, and friends, by Thomas Wright and Joseph Stokes churchwardens; John Rutter, John Ackerley, Joseph M. Baguley, William Nixon, and John H. Horton, sidesmen. The purse contained £67 7s. Eld., and was presented by Mr. Joseph Stokes. There was a good attendance of prominent 'Churchmen.

SETTING FIRE TO A WATCHMAN'S CABIN' AT WIDNES.-- On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Messrs. T.Sutton Timmis and H. Wade Deacon, four young men named Charles Beesley, of Foster-street, William Dufton, John Bedon, and John Bancroft, Chester-street, Widnes. were summoned by the Widnes Local Board for having set fire to a cabin in Deacon-road. 13ecidon did not appear. Bancroft and Dufton pleaded witty, and Beesley not guilty, Mr. T. T. Allen, clerk to file Local Board, said the Board had been laying some gas pipes in Deacon-road. adjoining Appleton quarry, and on the night of the Ist October there was a watchman in charge of the trench. About eleven* o'clock the watchman was sitting in 1114 cabin when one of the defendants Came to him and told him alt his lamp was out. He went to relight it. an the other three defendants came to the cabin. Tie Witl not got above twenty-five yards whc.n he heard a noise, And on looking round SAN that the Are- grate had been overturned into the cabin. He returned to. the cabin, to prevent it being burnt. The men ran away„ and Police-constable Almond, who then came on the scene, assisted him to put the flre out, after which the officer went and found tho defendants, who were

_ . liable to a fine not exceeding 4_:5 for what they had done. The three defendants Who appeared were fined 10s and 9s 6•1. costs, and had to Pay is. dainago, while Beddon was fined 153., with the same costs and damages as the others.

NORTIINVICII DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION AND E4nt. GRANVlLLE.—Yesterday Mr. E. H. Moss. Mr. T. Handley and Mr. G. 11. Deakin appeared before Earl Granville, and on behalf of the, Northwich Division Liberal Association presented that nobleman with the following addres,k;—" To the Right Hon. Earl Granville. The Northwich Division Liberal Association desires most cordially to concur in the expressions of confidence in your Lordship, as one of the, most consistent Liberal statesmen of the age, which are evoked by your visit to the Metropolis of the Nerth. During the Iwhole period of - parr public • life, your Lordship has been in full sympathy with the people and in all struggles for public rights, during the last 40 years your political foresight and your well earned powerful influence have very largely contributed to the successful issueof those struggles. More especially does this Asso- ciation desire to acknowledge the loyal assistance and support which your lordship is now giving to our rever- ed leader, the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, in his efforts to promote loyalty and attachment to the crown and constitution amongst our hitherto misgoverned fellow subjects in Ireland, and to express its earnest hope that you may be spared to see another triumph of the cause of justice and humanity in the grant of freedeni of local self government to this unhappy portion of the Kingdom Adopted at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Northwich Liberal Association, held on the 18th October, 1888. E. 11. Moss', President of the Association." The address, which is a most artistic production, is in the form of an albuct, the coverbeing of royal bluemorrocco, in gilt ,elegant. The letter press is printed in crimson and violet, set off with rich gilt, and is surrounded by an ornamental border of, pleasing design. The whole is a triumph of the bookbinder's and printer's art, and refiectsgreat credit upon Mr. G. Bellamy,of the:Examiner Office, Runcorn, whose production it is.

ALLEGED GRIEVOUS ASSAULT HY A WOMAN AT, WIDNES. —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Ellen Roach, a woman living at 13, Peel-st., was charged with haying caused grievous bodily harm to a woman named Catherine Lancaster. A labourer, named Hammond, of 11, Peel-st., said that on Wednesday night he was in Lancaster's house, and gave the prisoner some money to go and fetch some beer. After she had returned, and while Mrs. Lancaster was pouring the beer out, the women began quarrelling, and he saw the prisoner lift the can containing the beer to strike the prosecutrix with it. SERIOUS FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT- .—About noon, on Wednesday. a serious accident occurred in the Potato Delph Mine of the Sherdley Colliery, near St. Helens, belonging to the White Cross Colliery,Comoany, Limited. Four men, including a drawer, were at work in a place about half a mile from the shaft when the roof gave way, and thirty or forty tons of stone and dirt fell, carrying props and bars with it. John Butterworth, a married man living in Fletcher's-row, Parr, who was nearest to the face of the coal, was completely buried, and John Swift, of Bishop-st., had his legs and ribs injured. .A gang of a dozen men were at once got le the place and commenced to clear away the debris, but the difficulties were so great that large atones had to be brqicen before they could be moved. Thomas Brakeley who was slightly injured by the fall, was one of the gang, and a few hours later he was struck by a falling stone and so injured that he ' had to go out of the pit and seek medical aid. Drs. ' Twyford and Reid attended to the injured men. Another workman named George French had a narrow escape. The body of 13utteravorth was brought out of the Pit at eight o'clock at night. It was crushed in a fearful manner, a tone about a ton weight having been found upon it. The sad event cast a gloom upon the colliers, and many of the night men could not be induced to descend. Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's. which for strength is uneouslied.—.Advt. ANOTHER MUNIFICENT CHURCH GIFT AT ST. Ilimnss.—The members of the congregation and friends worshipping at St. 'Mark's Church, Cowley Hill, St. Helens. have been. gratified by an intima- tion from Mr. William Pitkington, fib., of Roby Hall, one of the trustees of the church, of his inten- tion of placing a new organ in the church at a cost of £BOO. Besides this,At is stated, he will defray the cost of panelling the front of the chancel, £3OO, and allow £5O per annum for the salary of an organist. St. Mark's Church, ,which has cost about £7,000, is a lasting memorial of the generosity of a few individuals. Colonel Gamble, 0.13., cave a site valued at £415, a clock and peal of bells £453, and £l,OOO towards the building fund. Mr. W. Pillcini4- ton contributed .£3OO, and the joint contributions of the same gentleman and his brother, Mr. Thomas Pilkington, to the repair fund, amounted to another £3OO, while the firm of Pilkington Bros., of which Mr. William is the head, gave 4'250 and his most recent gift is nearly £1,200. .Stlss Bishop gave £2OO, lessrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. £4OO, the Marquis of Salisbury .£lOO, Mr. J. C. Gamble, Mayor- elect of the borough, £lOO, and the Diocesan Church Building Society £350. For twenty years Colonel Gamble paid the stipend of a curate in the parish, and maintained schools, and on the church being consecrated, and the question arising how the vicar's stipend should be raised up to the time a grant could be obtained from the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, Colonel Gamble guaranteed to pay £2OO for two years. That time, having expired without the grant being made, the seven trustees—, Messrs. W. Pilkington,`Thomas Pilkington; Joseph Robinson, J. C. Gamble, W. Gamble, and G. J. Critchley—and the representatives of the late Rev. Candn Carr and Mr. H. S. Hall, have jointly under- taken the Payment of the money for a further period. The new , organ will supersede the harmonium which has been used, and will thus render the musical portion of the, services more attractive and devotional.
