div.head: PRESENTATION TO THE REV. S. B. HANDLEY
div.p: PRESENTATION TO THE REV. S. B. HANDLEY

AT STAFFORD. We take the following from the "Staffordshire Chronicle" of Saturday last, the rev, gentleman concerned being a .native of Runcorn :—The Rev. S. B. Handley, who for 23 years has been the minister of the Stafford Congregational Church, completed the fiftieth year of his age last Sunday. As a token of their affection and esteem for their pastor, the mem- bers of the church combined together to make him a birthday present of a purse containing the Jubilee number of 50 gt.ineas„ to correspond with the years of his age. The gift, whch had been kept entirely secret from Mr. Handley, vias delivered to him very late on Saturday night, accompanied by a letter signed by Messrs. W. F. Woolley, W. H. Peach, J. Williams, W. Woodall,'E. Edgar, and W. Peach as deacons and Com- mittee of Management on behalf of the church and congregation. The letter set forth that the church and congregation over which Mr. Handley had so long been pastor, desired to congratulate him heartily on having • reached his jubilee of years and , begged his acceptance of the gift, at once as a souvenir of the event and an expression of ' their personal love and regard. The idea entered many minds spontaneously and was taken up with spirit, and carried out in a warm-hearted manner, and in making the present, they thankfully recognized the value' dills faithful services amongst them, and prayed that the vigotv.ts heAlth of mine sand body with which he had ilitiVbrio been blessed, 'night be Tong Continued, Wad that he might long be spared to do still greater work for Him whom it was his delight to serve. The letter closed with thdir kindest regards to Mrs. Handley and daughters, and the expression of a fervent wish that Mr. Handley might have a happy birthday and many still more happy returns thereof.—On Thursday the annual conversa..ione of the church and congregation took place in the schoolroom. In the course of the proceedings Mr. Woolley, in the name of the church and congregation asked Mr. Handley to accept a handsome timepiece as a lasting memento of his birthday. The clock, which was of fine appearance, chimes the quarters and strikes the hours.—Mr. Handley, who was much affected, said that nothing which had been said or done by his people during the whole of his ministry had wrought 89 mightily upon his heart as their great and spontaneous ' genrosity on this occasion. Ile felt bound to them by ties more sacred and close than ever before, and he I should try to approve himself increasingly among them a worker of whom they need not be ashamed, and to I show himseff worthy of their confidence. Mrs. Handley ' and his family entered fully into his feelings of joy on I this oceasion

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting of the Board was held at at the Town Hall on Thursday, Mr. W. Fisher, presided. and there were present 3lessr3. Lake. Taylor, White, Pritchard. Wiswall, Lightburn, Wass, Smith, Mellor. Imison, Hankinson, Grice, Timmins, Speakman Dobson, Linaker (law clerk), Marshall (surveyor.)

div.head: WAVE OF SCARLET FEVER.
div.p: A WAVE OF SCARLET FEVER.

The Medical Officer of Health reported that the num- ber of deaths registered last month amounted to 35, three of which were inquest cases; and of the remaining 32 deaths 6 were due to mesenteric disease, 4 to bronchitis, 4to natural decay, and 2to diarrhcea. There was also one death from scarlet fever. The above 35 deaths show an average death rate for the year of 23.6 per 1,000 of the estimated population, and, exclusive of the three inquest cases, of 21.6. He regretted to observe that there was a death recorded from scarlet fever, and at present unfortunately there seemed to be a slight wave of this fever passing over the Authority's sanitary district. The indiscreet behaviour of some parents in allowing children to mix with infected children, during the most contagieus period, and also of parents of infected children, allowing their children to expose themselves on the streets, and to mix freely with other children, when the risks of communicating the disease is in its most active form. An incident of this descrip- tion came under his notice very recently. He had occasion to visit a ehild with scarlet fever, and on a subsequent visit, he found no less than six healthy children playing with this very child in a very close room. Reprehensible conduct Of this description was likely to be a fruitful source of propagating this disease, and parents did not seem to appreciate the gravity and responsibility when infected children were allowed to mix so freely with uninfected ones, a condition which was calculated to prolong indefinitely an epidemic of this description. There was also a case of fever of an indefinite character registered during last month.—The Surveyor stated that during the corresponding month ytst year there were 48 deaths. • THE snip CANAL COMPANY AND THE SEIvNES. _

The minutes of the Highway Committee contained the 'following :—Recommendation that instructions be given to the Law Clerk and the Surveyor to enter into communication with the Manchester Ship Canal Co. with a view to obtaining facilities for constructing a sewer or sewers under their canal, at such place or places as may be deemed advisable, and that subject to such facilities being obtained, that their application with reference to the proposed navigation improvements at the Sprinch be granted.—Recommendation that instructions be given to the Law Clerk to communicate with the Man- chester Ship Canal Co.', with a view to obtaining infor- mation as to how. they propose to deal with the sewer outfalls of the town.—Mr. Taylor moved, and Mr. Grice ;seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—The Law Clerk said at the request of the Chairman Of the Committee, the secretary, the surveyor, and himself visited Man- chester on the previous day and had an interview with Mr. Collier who showed by a plan exactly how the Ship Canal Company intended. to improve the Bridgewater Navigation at the Sprinch. He (the Law Clerk) informed Mr. Collier that his instructions from the Board were that at the same time as they arranged to give the Company consent to de the work; they should arrange the terms upon which the Board could take a sewer under the canal for the pur- pose of draining the district behind the works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company. Mr. Collier was indignant at this; and said his Board ef Directors were very much annoyed at the way, in which the Commis- sinners had treated the Company's application. The Law Clerk replied that the only information Mr. Collier could have got about the matter mtist have been from one of the two representatives of their own. This Mr. Collier denied and said he rould not recommend his board to mix up the two improvements at all. He would rather wait fora clause in the nest Act of Parliament; and he de- , clined to advise his Board of directors in the present stage, so consider the project of the sewers tinder the canal; When Mr. Collier took this line he (Mr. Linakcr) turned to Mr. Marshall and said "If the matter is to be dis- cussed in this manner, the sooner we terminate the inter- view the better." Mr. Collier intimated that he should want a direct reply to his letter to the Commis- sioners and then he would take the instructions of the directors. He was annoyed at the way in which the Commissioners had riceived the recommenda- tion. • He (Mr. Linaker) told him that his mind had been very much abused and that there was only one feeling shown by the Commissioners, and that was to assist the Company in their undertaking and to see whether, while assisting them, they could not make some arrangement with regard to the right of going under the canal.—The Secretary said Mr. Collier desired all communications to be in writing.—Mr. Lightburn: I think the less said about the matter in the present cir- cumstances the better.—Oß the suggestion of Mr. Speak- man the Committee were empowered to reply to Mr. Collier as they deemed advisable.—During discussion on the second recommendation the Chairman said he had it

from good authority that Mr. Walker was determined to push on at all hazards with the sewer work, and it was desirable that the Board should know as early as possible how the Ship Canal Company intended to deal with the sewers. (Hear, hear.)—Whe minutes were adopted.
FINANCE.

The report of the Finance Commiteee was adopted on the motion of Mr. Imison. It is stated that the receipts for the month amounted to £554 Bs. 6d. and the pay- ments to £293 16s. 10d. THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S SALARY.

The Health Committee recommended that the salary of the Medical Officer of health be increased by £25 per annum, the increase to date from Ist Nov.—Mr. Mellor moved and Mr. Lightburn seconded the adoption of the minute, the latter gentleman remarking that Dr. McDougall did a great deal of work.—Carried. There was no other business of public interest.

CURIOUS MATRIMONIAL AFFAIR AT WIDNES. On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Messrs. F. IL Gossage, T. Sutton Timmis, and Wade Deacon, a middle-aged man named John Tinkle; of 19, Wellington-st., appeared in response to a summons asking him to show cause why he should not contribute to the support of his wife. Mr. Rideal was for the complainant,and Mr. linowles for the defendant. Mr, linewles Mid that his client wished that I/16 Wiffo Would Come and live with him at 19, Wellingtou-st. Before the parties were married lit February last they both had furnished houses, and after the marriage they lived in the complaipant's house. She had, however, been continually tormenting him about the furniture being hers,and he onlybeing a lodger, that he had left her and gone to his own house. Mr. Knowles asked for an adjournment to see if the parties could not settle the case. Mr. Rideal said that on Saturday. the 13th October, the defendant took his clothes and left the house, 44, Wellington-st.owhere he was living with his wife, and went to live at 19, Wellington-st., with his step-daughter, and he had lived there ever since. He protested against an adjournment, as it was clear that the defendant had deserted his wife.—Mrs. Tinkler, who is advanced in years, gave evi- dence in support of this statement. Defendant gave her 16s. on the Saturday he left her. Be earned 30s. a week and overtime. He had said that he would never live with her again.—ln reply to Mr. Knowles she said that • she would go and live with the defendant anywhere except with the young woman (his step-daughter), with whom, she alleged, he had been guilty of immoral con- duct.—Sarah Ann Jones, 44, Davies-st., and Elizabeth Riordan, 1, Sankey-st., gave evidence, after which their Worships decided to adjourn the case for three weeks, to see what the woman would do, in view of the defen- dant's offer.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. By "Anna."
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. By "Anna."

That with regard to the proceedings in connec- tion with the laying of the corner stone of the Widnes Conservative Club, on Friday last, anything more dolefully dull for a political gathering it would not be easy to imagine. The crowd that occupied Victoria-road were very undemonstrative, and appa- rently had not energy to raise a hearty cheer, even when tho stone was "well and truly laid." That the upholders of the "great Unionist cause' were even more careful of their coin than of their cheers, and not even a "red cent." was placed upon the corner stone, in response to the appeal lot it.

That Mr. Parnell acted .the part of the candid friend. He acknowledged that inWidnes the Toriew were in a great minoritVand complained that the aristocratic Conservatives of the rural districts, repelled by the unaesthetic appearance of W idnes, did not cows forward to make up the deficiency in that generous fashion that might be expected. That doubtless the fact that 1,300 shares were yet unappropriated weighed upon the minds of the. party managers like a nightmare, and already before the bricks have risen much above the level of the ground, • The Club" is isiveu the title of " White Elephant."

That - Maier Cross seemed gifted with the unnaral power of prophecy when he dubbed the building "Liberal Club," Who knows I Perhaps when Ireland has gained legislative independence, and the Liberal axe iA being applied to the root of our iniquitous land laws, the Tories will be glad to dispose of the "White Elephant" to their political rivals for a "consideration."
'That the SpeMl f "our member 13 was rather ot a humdrum character, and did not evoke much enthusia2m.

That there were very many Home Rulers in the meeting, who frequently expressed their opinion by applause and otherwise. That some of the more sanguine Radicals are already predicting that Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss will fail to retain his seat when the next election comes. That there is much virtue in a "when."

That Widnesians should read' the speech of Mr. E. K. Mospratt to the science students and endeavour to provide' that. better education for which he so ably pleaded. That although theexamination system may havo its faults, yet the examinations and the prizes are an incentive to study, and many a youth thus induced to start on the high road to learning, will continue for the. love of the knowledge to be obtained.

That there are still strong hopes that Widnes wilt obtain its due representation on the Lancashire County Council by Rending two members. That in Runcorn, where there is no doubt in the matter, the great question under discussion is, who will be the representatives. That the Tories seem to have already decided for themselves that the election should be decided on political lines, and the Conservative Association is first in the field, and have adopted Mr. J. Brun- drit, J.P., and Major Razlelfurst, J.P., as their candidates.

That the Liberal Association have not as yet considered the question, and have yet an open mind in which to initiate a policy which shall be best for the interests of the town and of the county. That should they decide to take up the gage of battle thrown down by the Conservative party,therer can only be one issue to the contest—the return of two Liberals by large majorities. That under any circumstances Mr. P. Speak- man will come forward as an independent candidate. and,like Hal of the Wynd," fight for his own hand. That time will show.
That the Catholic bazaar has so far been a grand success, and all friends of religious freedom, of which our member Mr. Brunner is not the least, will rejoice.
-4-- ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER AT WIDNES.

• At the Widnes Police Court, on Thursday morn- ing. before Mr. F. 11. Gossage and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, a respectable-looking man named John Broom. of Appleton, was brought up in custody charged with causing the death of Thomas Maley, a foreman who was employed at the chemical works of Messrs. Mort, Liddell, and Co.—Mr. Glover, chemist a'; the works, stated that on the afternoon of the 29th ult., Maley came to him at the office, when he noticed that he was bleeding from the nose and right hand. Deceased made a complaint to him, in conse- quence of which he went into the works, and saw the prisoner. Witness asked him if he had strilck Maley, and he replied "Yes, I did strike him, but I had to do it in self-defence, as Maley had a hammer in his hand, and if I had not struck him he would have hit me with the hammer." Maley was the foreman of that part of the works and witness told Broome that ho should not have a person in authority, and he would be paid up and then leave the works. Broome refused to go, but witness pursuaded him to see Maley, who said that he, did not wish Broome to work under him any longer. Broome Wain admitted having struck Maley, and added that he had not yet finished. Deceased then said, "If he had not taken me unawares, he would not have done this to me." Broome then offered to fight Maley, but as the latter was an elderly man, and the prisoner was. much younger, witness told the • latter to go away and fight someone his own age. Broome then received his pay aid left the works, but he stated to witness that he was going to wait outside for deceased, but the latter left the place by another way.—Prisoner, who now denied having struck the deceased, was remanded for a. week on the application of Superintendent Johnson.

THB BIRTII AND DEATH RATB OP WARRINGTON. —For the week ending Saturday, October 27th, 1888. The mean temperature was 47-5 Fahren- heit, and therefore 2 deg. warmer than the pre- teding week. The maximum temnerature, 66 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 26th inst., and the minimum temperature, 26 Fahrenheit, on the 21st inst. The rainfall measured .14in. The general direction of the wind was South-west. During the week, which was the 43rd ,of the current year, 38 births and 22 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 25.8 per thousand, against 20-9 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 15.3 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from whooping cough, 6 from scarlet fever, 2 from diarthica, 3 from brain disease, 3 from lung disease; 23 eases of scarlet fever were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament. —JOHN 11. APPLETON:MC.3e teams met at Moss Bank, on Satur- day, and af er a splendid game, the home team came off, victorious, the score standing—Moss Bank, one try and three minors, to the Wanderers, four minors. RUNCORN RECREATION' V. SWINTON HORNETS.—The " Reca" paid a visit to Swinton on Saturday, when they met the Swinton Hornets, who had the best of the play throughout, but towards the close of the game the -visitors forced the pace. Pearson.on behalf of Swinton, landed a goal in the first half, and in the second Runcorn scored their two miaors. Result: Hornets, one goal, one try, and five minors; " Recs," two minors. RUNCORN PARISH OHLIE.CH V. WIDNBS POST OFFICE.— This match was played on the ground of the Church. The Post, Office started the ball; but, although the wind was against the Church, they, with a bit of good play, soon scored a try. The ball was again started by the Post Office, and after a bit of excellent play half time was called. When the Church kicked off after half time, Widnes had the best of the ' play, and soon scored a try; but failed at goal. The Church re-started the ball, and soon scored another try. but Ward failed at goal, the wind blowing very strong. Dunbavand scored both trios for the Church, and Flanagan for the Post Office. Sr. Paum's V. POOLSTOCE.—PIayed at Warrington in rough weather. Poolstock did not arrive till late, caus- ing the kick-off to be delayed till 4.20,the last half being played in the dark. Russell kicked off for St. Paul's, and the forwards dribbled to the line, forcing the visitors to save. On re-starting the kick was returned by Lawless, and a minor quickly followed. St. Paul's had hard lines, Poolstock not advancing par the Saints' quarter flag. On change of ends Poolstock pressed but did not score until through a misunderstanding by the Saints' forwards Poolstock scored a try. After the kick out the Saints had again hard lines, losing the ball near the line, Poolstock again scoring. Result:—St. Paul's 5 minors, Poolstock 2 tries. WIDNES V. CROMPTON.—A good game between these two teams was witnessed by a large number of specta- tors on Saturday, on the ground of the Widnes Football Club, Lower House-lane. Crompton managed to put in the field a full team, with the exception of Kershaw, who was the only man absent, but Widnes were again behind with their men, having to play without the services of three of their prominent men, Plumpton (captain), Bingham, and Barber. Nevertheless they succeeded in scoring well, and the final result of the contest would have presented a better appearance but for one or two tries, which were alleged to have been obtained, being disallowed. When half-time was called the score was— Crompton, one try and one minor to Widnes one minor. After the change of ends the homesters had the best of it, and Farrell altered matters for his company by gain- ing a try in a really brilliant manner. When the signal was given for the last time, the result was a draw—one try and two minors each. -- RUNCORN lt. NEW BRIGHTON (A Temes)—Played at Liscard on Saturday, the home team only mustering thirteen men. The visitors started, and soon showed their superiority, and had matters all their own way during the first half, Woods, Evans, Lunt, and Dutton scoring tries, Woods kicking a goal from each place. The score at half time stood four goals and three minors in favour of the visi ors. After the usual interval the home team restarted, and played up much better during this half, and some good passing was witnessed by both sides, Holt soon after getting over for the home team, Tomlinson failing at the place. After the kick-out some give and take play was witnessed. Neither side could claim much advantage, until just on the call of time Lunt secured, and made a grand run in close to touch. Woods, however, failed at the place. No side was now called with the score as follows :—Runcorn 4 goals, 1 try, and 7 minors New Brighton; 1 try. Teams : _s. Booth, back • E. Lunt, T. Woods. and W. H. Cawley, three-quarter backs; S. Abram* and W. Evans, half backs; J. Gatley, W. Shaw, H. Barker W. Rigby, J. J. ' Bowyer G. Lee, T. Whingates, R. Hlilwood, and J. Button forwards. Cansztree V. WESTMORELAND.—The representatives of these countirs met at Runcorn on Wednesday . The weather was all that could be desired, and a large attendance of spectators assembled to witness the contest. Westmor- land antieipated receiving the assistance of their scattered exponents in Lancashire and Yorkshire, but, with the exception of Allen, who is now showing brilli- ant form for St. Helens, the rest were unavailable. • Cheshire played their originally selected team, but the visitors had to some extent to rely on their reserves. A start was effected by the visitors kicking off, and a not very satisfactory return on the part of Luya, gave Westmorland immediately a decided advantage, and a minute later Cheshire conceded a minor. The home county then showed up to great _advantage Brazen- dale, Male, Hughes, and 'Wainwright exhibiting capital bits of play, and eventually. Muir, securing an opening, made the best of the opportunity, and gained a grand try, but Male failed to improve the point. Cheshire continued to have decidedly the best of matters, and Wainwright on two occasions made a couple of brilliant tries, but Male in both instances failed to improve the points, and at half-time Cheshire were leading by three tries and three minors to three minors. On changing ends and resuming, the north- countrymen wi•h the wind in their favour, exhibited greatlyimproved form, and harassed the rival defence considerably, but the home backs were equal to the occasion, and frustrated the visitors' from accomplishing their designs, although Exley, on one occasion, was within an aco of effecting the down- fall of Cheshire's goal with a capital drop; but ultimately Westmoreland were defeated by three tries and three minors to six minors. Teams :—Cheshire: J. Brazendale (Runcorn), back; C. J. Luya (New Brighton), S. H. Davies (Runcorn), and W. H. Male (New Brighton), three-quarters; H. Hughes (Runcorn) and L. R. Patterson (Birkenhead Park), half backs; A. G. Wood, N. Allardise, P. H. Lockwood, K. Monteath (Birkenhead Park), P. Riley, T. Wainwright, W. Faulk- ner (Runcorn), R. F. Muir (New Brighton), and H. A. Howes (Sale), forwards. Westmorland: J. Allen 1 • Kendal Hornets and St. Helens), back; G. Webster Kirby Lonsdale) and E. Hoggarth and W. G. Hoggarth Kendal), three-quarters; W. A. Banks and F. Exley Kendal), half backs; R. C. Beard, W. Parsons, E. Wilson (Kendal Hornets), S. Hadwin, J. Caradice, J. . Parkinson (Kendal), L. Beatham, H. R. Moore (Amble- side), and R. Richardson (Kirby Lonsdale), forwards. Referee: Mr. A. T. Kemble (Liverpool P.C.) WARRINGTON "A" V. HOLLINWOOD 1.9 T Thum—This fixture was brought off at ilellinwood on Saturday, before a moderate number of spectators, in dull weather. Bate (the visiting captain) having won the toss elected to play down hill, and Kay kicked off for the home team, Thorrdey charging. The home forwards broke away, and carried play to the visitors' quarter flag, where Smith getting possession from a scrimmage passed to Chad- wick, who transferred to Tetlow, and this player after a brilliant effort gained a try, Kay kicking a goal from the place. This early reverse was not relished by the visitors, and after Bate had restarted the visiting forwards ' followed up and prevented a return. F. Bate, Beard, , and Isherwood rushed the ball over the line, Edwards being! forced to kick dead. Hipwell dropped out, and the ball being charged down Asher, Parr, and Headon dribbled up the field, Bibby stopping their career. J. Bate gained possession from a scrimmage, and passed nicely to Law- less, who threw across and Appleton receiving the ball made a splendid run, gaininga try. Isherwood kicked a grand goal from a difficult position, the oval striking the bar and dropping ever. Headon kicked off, and Holmes replied with a run to centre. Speakman was here prominentwith a good kick to Edwards, who led but saved his side by kicking dead. Bibby return elt the drop out, and Molyncaux collared Flipwell before he could part with the ball. F. Bate put in a nice run, being tackled on the line by Edwards. The visitors now pressed their opponents forsometime,Speakman at length having a shot at goal, a dead ball being registered. Headon dropped out, Appleton returning intatouch. A lot of ground was now lost owing to a bad pass, the leather travelling into touch near the Warrington line. Jolley took the ball from the throw-out, and put in a grand run and kick, sending the oval into touch at the Hollinwood 25. Tetlow replied with a brilliant run and kick, forcing Jolley to kick dead. Half-time was then called, the score standing—Warringt.on 1 goal and 4 minors to Hollinwood 1 goal and 1 minor. J. Bate re- started, and Chadwick returned to Appleton, who failed to get the oval away, Hargraves bringing him down. thornley relieved the pressure, and Hulmes was promin- ent with a grand run, having hard lines in not scoring,

Smith collaring him near the line. Chamber Bartlett, and Parr, worked the oval away, but good exchanges by and Lawless to Appleton enabled this player to make a grand run, finishing up by passing to Bibby, who gatitsted a smart try. Isherwood failed at goal Both Donohue and Lawless afterwards got over, but the tries were disallowed, and on time being called, the score read —Warrington, 1 goal, 1 try, 5 minors; Hollinwood, 1 goal 1 minor. Jolley was in rare form, his kicking being much admired. Teams :—Warrington : Jelley,f ull back Bibby, Appleton, and Speakman, three-quarter backs; J. Bate' (captain) and Lawless, half backs; Donohue, Isherwood, Beard, Molyneaux' Thornley, F. Bate, Holmes, Warburton, and Acton, forwards. Hollinwood Edwards, full back; Tetlow, Chadwick, and Hipwell, three-quarter backs; Shaw and Smith, half backs; Powell, Ileadon, Asher, Chambers, Parr, Green, Bartlett, Astall, and Kay, forwards. RUNCORN Y. NEW BRIGETOX.—These teams met on the Irwell-lane ground, Runcorn, on Saturday, ,in the pre- sence of a large body of spectators. The weather was dull but fine, and a very fast game was witnessed. W. Hughes kicked off for the home team; but Rig was equal to the occasion and returned the ball, which fell into Brazendale's hands, and was sent into touch. Davies then gave the spectators a splendid example of his Powers as a runner. He put in a grand spurt, and, with his accustomed pluck, endeavoured to draw first blood for his team. Unfortunately, his career was checked, and F. W. Jones succeeded in collaring him before the danger was completed. Davies, however, was only brought to the ground near the line. Then followed a series of excellent pag-ses, and the ball was dribbled by the visitors into the Runcorn 25. The smart exchanges which followed between Wainwright, Crompton, and Riley put the visitors on their mettle, and a great amount of trouble was occasioned Newßrighton L.iy these tactics. When Davies obtained the ball he put in one of those screw runs for which he is well-known; passed to Crompton, and the latter re-passed to Riley, who ran in and scored a try near touch. Brazendale, however, who, essayed to convert the try into a goal, failed at the place. The play of the forwards after- wards became very fast, Dawson again relieving with commendable pluck. Hugh Hughes obtained the ball, passed nicely to Crompton, and the latter afterwards followed this up by passing to W. Riley. The latter made a grand effort to add to the score of the home team by running in. Unfortunately, through some technical breach of the rules, the ball was ruled back. A drop at goal by Crompton had the effect of compelling New Brighton to touch down. The New Brighton forwards came up to the line, and Male made a capital run. After a brief scrimmage, Simpson drib- bled over the line, and Brazendale kicked the ball dead. Fieldwick, on behalf of the visitors, next took a drop over the line and scored a minor. The visitors' for- wards succeeded in keeping the play in the Runcorn 25, until Brazendale came to the rescue, and relieved by bringing the play to the centre. H. Hughes punted well, whilst W. Hughes did his utmost to improve affairs. The play, by great energy, was carried into the New Brighton quarters, where the homesters Dressed them unrelentingly, and Leitch touched down. After some further play the whistle blew for half-time, with the score as follows :—Runcorn, 1 try, 3 minors; New Brighten, 2 minors. The second half of the game proved even more exciting, and the local men gave an example of their unqualified superiority. Play was re-started by F. W. Jones, who took the ball into the home team's ground, but H. Hughes, who was on the alert, dodged well through. Wainwright picked up, and a capital run was made, and the ball was passed to Davies' and after- wards to others of the Runcorn team. Eventually Crompton succeeded in obtaining a try, which, however, was not converted into what was desired, viz., a goal. Wainwright showed excellent form and although the fates seemedto be against the home team so far as goals were concerned, yet he was not to be denied. He put in some excellent runs, and shortly before the call for cessation of hostilities he obtained another try. H. Hughes had the honour of dropping the only goal of the day, and this was done in beautiful style. At the close of the play, the score recorded was: Runcorn, 1 goal, 5 tries, 6 minors ; New Brighton, 2 minors.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. COVENTRY.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. COVENTRY.

One of the most pleasantly-contested matches that I has been played on the Warrington ground was wit- nessed on Saturday, when the above Midland organiza- tion journeyed to Warrington to fulfil their return engagement. It will be remembered that Warrington opposed Coventry when on tour last season, the result being a draw—although it is only fair to state tirat the Warriagtonians were severely handicapped by several of their players being on the injured list. However, on Saturday, Warrington were again placed at a disadvan- tage, Jolley and Randles both crying off. This nec- cessiated a reorganization% of the team. Nevins was withdrawn from the forward ranks and transferred to the position of full back, Massey going to his old position at three-quarter. Ashurst, of the second string, , was included in the forward ranks, and acquitted him- self in a creditable manna, The,visitors were somewhat late in arriving, and it was almost an hbur after the advertised time before Coventry started the leather against a strong wind. Owing to an infringement ot the off-side rule, a scrimmage was formed at mid-field, and though the visitors were seen to advantage in the first pack, Barnes neutralized the effort by a lofty punt to the Coventry twenty-five. Hill, however, was equal to the occasion, and was the means of transferring the sphere to the Warrington quarters. Antrobus tackled accurately here, and although Riley made an extra effort, he found more than a match in the wily Warringtonian. Massey effected a. splendid punt to Hill, but the tatters coolness was loudly applauded. Hill responded splendidly, but a dribble by the home forwards, in which Frank Turner, Povey, and Dillon played a prominent part, looked like scoring until Gray saved his side by a smart save. Massey next became conspicuous with a tall kick, and Gray failing to hold the oval Massey raced up at top speed, secured possession, and safely planted the oval between the posts. Barnes took the place, and landed a goal. Fair Turner responded to the restart, and Barnes put in a tricky though ineffectual run. Massey, Antrobus, and Speakman were each applauded for sterling work; and after ...Riley had put in a well-timed kick to the halfway flag. Barnes passed smartly to Evans, who again placed the Coventry team on a defensive attitude. Barnes almost got in from a good run, Rotherham stopping him close to the line. Speakman, Antrobus, Barnes, and Evans passed splendidly, and again the Coventry goal was threatened, but the good play of the visiting custodian changed the venue to neutral ground. Fair Turner came through a pack, and a shot at goal by Massey forced the visiting team to concede a minor. Fair Turner, Dillon, and Creaghan put in good work, but a miskick by Barnes almost ended in disaster for his side, a minor point accuring, from Riley's good run. j Soon after the drop out grand passing by the home divi- sion deserved a better fate, and although the oval was got to within a yard of the line, the whistle sounded half-time, the score tlaqn standing—Warrington, 1-0-2; Coventry, 0-0-1. Frank Turner re-started hostilities, and after give-and-take play, Ashton executed a neat dribble and almost scored, but Hill stopped his career. A wild pass served as relief, but tricky transfers between Antrobus and Speakman tot* the game to the line. Hill got the oval away, and splendid exchanges were witnessed between Barnes, Evans, and Hill. Oldfield took play to the half-way flag, and after Speakman and the elder Turner had shown good form, Nevins for the first time this half got a good kick well into the visitors' quarters. Not to be denied, the home team kept up the pressure, and although Barnes had a try disallowed, Dillon gained a legitimate point from a pack near the visitors' goal. Barnes was again aftrusted with the place, and landed a goal. The game was now virtually ever, for although Fair Turner and Ashton had hard lines in not adding to the score the visitors managed to keep the Warringtonians at bay, and finally the whistle sounded" no side," Warrington still maintaining their unbeaten eertificate this season, gaining their seventh victory by 2 goals, 4 minors, to Coventry I minor. The game wasla most pleasantly contested one, but it was a sad loss to the Coventry team when Goodrick had to retire through having spr tined the muscles of his right arm. However, Warrington must be compliment- ed on defeating such a strong organization in so decisive a manner. All the home division played well, and a marked improvement was noticed as regards combina- tion, although there were very glaring instances of being too eager, and golden opportunities were lost. Barnes, Massey, Speakman, Antrobas, Dillon, Ashton, and the brothers Turner are to be complimented on their display. Oa behalf of Coventry Hill, Riley, and Rotheram, and Richardson are deserving of special notice. Teams :—Warrington: Nevins,. back; Evans, Barnes, and Massey, three-quarter backs; Antrobus and Speakman, half backs; Fair. Turner, Ashton, Dillon, Hayes, Povey. Littlewood, Frank Turner, Ashurst, and Creaghan' forwards. Coventry; Hill, beck: Goodrick, Grey, and Oldfield, three-quarter backs; Riley and H. , Rotherham, half backs : Frith, Carpenter, K. Rotherham. . Richardson, Newsome, Sargent, Atkins, Harold Bother- ham, and Newark, forwards.

ASSOrIATION. rimsear v. NEwTox-fs-WlLLows.—At Prescot on Saturday. The visitors kicked off, but the ball was returned and kept in the visitors' quarters, they rarely getting past the half-way flag. Score at half-time.— Prescot, 4 goals; Newton, 0. On restarting the visitors played better, but they were never very dangerous except once, when the right made a run and scolvd. The home team added four further goals. Final result.— Prescot, 8 goals; Newton-le-Willows, 1 goal.

THE ZOMO TEA AND COFFEE COMPETITION.—The Zomo Tea and Coffee Company announce that their monthly competitions, which were suspended last July, have been resumed in a new form, and that they will communicate particulars by circular on November 17th to all who formerly competed. The British Government have congratulated the Czar upon his escape from injury in the recent railway accident. The summons by Mr. Robert Miller, Radical candidate for Dewsbury, against a constable, for assault, was dis- missed on Thursday.

Bartington, for moving four pigs, on the 15th October, was fined 4s. and costs.

JUVENILE HAIVICERS.—Three boys, named William Long- thaw, Thomas Howard, and Edward Howard, belonging to Warrington, were summoned for hawking without a licence at Grappenhall, on the 25th Getober.—The defendants were cautioned, and the summonses withdrawn.

HIGHWAY OFFENCE.—WiIIiam Lightfoot, wheelwright, Aston, was fined is. and costs for allowing a pony to stray on the highway at Aston, on the 23rd September.—Bdward Carroll, a hawker, was finect, 7s. 6d. and costs for allowing four horses to stray on the highway at Little Leigh, on tho 19th, May, 1887.

, GEESE STEALING.—Five rough-looking men, named William Yarwood, Samuel Davies, John Lowndes, Thomas Moreton, and Joseph Blease, all from Northwich, were brought up in custody charged with stealing, on the 28th October, two geese, value 165., the property of Joseph Ash- brook ; alto with stealing a half-pint glass on the same date. —The prisoners went into the Horns Inn, Little Leigh, on Sunday morning, and after having some drink went away, taking a half-pint glass with them. A few hours later they were seen chasing some geese in a field on Mr., Ashbrook's farm, Little Leigh, and were observed to kill to geese and make oft with them. They were followed and overtaken at Winningitin. when the geese and the glass were found in their possession.—All the prisoners pleaded guilty to the first charge, and Moreton and Davies to the second. They were each committed for one month's imprisonment with hard labour.

div.head: INCRBASB OF POLICE CASAS.
div.p: INCRBASB OF POLICE CASAS.

The total number of persons dealt with , during the year is 2,352, against 2,014 in 1887. The number sum- marily disposed of is 2,325, and for indictable offences 27. Of the former 1,548 males and 339 females were convicted, and 311 males and 127 females wsre dis- charged; of the latter 15 males and 4 females were committed for trial, and 7 males and 1 female were dis- charged for want of evidence or prosecution. Total in- crease over last year, 33' 8 • which may be mainly accounted for by the increased number of strangers attracted to the neighbourhood by the making of the Manchester Ship Canal, This increase is to be found chiefly amongst those brought up for drunkenness, and for begging and sleeping out, the numbers being—for drunkenness Ste., 780 this year against 573 last year, increase 187 ; and fin, begging and sleeping out, 185 this year against 100 last year, increase 65; thus accounting for 252 out of the increase of 338.

div.head: DBCBRASI4 OF ROBBBRIBS.
div.p: DBCBRASI4 OF ROBBBRIBS.

Oil the other hand, the number of robberies, Sfc., reported to the police kas decreased, as also the value stolen the robberies being 143 this year, and 183 last; the value stolen £123 lOs 2d. this year, and £2BO 9s. 3d. last year. This favourable state af crime may also be partially traced to the influence of the Ship Canal works, as quite a number of people who would otherwise have been out of work, and consequently destitute, have found employment on same. INDICTABLE OFFENCES.

The indictable offences are: 1 wounding with intent to do bodily harm, 1 manslaughter, 1 rape, 1 defilement of girl under 13 rears of age, 7 burglary and house- breaking, 4 breaking into shops, warehouses, &c., 1 rob- bery on the highway, 1 larceny from the person, 18 simplelareenies, 4 embezzlements, 4 frauds and attempts to defraud, 1 malicious injuries to property exceeding £5 in value, 1 forgery, 1 perjury, and 1 attempted suicide, total 47 ;as against 42 last year. The number of persons apprehended being 27, 19 committed for trial and 8 dis- charged.

div.head: CASES 917MMARILT DEALT WITH.
div.p: CASES 917MMARILT DEALT WITH.

The offences which have been summarily dealt with, and which are the most numerous, are assaults on the police, 22 this year, 28 last; common assaults, 164 this year, 198 last; breaches of the peace, &c., 188 this year, 153 last; Elementary Education Acts, 230 this year, 178 last; drunkenness, Arc., 760 this year, 573 last; local Acts and borough bye-laws, 223 this year, 262 last; neglect of family, 46 thisyear, 41 last; simple larceny, 114 this year, 107 last; vagrancy, begging, &c., 165 this year 100 last. Ten children have been sent to industrial schools and 8 to reformatory schools during the last twelve months ;13 were sent to such schools, in 1887. For keeping dogs without a licence, 7 persons were sum- moned, 5 being fined and 2 dismissed.
LOST -CHILDREN AND ANIMALS, WARNINGS TO HOUSE- HOLDUPS, INQUESTS, &C. _

During the year 75 chilciren-reported to the police as lost were found and restored to their parents. Forty head of cattle and horses were found straying and restored to their owners. One hundred and seventy-four doors, cellar grids, and windows of dwelling-houses, lock-up shops, &c., were found either open or insecure, and the tenants warned. Warrants for apprehension of offenders issued, 123; executed 108. The Coroner resolved from this office reports of 80 deaths, upon 42 of which he or his deputy held inquests, and 38 were referred to the registrar; the verdicts where inquests were held being-23 accidental, 14 natural causes, 2 found dead. 1 manslaughter, 1 found drowned, and 1 suicide by strangulation in the police cells, felo de se.

div.head: LICHNSING TAATTBRS.
div.p: LICHNSING TAATTBRS.

There are 87 public-houses, 48 beerhouses, and 70 off- licensed houses (including one refreshment house) in the borough; 3 persons are licensed to sell game, and 1 holds a billiard licence. Sixteen public-houses, 8 beerhousee, and 10 off-licensed houses have been transferred during the year. Two licensed victuallers were summoned for ' selling during prohibited hours on Sunday and permit- ting drunkenness respectively, both dismissed; 2 beer- hVuse-keepers for permitting drunkenness, 1 being fined in the costs, ss. ed., and the other dismissed; and 2 off-licence holders, for selling in prohibited hours on I Sunday, 1 dist/Feed ; and for allowing drink to be con- sumed on the 151-emises 1 fined is. and 9s. costs.

div.head: wntic OF THE FIRE BRIGADE,
div.p: wntic OF THE FIRE BRIGADE,

The Fire Brigade has had to contend with six fires in the borough and 3 out, the estimated damage done amounting to £1,657. There was one false alarm, which caused the Fire Brigade to turn out unneressarily.
IiXTINT AND VALUATION OF THB BOROUGH.

The population of the borough, taken at a local census in May last, was 47,325, but it is now estimated at quite 48,000, owing to the large number of strangers come to work on the Ship Canal. The acreage is 1,442, and the 'valuation £147,844.

div.head: Titll POLICE ESTABLISHMENT.
div.p: Titll POLICE ESTABLISHMENT.

The police establishment- is made up thus: 1 chief constable, 3 inspectors, ' 4 sergeants, and 34 constables; total, 42. An additional constable under my control is employed constantly at Dallam and Bewsey forges, but the com- pany pays his wages and buys his uniform clothing. The leave of absence granted to all ranks amounted to 300 days, sick leave to 394 days, and hurt upon duty 70 days; total, 764 days. Of this P.C. 7, Hennessy, absorbed 97 days, and P.S. Shaw 117 days. The cost of the police establishment for 1888 amounted to £3,888 15s. id. Owing to the very decided increase of population since 1881 it is contemplated to augment the police force by 6 men, making the strength 48, or 1 to the 1,000 of popula- tion. The force was inspected by the Hon. C. G. Legge, Inspector of Constabularies for the Northern Division,on the 22nd March last, when the result appeared to be satisfact,ory. It appears from the report that the police force in 1879 numbered 36, and in 1888, 43. The total charges of the police establishment in 1879 amounted to £3,302 us. 3d., and in 1888 to £3,888 15s. ld.

div.head: TRAMPS.
div.p: TRAMPS.

The number of tramps sent to the vagrant, wards of the workhouse during the last ten years is as follows —1879, 12250; 2880, 11,772; 1881, ,090;9 1882, 8,775; 1883, 5,099; 1884, 5,565; 1885, 6,287.1886, 6,687; 1887, 7,102; 1888, 8,080..

SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A GAMBKEEPER'S WIFB.—Mrs. Carlton, aged 40 years, the wife of a gamekeeper on the Inglewood estate, near Penrith, committed suicide on Wednesday in a most determined manner. In the absence of her husband, who was going his rounds, she loaded one of his guns and fastened a string to the triggers. She must have looked down the barrels and pulled the string, for when her husband returned home to tea he found his wife dead, with the top of her head blown completely off. ThrucxxSan lfswxnns.--darnes Johnson, of New Mills, Derbyshire, was fined ss. and costs 6s. 6d. for hawking with- out license. in Walmsley-st., on Saturday afternoon.— Thomas Barrett. of Oldham, was charged with hawking, with- out license, in Walmsley-st. ; and further with assaulting and resisting P.C. Maitland in the execution of his duty. On Saturday afternoon Maitland took the prisoner into custody on the former charge. After walking quietly a few yards, the prisoner attempted to trip the constable, and failing to do so kicked him on the legs, and struggled desperately to make his escape. A pane of glass in the shop window of David Wright. provision dealer, was broken during the struggle.— The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Ihrriett Kay, an old woman, wife of a boatman, was fined 10s. and costs 9s. 6d. for being drunk and disorderly on the premises of the Albion Inn, on the 22nd September. P.S. Wooley and P.S. Gosling proved the case.—Samuel Heyes, a young man, pleaded guilty to basing been drunk and disorderly in Devonshire Place.on the 23rd Oct. He was fined 10s. and costs.—Wm. In his possession. He was fined ss. and costa for beingdrunk, and the second charge was dismissed,—Samuel Stubbs, a , boatman for the "Dukes," was fined 10s. and costs for being ' drunk while in charge of two horses. For lying across the footpath in Church-st. in a helpless state of drunkenness, and John Crompton was fined ss. and costs.—A navvy named John Jones was mulcted in the sum of 10s. and costsfor being drunk and disorderly In Cooper-st, on Saturday night, and a similar penalty was imposed upon Edward Saunders, a young sailor fromVersvick-on-Tweed,for being drank and disorderly in High-st.—Patrick Duffy was charged with being drunk in Bridge-et, on Sunday morning. FRODSHAM POLICE NEWS.
At the iiddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, the follow- ing Frodsham police cases were heard

BROTHERS AT VARIANCE.—Win. Clarke summoned Thos. Clarke for assaulting him at Kingsley on the 22nd Sept.— Defendant did not appear.—The parties are brothers, and live at Weaverham, and it appeared from the complainant's statement that he was returning from Kingsley. shortly after nine o'clock on the day named, after having been to see his parents, he met his brother, who was drunk. Without any squabbling his brother immediately knocked him down in the road, and then into the ditch, and ill-used him very badly.-- A fine of 108. and costs was imposed. WIDNES MEN AT FAULT.—Samuel Hunt and George Richards. Widnes men, were charged on remand with steal- ing a brass match box, value 3s„ and the upper portion of a table call bell, value 35., the property of Thomas Fletcher, of the Golden Lion, Frodsham, on the 18th October.—Hunt only appeared, and said Richards had absconded last Tues- day.—lt appeared that these defendants, along with several ' other men, were having refreshments in the Golden Lion on the day named, when, thinking -they had been charged too much, Hunt, according to his own statement, took the ' articles and gave them to Richards. saying " We'll have our money's worth."—Mr. Pletcher said he believed Hunt was Sorry for what he had done, and was led away by Richards,

and he did not, therefore, wish to press the case against him. —Hunt said he did not take the things out of the house.— The Chairman said it appeared to be more a case of wilful damag., and considering what Mr. Fletcher had said, the, defendant would be discharged. SCENE WITH A NAvvr.—Joseph Allan, navvy. whose wife appeared for him, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in the Commercial Inn, at Frodsham, on the Ist Oct., and with refusing to quit when requested.—He was also charged with assaulting Sergeant Turner, and with damaging his clothes.—Sergeant Turner proved apprehending defendant after a severe struggle, in which he had his trousers torn, the damage being Is., and he was also injured.—Superintendent 'Naylor said he withdrew the charge of assault.—Defendant was fined £2 inclusive of costs.

ANOTHER NAVVY IN ThoußLE.—Thomas Davies, a navvy, was charged in custody with assaulting Samuel Spruce, in Main-st., Frodsham, on the 23Cd October.—Prosecutor said defendant asked if he had any money, using an oath, whilst near the Queen's Head. He replied that he had, but he had a family of children too, but if he wanted a drink he would give him one. They went and had it in the Queen's Inn, whilst there prisoner said "You are not good enough for me," and struck him on the face, knocking him down on to the fiber. The prisoner kicked him once, but he could not remember what took place afterwards. When he recovered conscious- ness he was being picked up. He was taken to Dr. Robin- son's, who put five stitches in his head.—Mrs. Spruce corro- borated.—A young man named Antrobus said prisoner kicked prosecutor twice on the head. The wound was over to Inches in length.—Sergeant Turner said Dr. Robinson had r said the wound was a contused one, and was such a wound as might be caused by a man's boot. It depended upon the man's system whether he would get better or not. —Prisoner was committed to gaol for one month.

WARRINGTON' MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. CANDIDATURE OF MESSRS. PIERPOINT AND FLOOD. On Monday evening a meeting was held in Wycliffe schoolroom, Bewsey-street, in furtherance of the candidature for North-West Ward, of Coun- cillor William Pierpeint and Mr. Thomas Flood. There was a very large attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. Thomas Morris, who was supported on the platform by the candidates, by Councillors F. A. Roberts, H. Roberts, and H. Fleming, and by Messrs. T. Birchall and John Walker. Councillor John Platt wrote explaining that. absence from home prevented his being present, and urging the claims of the candidates. A COMPLIMENT TO THE CANDIDATES. A letter was also received from Mr. McMinnies, J.P. who said :—" The state of my health prevents me being out in the evening. I cannot therefore be present to- night at your meeting in support of Mr. Pierpoint and Mr. Flood, but I shall be glad to do anything I can to promote their success. They have both proved the earn- estness of their Liberalism by many years' service in the cause. Mr. Flood has made personal sacrifices that few of us have had to undergo, and I hope the Liberal electors of the north-west ward will recognise his claims on the grounds of political fidelity and eminent fitness to render municipal services." AN EXPLANATION. The CHAIRMAN', in the course of references to the claims of the three candidates in the field, had a word to say in regard to Mr. Hedgcock. Be could not understand Liberals fighting each other; there seemed to be no sense in it. When a candidate went against his party it reminded him of two lines he read the other day— "A merciful Providence fashioned us holler. 0' purpose that we might our principles mailer." There would have been no contest at all in that ward had not Mr. Hedgdock been put forviard after both Mr. Pierpoint and Mr. Flood were in the field. A party of friends had cajoled him to provoke a eqntest. But he trusted the electors would go straight for Pierpoint and Flood (Applause.) MR. PIERPOINT ON SANITARY MATTERS. Mr. FIERPOINT, reminding his audience that he had not before had the opportunity of giving an account of his stewardship to the electors of the ward, reviewed his policy and votes as a member of the Council. Referr- ing to Longford, he said he thought that die time was near at hand when the question of Longford should be earnestly and thoroughly gone into. Some of his friends on the Sanitary Committee might say that the whole thing was perfectly right, but there were a few of them in the Council, who happened to know that two and two made four, who were not satisfied with the existing order of things. '(Hear, hear.) In the interests of the town, and of the Sanitary Committee, it was desirable that some investigation should take place. In the year 1878-9 the amount of rates collected in Warrington was 419,855. In 1887-8, last year, the rates collected amoun- ted to £28.485, so that the increased rateable value of the borough had resulted in £B,BlO more being paid in rates than was paid nine years ago. The rates, how- ever, did not decrease. The money had gone some- where. He had a good idea where a good deal of it had gone, and he wanted to have a stronger party in the Council, who were determined to know where it had gone. (Applause.) An individual Councillor could not do it; united action must be brought to bear: There was the dead weight of aldermen to overcome. As a rule the aldermen always voted straight with each other. He desired to continue to do his best towards lessening the rates. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Pierpoint next urged the desirability of the wosking class in the ward having a direct representative through such a man as his col- league. (Applause.) MR. FLOOD'S OPINIONS. Mr. FLOOD in the course of his address, said that some- thing of an exceptional character must have existed for years, or there would not now be such a strong agitation against- the management of the Sanitary Committee The closest investigation would be required of him in this matter, and he should watch every movement, to discover where the weakness lay. There was no class more affected by this question than the one that he belonged to, and he knew that there were insanitary! conditions of the worst kind in the neighbourhoods where working people lived. The ventilation of the sewers- was a matter that required attention, for some grids situated in the centres of population emitted very obnoxious vapours and the poor were sufferers thereby' (Hear, hear.) Then there was the question of the paving of streets. If a man owned a cottage, he was confronted with an enormous expenditure in paving. He himself, lived in a cul-de-sac, where was very little traffic, but it was laid down that the same class of paving should be adopted, and that the same cost should be charged to the cottage own6r, as was the case in regard to streets like Sankey-street and Bold-street. He was met with the argument that it was necessary from a sanitary point of view that this should be so, but in other towns the paving varied in quality according to the requirements of the thoroughfare. Again he did not consider that the streets were sufficiently lighted in the poorer quarters of the town. Better lighting was required in the back- streets. These and other such things he should make it his business to attend to. (Applause) WORKINGMEN REPRESENTATIVES. Mr. Thomas Birchall, in proposing a resolution declar- ing Messrs. W. Pierpoint and T. Flood "fit and proper" persons to represent the ward in the Town Council, said that workingmen should have a due representation on local bodies. Mr. S. Beaman having seconded the reso- lution, and Mr. L. Weir having supported it, Councillor F. A. Roberts also spoke in its favour. If Workingmen, Mr. Roberts said, felt that they wanted direct represen- tation, they had a perfect right to it so long as they were strong enough to give due effect to their wishes. That ward had in the past proved strong enough, and they had a perfect right to send to the Town Council a man of their own order. The resolution was also sup- ported by Councillor H. Roberts, who, after referring to the candidature of Mr. Hedgcock, said that it was well known that for the last two years he had been a member of the much-abused Sanitary Committee. He was pre- pared to defend the general policy of the Committee, which was undoubtedly in the best interests of the health of the population as a whole. While admitting that a reduction of the rates would be welcome, he said that it must be borne in mind that several expenses had during the last nine or ten years cropped up which per- haps no one would like to see done away with. The annual cost of maintaining the Park, Town Hall, and Baths, amounted to £1,322. The annual cost of the School Attendance Committee was £350 a year, and, in addition, £265 was disbursed in school fees by the Board of Guardians. There was also the cost of the Fever Hospital, some £9OO or £l,OOO a year. These were expenses that co'uld not be dispensed with. The resolu- tion approving the candidature of Messrs. Pierpoint and Flood was then carried, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: MEETING QF MESSRS. GREENALL AND VOISETS SUPPORTERS.
div.p: MEETING QF MESSRS. GREENALL AND VOISETS SUPPORTERS.

A meeting of the supporters of Messrs. E. Green- all and L. Voisey, two of the candidates for South- west Ward, was held in .11oly Trinity schoolroom, Museum-st., on Monday evening. There was a good attendance. Mr. W. Owen presided, and besides the candidates, there were on the platform Alderman Burgess. Councillor J. E. Wright and H. Roberts.

div.head: POLITICAL NULENNBIK NOT YET COKE.
div.p: THE POLITICAL NULENNBIK NOT YET COKE.

The CHAIRMAN, having mentioned that he had received letters of apology for non-attendance from 'Messrs. J. White and W. Robinson, said they had only to look around that room and on that platform to quite under- stand that that was not a political meeting. The political milennium had not yet arrived, when the political hatchets would be buried, but he thought it spoke well for their cause, and was a good omen of their success, that men of all shades of pehtical opinion were gathered together with the one object of returning Messrs. Greenall and Voisey to their local Council. (Applause.)

_ _ MR. OREENALL AND TEE SANITARY COMMITTEE. Mr. E. GREENALL said it was only at the urgent request of many influential fellow burgesses that he had agreed to join Mr. Voisey in that contest. He felt strongly that the south-west ward could find its repre- sentatives within its own boundaries. They felt that they should not submit to be represented by the nominee of any Association, and that they should not bow to the dictation of any body of men, without at any rate having an opportunity of saying at the polling booth whether or not such was the wish of the ward. (Hear, hear.) He had been the victim of the usual stab in the back. An anonymous correspondent twitted him with being a thick and thin supporter of the Sanitary Com- mittee. He was not on that Committee nor would he support it unless he considered it was honestly doing its duty for the benefit of the borough. If, after due con-

sideration, he at any time thought their action extrava- gant and mistaken he should not support them for one single moment. (Hear, hear.) He felt sure that if his friend Alderman Burgess would more fully take them into his confidence from time to time they would realize that his efforts in sanitary management were with the best intentions, and they would more fully appreciate the enormous difficulty of the question with, which he had to deal. (Hear, hear, and applause.) MR. VOISEY ON THE CORPORATION ACCOUNTS. Mr. VOISEY said his policy would be to get the best possible management of the town's affairs at thelowest possible cost. That proposition meant a reduction of jthe rates where a reduction could be reasonably made, but he was not going to join in the chorus that the rate should be brought down'from Ss. 6d. to 45.6 d. or 3s. Bd. He should like to know how many of those people who talked so much about reducing the rates had gone( into the annual accounts published by the borough treasurer. He found there that the bonded or eapital debt of the town was nearly £300,000. That in itself was an item and there was a very large expenditure in meeting the capital redemption and the interest upon that sum. That alone,he thought,must,speaking roughly, represent about one-third of the entire expenditure of the town. If begot into the Council he thought there would be room for suggestion as to the mode in which the accounts were set forth, as he thought there was rOom for amendment there. (Hear, hear.) He should speak out very frankly as to anything which he thought wanted suggesting, and he believed he could made sug- gestions whereby the accounts could be made a little clearer. (Applause.) Councillor Witicurr moved " That this meeting con- siders Mr. Edward Greenall and Mr. Lewis Voisey are fit and proper persons to represent this ward in the Town Council, and that it pledges itself to use every legitimate means to secure their return at the forthcoming election." Councillor H. Romurrs seconded this Proposal, and in doing so criticised some of the statements in Mr. T. Jones' address. AN ASSERTION AND A CHALLENGE. Alderman BURGESS, supported the proposal, and, referring to the work of the Sanitary Committee, said they had none of the ratepayers' money at Longford. They had had the authority of the ratepayers to borrow money in their name, and out of the material taken to Longford—which was of no value when collected but a source of disease and death until they got it removed— they got that which pays the interest on the borrowed capital and provided a sinking fund for the redemption of the capital within the time it was borrowed for, and along with that they had a very handsome sum of money at the end of the year. Something had been said about an account being given. Too much had already been said of an ill-natured character to allow of that question settling down on the Sanitary Committeee giving an account. He should demand that there be a most thorough, complete and searching inquiry on the spot as to the working of the whole of the sanitary systan that had been spoken so much of. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Burgess, in conclusion, repeated that from the material taken to Longford a sum of money was derived that paid the interest on the loan and provided a sinking fund for the redemption of the loan, and, in addition, contributed handsome sum towards the rates of the borough. Upon that statement he was prepared to stake his reputation, and he challenzed any gentleman either inside or outside the Council ghamber, in the Public Hall or any other' place to disprove the statement. (Hear, hear, and applause.) '
The proposal was supported by Mr. Westwell, and Mr. A. Browne, and carried unanimously. A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close.
A SI7PPLEMENTARY MEETING.

A second meeting of the burgesses of the South-west ward, in support of the candidature of Messrs. Greenall and Voisey, was held on Wednesday evening in the I Workingmen's Mission room, Bank Quay. The chair was occupied by Mr. R. Williamson, and amongst those also plesent were the candidates, Councillor J. E. Wright, and Messrs. W. W. Westwell, and W. Bennett. There was only a smallottendance. After the Chairman had spoken, Mr. E. Greenall gave an address similar to the one that he delivered at the meeting on Monday I evening.—Mr. Voisey, in the course of his remarks, said that in the Corporation accounts for the year end- ing March, 1888, in the improvement Rate account, there was an item of expenditure of something like £2.268 in the purchase of a field at Howley for the purpose of a store-yard. The whole of the capital cost of that place was charged, and the ratepayers had to pay it in the rate for such year. It seemed to him utterly wrong to ask any set of ratepayers to pay for a capital purchase of property in that style, because those who were 'the ratepayers for that year, although they might be resident in the borough for that year only, had been made to contribute towards the entire purchase of that property. The money for the purchase was found by the bankers, and it would be quite right to say to the ratepayers that they must contribute the interest of the purchase money, but cer- tainly not to contribute to the capital cost in one year. Had it been a matter of £lO,OOO, they would see what a great hardship it would have been to charge it in that way. He wished to point out the necessity for sending men to the Town Council who were able to deal with questions of that kind. Mr. Voisoy then proceeded to refute what was termed an insinuation on the part of Mr. Jones that he and Mr. Greenall we the nominees of the Sanitary Committee. An insinuation of that kind, he said, was entirely unworthy anyone who aspired to a seat in the Town Council. (Applause.)—A resolution approving of the candidature of Messrs. Geeenall and Voisey was then passed on the propbsition of Mr. Westwell, seconded by Air. Bennett, and supported by Councillor Wright.

MEETING OF MR. BARLOW'S ST/PPORTERFI In support of his candidature for the north-east ward, Mr. S. Barlow convened a meeting which was held in the Brick-street schoolroom on Tuesday evening. Mr. W. Willett was elected to preside. There was a good attendance.—The Chairman, in the course of, his remarks, said that the sanitary arrangements of the north-east ward were very bad, and anyone walking up Battersby-lane and along the streets in that neighbourhood would find them in a very bad state. They were told that if they lived any- where near the residence of a town councillor the sanitary arrangements were in a good condition, but he was sorry to say that they had no town councillors living in that ward; it would be a good job for them if they had. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. S. Barlow said, with regard to the outcry that was being made as to the intercepting depots, that he had a large property in the neighbourhood of the depot in that ward. There was no doubt that the depot was a nuisance,—they all admitted that—andhe should do his best to see how far a better mode of working would make it less unbearable, but after thousands of pounds had been spent on the depots it was nonsense to talk about doing away .With I them. By careful management he believed a great deal of the nuisance would be avoided. As to the reduction of rates he believed they could be reduced to less than ss. in the £. (Applause.)—Mr. Bate moved that Mr. Barlow was a fit and proper person to represent the burgesses of the north-east ward.—Mr. James Hemmingway seconded this proposal which was agreed to unannuously.—ln answer to a question Mr. Barlow said he was in favour of the front of the Town Rail being improved.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: MR. HEDGCOCR'S CANDIDATURE. LIVELY MEETING.
div.p: MR. HEDGCOCR'S CANDIDATURE. LIVELY MEETING.

On Tuesday evening a meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Hedgcock for the North-West Ward was held in Wycliffe Hall. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Pendlebury, and amongst those who were on the platform were the candidate, and Mr. W. 11. J. Jenkins, George Woods;W. Law- less, H. T. Bowers, B. Marshall, J. Banner, and W. Kerfoot. There was a good attendance. MR. HEDGCOCK'S PROGRAMME.

In the course of a short address which. Mr. Hedgcock read, he said that if he was returned to the Town Council he should be proud of the honour eonferredupon him,but if he was not successful, although it would be a loss, he did not intend to shed many tears. If he was re- turned he should endeavour to do his duty. It was in Committee where the work was really done, and if he regularly attended to that particular business, they must excuse him if they should not see his name amongst the speakers, assuming, of course, that he was elected. He should to the best of his ability vote for anything that vffluld be a judicious saving to the pockets of the rate- payers. Economy must be the main point, but-proper improvement must not be lost sight of, and whatever was done must be well done. The same principles that guided a man in the conducting of his own business should appertain in the coaduct of the town's affairs. (Applause.) MR. WOODS AND THE RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION. Mn. GEORGE' WOODS proposed 'That Mr. John Hedge- cock is a fit and proper person to represent the rate- payers of the North-west Ward in the Town Council of this town." Referring to the candidature of Mr. Flood as a nominee of the Ratepayers' Association' Mr. Woods took occasion to remark that that Associatitc was not a representative body. There were, he remarked, 8,000 ratepayers in Warrington, and yet the Association did not number mote than 100 members. What was wanted was an Association of an entirely different composition —onke of the manufacturers, tradesmen, and working men .du He condemned the nomination of political parties in regard to the election of Town Councillors, but opined that in this instance the Rayepayers' Association had been formed principally for the purpose of sending ambitious men to the Town Council, on the cheap. The Association had tried to bring an honourable body of men into_gontempt but had only succeeded in dis- gracing itself. (Applause.) Mr. Woods then referred to the qualifications of Mr. Hedgcock.
WARRINGTON AND THIS SHIP CANAL.

Mr. WILLIAM LAWLESS, who seconded the proposition, said that he failed to see that the Town had got much advantage from the large expenditure incurred at Long- ford. Now that the construction of the Ship Canal was in progress there was every prospect of Warrington being extended, and if those in authority could only see their way clear to reduce the rates, it would tend to the material benefit of the town, because it would be an inducement to employers of labour to establish works in or near Warrington. (Applause).

A GLANCE INTO THE FUTURE. Mr. W. H. J. JENKINS supported the resolution! doing so he expressed the belief that there was determination on the part of the ratepayers not t. dictated to by either political party, or by as to the persons whom they should send to the Council. He believed also, that this was a " sign Of When it came about that the burgesses, of their oWn will and choice, sent men to the Council Chamber, they believed to be blessed with intelligence, with n't rity, and with an honest determination to do their WA for the town' it would be a blessing for all of then2-,1,' believed that we in Warrington were on the herder ricg of great success, and that the construction of the a'7, Canal, with its attendant works, would be the making' r.riefff Warrington. (Applause) .Mr. John Banner supported the motion, and the Chairman was abow put it to the meeting, when A SCENE OCCURRED. o Mr. John Walker asked to be allowed to submit 00" two questions before the resolution was put to the roetad ing. He himself some mentioned to Mr. Hedgcock that he thought that (Mr. Hedgcock) would be willing to come forward candidate he would be suitably: received, but Mr. Ile; cock did not think fit to move in the matter. Deputy-Chairman for their valuable services during the past year." The Committee also recommended that "a sewer be constructed in a street off Wharf-st., to receive the sewage from the now premises belonging to the Castle Rubber Company, Limited." Alderman DAVIES proposed the confirmation of the minutes. Regarding the brook at Howley, he said that he believed that the responsibility rested upon the owners. The Committee felt, however, that the Corpora- tion were to some extent responsible in so far as retarded the flooding of the brook by tidal waters, and they therefore resolved to putin a penstock at the river end of the brook. That, they expected. would for all time prevent the tidal waters of the river " backing up" the brook. Having done that, they had done their duty as a Corporation. Councillor H. FLEmixo seconded the confirmation of the minutes. _ _ _

Cd(incillor BOLTON asked why, if the brook was neither more nor less than an open sewer, it could not be turned into another sewer and the brook filled up. As it was it constituted a serious nuisance. _ . .

Councillor F. A. ROBERTS, referrlhg to the minute regarding the street off Wharf-st., said that the minute of the Committee was one that should not pass without comment. He was given to understand that the street in question was a private roadway. Councillor H. Roberts, referring to the Howley brook, said that he was sure that the Chairman of the Committee would not misunderstand him when he said that they could not give the question more serious consideration than it deserved. The death that occurred at the brook only a few weeks ago was not the first, and, he believed, not the second, that had occurred owing to the insecure condition of that dangerous watercourse. Whether the resolution on the minutes would make the owners liable for anyimilar misfortune that might occur in the future he did trot know. He hoped that it would. It did certainly seem to him that someone should be responsible for the loss of innocent livesksuch as those that had recently occurred. Whether the construction of a pen- stock would be sufficient to make the brook no longer dangerous to life or not he did not know. If it did not he thought that the Paving and Sewerage Committee should take all necessary steps for preserving life, either by enclosing that portion of the brook that was in the municipal borough, or by some other plan. Councilor TINSLEY' asked if Wharf-st. was public or private property 20- The MAYOR: Wharf-st. belongs to the town. Alderman DeviEs said that the street in question was one that runs off Wharf-st.

The Towe CLERK said that it was a private street with a right of public footpath over it. Alderman Devias, replying, expressed willingness to withdraw the recommendation from the minutes regard- ing the street off Wharf-st., if the Town Clerk thought thtt the recommendations of the Committee was not a legal one. The Towx CLERK : I think it very desirable that the matter should be re-considered by the Committee. The minutes of the Committee were then passed with the exception of the part referring to the proposed sewer off Wharf-st. it being understood that 'the matter would be re-considered by the Committee, and again brought before the Council.

Recorded iii—ilie—Minutes of this Committee was a resolution that the best thanks of the Committee be given to Mr. Alderman Webster for his able and valuable services as &airman during the year. The Council confirmed the minutes of this Committee on the proposition of Alderman HoLmEs, seconded by Councillor BLACICHURST.

, MCSEITAI, LIBRARY, AD ARTS COMMITTEE. The return for September showed that the number of visitors to the Museum during the month was 2,285 being no change in comparison with September, 1887; books issued in reading TOMB, 1,843, decrease 21 per cent;; do. from lending department, 2,142, increase 41 per cent. The Committee gave its best thanks to Mr. Beamont for his valuable services as president during the past year. Alderman WEBSTER, in proposing the confirmation of the minutes of this Committee, said that since the last meeting of the Committee the Muesum had lost one of the most enthusiastic curators, Mr. William Fell, who for a number of years was associated with one of the departments of the Museum, It would be very difficult to replace his services. Perhapit there was only one gentleman who might be said to have , surpassed Mr. Fell in his particular department—that of making casts of fish—and that was Mr. Frank Buckland.

-- COuncillor PERCIVAL, who seconded the confirmation of the minutes, fully endorsed what the proposer had said with regard to the late Mr. Fell. Aldermen Pipkmere, Davies, Holmes, and the Mayor having referred to the valuable services rendered by the late Mr. William Fell, the minutes were adopted without further comment. CEMETERY COMMITTEE.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. Mr. Edward Milner having resigned his appointment as one of the representative governors under the scheme for the administration of the Warrington Grammar School Foundation, the General Purposes Committee recommends that Mr. Alderman Webster, the Chairman of the School Attendance Committee, be appointed a representative governor in his stead. The Milton proposed the confirmation of the minutes of this Committee. Alderman BURGESS seconded the proposition. He entirely agreed with the appointment of Alderman WEBSTER, but he thought that -when the time came round for the appointment of three' members of the Council on the Board, some members of the Liberal party should be selected as one of the representatives. 'Pile resolution was carried.
