THE LATE FIRE IN CHURCH-ST. Sir,—Would you kindly permit me, through the medium of your paper, to thank all who so kindly helped to extinguish the fire at my shop in Church-st., on the 27th ult. Great as was the damage done,it would have been much greater had it not been for the valuable assis- tance rendered by the men from Mr. Brundrett's Brewery, and from Messrs. Rylamds Bros., and chiefly by Mr. Brvndrett, who spared himself no' trouble. To them all I beg to give those thanks which personally I may not be able to do.—l am, yours obediently WILLIAM SAVORY. Church-st., Warrington, Nov. 2, 1888.

THE RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION. Sir,—Whatever may be the result of these November elections—and I write this letter before the results are known—l think we have already had ample proof that the Ratepayers' Association has done a useful work in the town. Before its outspoken criticism, all that indifference to outside opinion which prevailed in certain quarters in the Town Council has disappeared, and we now have gentlemen who were in the habit of riding rough-shod over a minority in the Council defending themselves in the mildest accents before the public. The association has entirely broken that compact which stifled public opinion on matters municipal, and it is really to it that the burgesses of the town owe their present opportunity of giving expression in an effectual and conststutional way to what they really desire in their local government. I trust, that the association will keep together, and that it will grow stronger for many years to come. As a Latchford resident, I must say that I am grievously disappointed that that ward should be sub- jected to another year's disfranchisement. It is to be hoped that the association will pay particular attention to the nomination papers of its candidates, and leave no opening for the petty, quirking ingenuity of people who are always ready to fix upon small technicalities to pre-1 vent the electors from selecting their own representa- tives.—l am, sir, A LA.TCHFORD VOTER. October 30, 1888. —4i THE MORAL OF THE ELECTIONS. Sir,—ln my opinion the moral of the elections is—that the intercepting depots are not so black as they are painted. Neither of the wards in which the depots are situated has returned the candidates who made the most of their hostility to these institutions. It may be said that Mr. Diggle—considering that it was Mr. Diggle—did very well in the South-east ward out of his cry against the depot there. Ido not agree with this. Speaking comparatively, Mr. Diggle was a fairly good candidate, and if the Howley depot be as bad as it is said to be, and if the feeling against it be as strong as it is represented, he would, on tiae very strength of his hostility to that depot, have been sent to the Council by a swinging majority. And then, again, as to the North-east ward. If the voters of that ward had been in search of two out of the five candidates who were most hostile to the intercepting depot, whom would they have chosen? Clearly, Messrs. Dixon and Thornton. Yet neither of these gentlemen has been returned to the Council. Mr. Garner, who was at the head of the poll, has, as far as I know, made no great protestation against the depot; and, Mr. Jenkins, the other successful aspirant, publicly and very senQihly, refused to pass a dogmatic judgment -on the action of men who have worked unselfishly for years for the sanitary welfare of the borough. Surely, all this, as I have said, carries with it the moral that the depots are not so black as they are painted.—Yours, Itc Warrington, November 2, 1888.
SANITAS.

LATCHFORD WARD. Sir,—Like many others, lam at a loss to understand the course which Councillor H. Roberts took at the Nomina- tion Day towards the candidate who came forward for Latchford Ward in opposition to Councillor Joseph Taylor. Ido not belong to the "Ratepayers' Associa- tion," and from what I hear do not agree with many things it has done, but apart from this and apart also from the juvenility of Mr. Taylor's opponent, these matters are cast into the shxde by the policy Mr. Roberts saw fit to adopt at the Town Hall on the 24th ult. lam afraid the next time this gentleman appears on the temperance platform he will not have it all his own way. It was only the other evening, at a Large temperance meeting, he said something to the effect that it must be "war to the knife on this question, and he for one should not red until the public-houses in Warrington were greatly reduced in number, especially in the neigh'bourhood of Iluttefitaaftete!,t,=4.t. :" and yet when a candidate comes forward,whe is,a.dmittelly, a Tory of the Tories,but who ' nevertheless gives a pledge that he would "bring what pressure he could upon the Watch Committee to carry out the existing law in reference to publicans who wink at drunkenness being carried on in their premises," Mr. Roberts raises objections at the nomination which prevent a contest. Through this action , the representation for our ward remains unchanged, or at all events we have been debarred from trying to effect a change in its representation. I for one think that an election for this sad of Warrington would have done no harm, and also ihinlc if Mr. Long,ton had been successful our friends of 'the trade" Mil thn COUIcI net baVQ complained of their share of representation.—Yours truly, A VOTER AND RADICAL.

THE REV. G. D. WRAY ON THE WAR PATH. Sir,—lt seems to me when a man gets into a pulpit he thinks himself at liberty to say anything he likes to his fellow men. It may be that parsons adopt this arrog- ant position tram the knowledge that the congregation dare not answer back, for I have heard some of the liveliest eastigations delivered from a pulpit, the recol- lection of which tickles me even yet. But of all the remarkable "sermons," I have heard or read perhaps the most remarkable was that delivered last Sunday by our youngest and latest cleric—the Rev. G. D. Wray, at St. Peter's Church. The sermon was an astonishing combination of ignorance and bigotry ; and clearly shows that it would be better for the rev. gentleman instead of burying himself in a paltry village like Halton, to take up his permanent abode in an industrial centre and make himself acquainted with national questions that are bound to come to the front. What for instance shows a more lamentable display of ignorance than the astounding assertion that the estabiehment of a school Board would disgrace our town? I should dearly like to know what town con- siders itself so disgraced. Perhaps Mr. Wray will kindly enlighten us. My conviction is altogether the other way—that we are already disgraced by the action of such men asMr. Wray who prohibit us participating in the educational enlightenment enjoyed by other towns. But this question of voluntary v. Board schools will shortly have to be finally decided, and I believe it will be decided in such a way as to save parsons having to refer to the " ridiculous excuses" of subscribers. Subscribers, as such, won't be needed .—Yours Sze. PROGRESS

THE TOWN COUNCIL'S "PRESTIGE." Sir,—At a meeting held last week in support of Mr. Joseph Taylor for Latchford, Alderman Chandlev told us that the prestige of the Town Council was being lowered, and that we should be particularly anxious to only send men, to that singularly well-conducted body, who could

be turned into Mayors in the future. Now, sir, if you' will permit me to say it, this, considering the circum- stances of the present election, is a piece of sheer snobbery. Alderman Chandley evidently means that he, at any rate, does not want anybody in the Town Council who does not carry with him the pewter badge of a shop-keeping respectability. If you will allow me I think I can give a better qualification for Council honours than that. I should say that the very best title a man could have to sit in the Town Council would be a majority of votes of his fellow townsmen placed in the ballot boxes. The very worst title a man could have would be the fact of his having been deposed from the chairmanship of a committee through not acting in accord with the wishes and interests of the public whom he is supposed to represent. It is not out of place to remind Alderman Chandley that he is under no sort of compulsion to sit in the Town Council. If those who are elected, this November, are not such as a gentleman of his fine qualities likes to associate with, all he has to do is to sit down and indite a second resignation. He has already broken the ice in this direction, and a thing of this kind is easier done a second than a first time.— Yours, lee.,
PLEBEIAN. P.S.—By-the-bye, what sort of prestige does the Council gain by the election of Mr. Joseph Taylor, and what sort of a Mayor would .he make?

THE WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY. Sir,—l see from your last week's issue that .Mr. J. P. Reynolds" has thought it incumbent upon him to put matters in a true light" as regards the unsatisfactory condition of the Musical Society, and his letter is a curious jumble of apology and defence. Mr. Reynolds admits that the annual meetings are often poorly attended, with the inevitable result,—which I gathea he deplores as much as any of us,—that the committee and other officers are usually re-elected, with slight altera- tions. This much being fairly established, it is, I submit, quite a matter of opinion whether the best way of seeking to .remedy these short-com- ings is for those who find fault with the Society to join it with the object of making their grievances known at its meetings, or, whether a discussion of the arguments pro and con in the public press does not offer be ter chances of success. Experience of the pro- ceedings of " annual meetings" teaches that feelings of personal diffidence and want of confidence in taking part in public debates coupled with the consciousness of being in a minority,often operate in preventing the expression of suggestions most closely connected with the general welfare of the members, or with the furtherance of the objects for which they meet as a body. And when by reason of effiuxion of time and by reason of the re-election time after time, with only slight alterations of the old officials, some degree of ossification of the framework of the society has taken place, and it becomes necessary that these "sug- gestions," to be effective, must be more and more drastic in character, the hopelessness of succPss by the method indicated is at once apparent. The fact is the Committee is far from being represent- ative of a musical Society, and the general tenour of Mr. Reynold's letter shews pretty clearly that he is, himself, conscious of the fact. But Mr. Reynold's defence of the society, of Dr. Hiles, or its president, does not particularly concern me. My intention is rather to say a word upon the subject of Mr. Reynold's con- nection with the instrumental part of the work of the society which he tells us has been "intimate." Your correspondent, "A member of the society," a few weeks ago took up the question of Dr. Hiles' unpopu- larity with the musical public in general, and with the instrumentalists in particular. While agreeing with your correspondent's views in the main, I am disposed to point out, as quite as remarkable, how peculiarly disastrous, from the society's.point of view, has been that " connection " of which, it would seem, Mr. Reynolds is a little proud. From a long acquaintance with many of the instrumentalists in the town, I am able to aver that Mr. Reynold's unpopularity amongst them is quite a match for that of -Dr. Hiles himself. Is there not a peculiar skmificance in Mr. Reynold's acknowledged failure of his efforts to reach the instrumentalists through Mr. Down's agency? I am quite sure that Mr. Down did not stand in the way on the occasion referred to; nay, I feel sure that his efforts are so far disinte-ested that he would be only too pleased to see established in the town a society worthy the title "Musical," backed up by an orchestra such as his own.

And with what good taste Mr. Reynolds sneers at the conceit of our local bandsmen and "their tendency to over-estimate their powers and take offence if, according to their views, sufficient trust is not placed in them." What, I should like to ask, is the measure of Mr. Rey- nolds' conceit, what the number of instruments he pro- fesses to play, and on which does he consider his profi- ciency such as to qualify him to enter an orchestra like that which played to a delighted audience in the Public Hall last Saturday night ? The existence, at the present moment, of such an or- chestra as Mr. Down's is, I think, sufficient commentary on that portion of Mr. Reynolds' letter which refers to the instrumentalists in relation to the Musical Society.—
lam. Scc., _ A MEMBER OF THE LATE ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

WESTON. This section continues to be the scene of busy activity, and the progress made week by week is palpable to the most cursory observer. On the Marsh the machinery is in capital order, and the amount of material removed by the German, French, and AmeriCan navvies in use is enormous. The line of the canal is now excavated to the length of half a pile, and is both wide and deep. The important and dangerous work of excavating for the foundation of the great lock at Weston Point has advanced rapidly during the past fortnight, notwith- standing the difficulties encountered. The foundations are to be of concrete, and there are many hundred tons of this material now on the ground. RUNCORN.

Greater activity prevails On this section than has been the c.ase for some time back. In the neighbourhood of the Big Field, two steam navvies have started cutting the canal on the second level, and as, at several points between Norton and Runcorn' a depth of 60 and 70 feet has to be excavated before the level of the canal is reached, it will be necessary to cut at a third level. The preparations for commencing operations in the bed of the river are progressing apace. A series of experiments have been made with a pile driving machine in the river, and now navvies are engaged tikking off tb tOP soil of "No Man's Land," which will 134 swept out of existence by the Ship Canal. As a prelude to the intended river work," No Man's Land" is being railed off in order to keep a curious public beyond the reach'of danger, and Messrs. Kirkham are also engaged in con- structing in Duke's Field a convenient and commodious building for the use of Mr. Gregson, the engineer. MOORE AND ACTON GRANGE.

_ The German steam navvy, which has been for some time one of the most important factors in the work of the Moore Section, has been taken down and removed to near Latchford, where it will no doubt be of great efficiency in the first lift of the cutting. At Acton Grange the construction of the railway embankment is progressing rapidly. The amount of spoil deposited there per day is immense. The Mission Hall services are very successful, and are attended by large numbers of people. The work in the cutting during the week has been anything but pleasant at times. STOCICTON HEATH AND WALTON. The alternategood and bad weather of last week has somewhat retarded operations. The large American navvy near Twenty Step Bridge is still standing, and has not been working during the week. A large number of men are busily employed at the new road, which is evidently to be a very good one. At its termination above Tom Payne's Bridge it is complete, but in the centre, where it touches on the Old Quay Canal, there is a large amount of labour still to be spent on it, and some time will elapse before it is ready for use. On the other side of the road two American excavators are tearing UM at a rapid rate what once was a beautiful lawn and shrubbery attached to the late Mr. Cunliffe's honse. The soil removed is of the lightest description, as the navvies are only in the first lift of the cutting, but the strata below is one of hard sandstone rock, which it is both slow and difficult work to remove. This is plainly demonstrated a little further on, where the second lift has been reached, and where the work seems to go on very slowly after the rapid progress higher up. THELWALL, LATCHFORD, &c. The cutting near the wooden hospital lengthens rapidly, and there are now three American navvies at work there. Cedar Lawn, the late residence of Alder- man Pickmere, is a scene of complete havoc. The house is still standing, bit it will probably be pulled down early next week. The river diversion at Thelwall is almost completed, a number of gangs of men having for some time been at work on the new river bourse, which has now, with the exception of a bank left at each end to prevent the river from breaking in, been excavated to the required depth. The soil, which is of a loose, sandy nature, has been deposited on the south side of the cutting, where it forms an immense bank. This bank is now being levelled off, and good soil is being placed on the surface, which will lv sown with grass seeds. Next week an iron footbridge will .be begun across the new channel, to preserve the footpath from Thelwall via the ferry to Martinscroft, which has existed for centuries. Before the river can be turned into the cutting, the banks will have to be lined with stone and concrete to prevent the action of the water washing them away. MERSEY AND TRWELL NAVIGATION.

The Ship Canal Company have issued notices stating that that portion of the Mersey and Irwell Navigation extending from Mode Wheel to 150 yards west of the confluence of the Mersey and Bonin, in the parish of Lymm, which is required for the purposes of the Man- chester Ship Canal, will be closed after the 15th of November next. The traffic between Manchester and Warrington will then be transferred to the Bridgewater Canal. The construction of the track railway on the southern banks of the Irwell at Barton has proceeded beyond the meadows in front of St. Catherine's Church.
ACCIDENT NEAR IRLAM. On Monday last a serious accident occurred to Thomas

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 3, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 3, 1888.

Abbey, a labourer employed en the Ship ,Canal works near Irlam. He was walking along the cutting when he saw a waggon being sent in his direction. To get out of the way, he climbed up the side of the cutting but fell back and his leg was badly crushed between the waggon and the rock. He was conveyed to the hospital at Latchford, where it was found necessary to amputate the limb. On inquiry yesterday, it was stated that he is progressing favourably. FATAL ACCIDENT AT ACTON GRANGE.

On Wednesday a navvy named William Hall, employed on the Acton Grange Section of the Canal, was standing on the waggons of a train which was being shunted, when from some cause he was thrown out on to the ground and terribly injured. He was conveyed on the engine to the hospital at Latchford, where he received medical at. ention, but died from the effects of the fall. An inquest will be held to-day (Saturday). CLAIM FOR COMPENSATION. _

An extraordinary claim for compensation for land required for the Slanchester Ship 'Canal, which will probably influence a great number of other claims which will follow, was concluded on Tuesday at the Surveyor's Institution, Westminster, before Mr_ W. J. Beadel, M.P., umpire. Sir John Whittaker Ellis, Bart, ALP was arbitrator on behalf of the claimant (Captain Park Yates), and Mr. A. M. Dunlop on behalf of the Manchester Shill Canal. The claim was for upwards of £73,000 for lan. at Ince and Thornton. Sir William Marriott, Q.C., M.P. (Judge Advocate General), and Mr. Sutton, were Counsel Ifor the claimant; Mr. Pember, Q.C.. and Mr. Balfour I Browne, Q.C. appeared for the company. Mr. Pember, Q.C, on behalf of the Ship Canal Company, summed up the evidence which had been given at the three previous days sittings. The property consisted of 2440 acres of tolerably good land, with fair sporting, knct it gave an average rental of £1 14s. an acre, making a total of £4156 per annum. The only way in which the Canal would affect this property was that they would take a narrow strip from its river frontage. It was, however, considerable in acreage-180 acres, by reason of its great length, which was eight miles. On the farms which were affected they took 155 acres of pasture land out of 1014, one-seventh of the whole' as they only took 24 acres of arable land out of 622, one twenty-sixth. They there- fore estimated it at various prices, which worked out at £lOO an acre on the average, being the very handsome allowance of 50 sears' purchase. Then there was nothing left but the residential damage—the temporary damage during construction, and the permanent damage. There was the interference with sport, as poaching was not unknown amongst navvies. There was the smoke from the contractors' engines of which the dairymaids complained, and then there was the noise, disorder, and ugliness of these unfinished excavations. All this would continue for three years more, and Mr. Dunlop allowed £1,400 for it. The smoke from the vessels using the canal would be very little nuisance. He (Mr. Pember) maintained there would be no perpetual damage at all, though his valuers had allowed £3,400 for it. There were other items for the lighthouse, powder, magazines, two cottages, and re- planting, which brought the total to £26,000; which would be a fair and reasonable remuneration. Sir W.T. Marriott, Q.C., in replying for the claimant, said his case did not depend ad much on matters of detail as upon broad principles. Instead of taking the intrinsic value of the land per acre, he took the value of the estate as an estate, plus the value to Mr. Park Yates himself. Mr. Pember' in his elaborate calculation, had taken the land at £1 14s. per acre, whereas his own witnesses valued it at £2; and he had taken the number of acres at 2,440, leaving out 220 acres of park land. He said the whole estate was worth only £124,000. Now, Captain Yates' father paid £BO,OOO for the Ince estate in 1804, and land had much increased in value since then. Twelve years ago the claimant bought the Thornton, estate for £48,000, and in Cheshire, at any rate, land had not depreciated. Further than that, £30,000 was expended in building the house. That made £168,000 as the actual cost, and this land that was taken was the very cream of the estate. Sir W. Marriott commented on the minor details of the claim, and urged that the lowest estimate put forward for the claimant—that of Mr. Robert Vigers, £B9,3B3—was an exceedingly mode- rate one. The Umpire said he would take time to con- sider his award, but it would not be long delayed. RATING APPEAL. adjournbd quarter sessions was held at Chester Castle yesterday, his Honour Judge Horatio Lloyd presiding, to hear an important appeal by the Manchester Ship Canal Company, who have acquired the Bridge- water and Mersey and Irwell canals, in the township of Runcorn, against the rating of these canals by the Assessment Committee of the Runcorn Unien.—Mr. Bat-' four Browne, Q.C., with Mr. E. H. Lloyd, represents the appellants, and Mr. Marshall, with Mr. J. E. Bankes, the respondent.—ln February, 1888. the union was re- valu and the gross valuation sibis stated at £16,677, • while the old valuation on the existing rate-book was £7,325, and it is against this increase that the appeal is being made.
RUNCORN AS IT IS AND AS IT OUGHT TO BE.

' On Sunday evening,the Rev.J. D. Thomas,pastor of the Bethesda Congregational Chapel, Runcorn, com- menced a series of sermons on the subject of" Run- corn as it is and as it ought to be." The rev, gentle.. man took for his text,Leviticus,l9 c. 30 v." He shall keep My Sabbaths, and reverence My sanctuary; I amthe Lord " ; and Ezekial 22 c. Bth v. "Thou bast despised Mine holiness and bastprofaned My Sabbath." Mr. Thomas said in this series of ser- mons care would be taken to avoid exaggeration: no attempt would be made to make the town look better or worse than it really was. It would be his duty to state some sad and sorrowful things, but they were things which actually existed in their midst. He had lived amongst them nearly ten years—he ought, therefore, to be in a position to know what was the real state of affairs. That evening he would speak of Runcorn in relation to Sabbath-keeping. On the Lord's Day there ought to be cessation from labour, and separation from what was unclean; work both for man and beast ought as far as possible to be laid aside; and all things which tended to degrade and materialize the human soul should be at all times. After giving Scripture proof that the Sabbath was intended to , be observed as a holy day and a day of rest, be said there was less regard in Runcorn for the Sabbath now than there was nine years ago. He would refer tlienl to the extensive operations which were carried on in the large manufactories of the loca- lity. He was aware that some of these did as little as possible on a Sunday, but there were others which did as much as they dared, without giving up the last shred of respect for God's law. When he had said to some of the poor workingmen—" How is it you have to work on Sundays as well as week days ?" they had replied "Sir,. it is a case of work or get the sack." Yes, and some of them, in their utter weariness had taken the sack, and had risked being unemployed or had accepted lower wages elsewhere. And the strange thing was that these men belonged with few exceptions to the same works. He did not know whether their concerns were under more worldly and keen manage- ment than formerly, but it was certain that Sunday labour was more extensive within their boundaries. If there was a break down in the week, the damage must be repaired on Sunday. If some portion of the machin- ery, or a sprained wheel, had got to be replaced, it must be done on a Sunday. There was an infinite concern for the profits of shareholders; and hence Sunday was called fri to yield its contribution to the half-yearly dividend. Look again at the increasing number of shops that were open for the sale of goods. It was not so many years since they might have gone through the town and not passed a single shop open on the Lord's day; but that day, that evening, there were many, and they were all of the class which might easily be dispensed with. It was an old argument for the sale of certain articles on the Sabbath, that they would not keep until Monday, but he had not yet heard that lollipops, and birds-eye honeydew, and cavendish ; Dublin stout and pale ale, old tom and Scotch whiskey, would not keep trom Saturday night to Monday morning ; and it was the vendors of such things 'that boldly threw open their doors on the Lord's Day. The growing lads and young men,seeing the tobacconists' shops open, purchased their cigarettes and cigars, and the children, walking innocently to Sunday school, saw, the shop wide open, and in an evil moment, ponce intended for the missionary box were sacrificed in the cause of humbugs and peppermint. He confessed he was afraid for the missionary contributions, but he was still more concerned for the honesty of his children. Hitherto they had agitated for Sunday closing only in the case of public-houses, but he conceived, that it would be necessary very shortly to enlarge the field of their operations and advocate the closing of all business houses except such as were absolutely necessary for the support of life and health. Another evidence of the diminished regard for Sunday was in the unblushing effrontery with which newspapers of the sporting type were offered for sale in the streets. It was now a regular occurrence, he was sorry to say, to see men and boys on a Sunday morning with bundles of these news- papers in their arms, ready to be distributed to whom- soever would buy, and it was not at all uncommon to see groups of half-a-dozen men, or more, gathered at different points reading the latest news of Saturday's football, or discussing the latest details of the latest outrage. He could speak with greater force in this matter if the hands of the religious bodies and organisa- tions were clean, but he was afraid that in more than one religious community it was the common practice to dispose of and receive pay for magazines and other religious periodicals on Sunday. From a commercial point of view there was quite as much to be said for the sale on the Lord's day of the "Sunday Chronicle," as for the sale of the " War Cry." Another evidence of the growing disregard for the Sabbath was seen in the diminished numbers who attended morning service. This was true, not alone of Bethesda Chapel, but of almost every other place in the town. "Yes," said a friendly whisper, "and that disposition to stay away from church will continue to grow unless the services were made: more entertaining and profitable." What entertainment or profit was there in lying a-bed until ten or eleven o'clock on Sunday?

He would make a bargain with them. If they would alter Saturday nights habits, and come to chapel on Sunday morning, he would try to give more interest to Sunday mornings services. Let it not be supposed that he was advocating a puritanical view of Sabbath observ- ance, although he believed ttiat the Puritans were a great deal better than we were. Looking at it in the broader, freer spirit of Chnstianity, it was easy to see that while adhering to the two main lines of rest and holinessit was possible to make the Sabbath the liveliest and best day of the seven. He urged working men to resist the introduction of the Continental system ot working seven days a week: and let them enjoy that heritage of rest which was theirs by Divine right, and which had been given to supply the eternal necessity of his being.
WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART SCHOOL. MR. E. E. MUSPRATT ON THE CHEMICAL INDUSTRY.

The annual meeting in connection with the Widnes Science and Art School was held, at the Baths Assembly Room on Monday evening. Mr. F. H. Gossage, IP., presided, and on the platform were Mrs. Gossage, Mr. E. K. Muspratt, J P., and I Miss Muspratt, Mr. and Mrs. Carey, Dr. Hurter, Messrs. W. A. Watts, J. K. Drilileld, and J. Morrisoa ( sec retary.) In opening the proceedings the Chairman com- mented with satisfaction upon the success achieved by the school. Mr. J. MORRISON read the fourteenth annual report, which stated that the school had been exceedingly well attended during the past session the entries to classes numbering 207 as compared with 168 in the previous year. 45 students were under instruction in art, and 162 in science. Last year the art class achieved its highest success, when 47 per cent. of those examined passed the Government examination, and this year showed a further improvement, for 53 per cent. had passed. The science classes had not done quite so well as in the previous year, but some of the students had distinguished themselves in the higher stages of science, and the committee congratulated Mr. W. C. Knowles, and Mr. W. V. Brown who had each obtained a first class certificate and a bronze medal in the honours stage of practical chemistry. 61 per cent, of those examined passed in science. The amount of fees the Government grant received was £129 145.; and subscriptions £126 us. Bd. The total expenditure was £256 ss. Bd., leaving a balance in bank of £23 13s. 4d.
_ Miss MusPokrr then distributed the prizes to th 6 successful students.

Mr. E. K. MuseaArr' who received a cordial greeting, impressed upon the students who had received prizes that they were only taking the first step in the ladder of education; true education would come in alter life; they were only preparing themselves for the future life that was before them. (Applause.) The depression in trade in this country for the pas: few years set people into inquiring the cause of that depression. They came to the conclusion that there was something wanting in the education of our people. In every country, except our own, they were making strenuous efforts to educate the whole mass of the people. They rushed to the conclusion that all they had to do in con- nection with the Science and Art Schools was to teach I technicology, and they seemed to have the idea that they could teach in schools that which could only be learned in the workshops. They could not learn in a I science and art school exactly how to make alkali. They could put the student in the way of benefitting by the instruction that he afterwards received in the :workshop, and of applying the principles of science to the industry which he was engaged. (Applause.) What was wanted in this country wasnot so much technical education in its narrower sense, but what was required was to teach better that which was taught at present (Hear, hear.) Unless we improved our education and applied scientific training and scientific methods more than we did at Present to our manufactures, we should be outstripped by the better educated nations on the Continent. Formerly in Widnes they had a practical monoploly of raw material, and had coal at a low price and in the immediate neighbourhood; and upon the cheapness of Coal and salt depended their great manufactures, and upon it, too, the welfare of Widnes depended. To-day there was a Salt Union, which was going to raise the price of salt 50 per cent., upon that great raw material which was the staple of the manufactures of Widnes. Coal, too, would become more expensibe. On the Con- tinent, in Germany, there were large salt deposits, and in Germany there was an educated people, who would know how to get the best results out of this raw material. Therefore the time had come, unless the trade of Widnes was to depart from it, and the great manufacture of alkali, comkr extraction, and other trades carried on in Widnes were to be transported to other countries, when they must give a higher and a better education. (Applause.) What was wanted was the more special teaching of science. He trusted, by the application dl science to industry, we should be able to make greater strides in the futute than we had in the past. If we were to hold our own against the compet- ing rivals on the Continent and in America, we must rely upon a more thorough and better education, and that education must be of a scientific and practleal character.

Mr. CAREY proposed a vote of thahlrs to Miss Muspratt for distributing the prizes, and to Mr. Muspratt for his address. ' Dr. HURTER seconded the motion, which was carried with acclama,ion and a similar compliment having been paid to the Chairman, whose generous provision of a laboratory was commented upon by Mr. Watts, the meeting terminated.
LORD CRANBORNE AT -WIDNES CON SERVATIVE CLUB.

- Last evening week a public meeting was held in the Drill Helm cotineetion with the opening of the Conservative Club. . The room was elaborately decorated for the occasion and of the numerous mottoes "Unity is strength " and "Peace with honour" occupied prominent positions. There was a large audience Major Cross presided and he was supported by numerous Tories of local light and leading in addition to Lord Cranborne ALP., Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss M.P., Sir G. Baden Powell M.P.,. and Captain Walker.—The Chairman referred to the presence of Lord Crauborne,who had that afternoon laid the foundaion of a "Liberal Club" (laughter) and claimed that be was the son of a legislator who had passed a measure which had shown more confid- ence in the people than any other measure ever placed upon the statute book. (Applause.) Referr- ing to the New County Councils he hoped that Widnes would send the best man as its represent- ative irrespective of politics. (Applause.) Lord CRANBORNE then addressed the meeting and • said he came to Widnes as the friend of their popular member. (Applause.) That meeting, he_presumed, in the first place testified to the popularity of Mr. Moss and in tho second place to the strong determination of Unionists and Conservatives to maintain the present Government. (Applause.) They knew the old catch- word of the other side—" peace, retrenchment and reform." He maintained that with regard to retrench- ment the present Government in the person of Mr. Goschen, Chancellor of the Exchequer, had introduced and passed ohe of the most important, if not the most important operations of our generation. (Applause.) By the conversion scheme, Mr. Goschen had saved the taxpayers of this country to upwards of 1* millions a year. (Applause.) The Government by their policy of national defence which they had introduced both into their administration and into their legislation had done more to secure the position of this country from any enemies there might be, than any Government which had held office in this country during recent times. (Applause.) The claim of the Government to the thanks of posterity, and to a favourable verdict at the next election would rest much more upon their aOminis- tration and especially the administration of a near relative of his—the Chief Secretary for Ireland—than upon the legislative programme they had carried into effect. (Applause.) Were the Irish cry for Home Rule granted and the loyal classes in Ireland handed over to be despoiled by their enemies, then similar demands would be made for England, Scotland and Wales • and sacredness of property and permanency of contract and the prosperity of the country would be destroyed. (Applause.) Mr. E. W. PARNELL moved a vote of thanks to Lord Cranbome for the honour he had conferred upon them by his visit and for his address. Mr. JAMES WHITE seconded the motion, which was carried.

Mr. G. Payrin then vroposed a resolution of confidence in the Government and satisfaction with the policy of maintaining the unity of the empire. Mr. T. C. EDWARDS Moss M.P., supported the motion, in a speech dealing with the legislation of the past session, especially referring to the Local Government Act. He asked the electors to send representatives to the County Council best calculated to do the work of the people irrespective of party politics. (Hear, hear.) " Alluding to the fact that Widnes had only one County Councillor with its 30,000 inhabitants, he must say that as the average was one member for seventeen thousand ' inhabitants, he thought the people of Widnes had a dis- tinct grievance. He heard that the question was to come up for discussion on Tuesday next at Liverpool Quarter Sessions. Personally he was not a magistrate, and therefore he should be unable to take part in the discus- sion but he had approached several of his friends who happened to be magistrates, and had secured the services of one in particular in whom he had absolute confidence, and who had promised to take up the cause of Widnes, and to help those who were trying to get for Widnes what he thought the town was entitled to—two representatives in the County Council. (Applause.) In conclusion Mr. Moss endorsed the policy of the Government in Ireland, and contended that the Unionist cause was gaining ground both in England and Ireland. (Applause.) The motion was Passed and shortly afterwards the meeting terminated.
STovEs in great variety at Garland's, 51, Bridge-st.,Warring- ton.—Advt.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, NiThiston, on Thursday week, when there were present Mr. J. Ken- wright (chairman), the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. J. Lowe, T. Eatock, J. Griffiths, James Mercer, J. Twist, Joseph Ellison, J. Burchall, E. Syder, Joseph Birchall, E. Birchall, J. Whalley, It. Ranson, It. A. Graves, J. W. Wareing, T. F. Hill, W. Middlehurst, J. Leatherbarrow, J. Fisher, C. B. Johnson, W. Tyrer, and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk). COUNCILLOR KIRKHAM'S DEsERTION.—CRUHL CONDUCT. —The Clerk remarked that the Eccleston Relief Committee had a case of desertion which they wished to bring be- fore the whole Board.—Mr. Ransom explained that that morning Mrs. Kirkham had applied for outdoor relief and the Committee had recommended. that a certain sum should be given to her.—The Clerk: The circumstances attending the Kirkham case are pretty well known to all the Guardians. The husband of this woman was sup- posed to haveigone to America, and at the time of his leaving this country he was not residing with his wife. He, however, had the custody of the children; but he left them unprovided for, and hence application was made to the Guardians for the relief of the children. The mother at the time was residing at Southport, but since then she had come to reside within the limits of the jurisdiction of that house and it was for the Guardians to say whether they would relax the standing orders, which required that a wife must be deserted for three years.—Mr. Middlehtust said they had occasionally relaxed the rules previously, and he did not wish it to be thought they were making an exception in that case alone.—Mr. Burchall: I think this is a case where you might grant outdoor relief. It is an exceptional case. The only tie Mrs. Kirkham has upon the children is her love for her children, though she may legally not have charge of them. I think the Guardians ought to grant some little assistance to these children through their mother. It is, no doubt, a disgraceful and shameful thing that they should be deserted, and I for one will vote that she has it.—On the motion of Mr. Ranson, seconded by Mr. Burchall, it was decided that 3s. 9d. per week should be granted to the children.—The Clerk: Do you order any proceedings to be taken against the hus- band P—Mr. Middlehurst Yes.—The Clerk: lam told that the grandfather of these children is in a position to repay this money.—Mr. Burchall : Well, that is enough.—lt was -then resolved that the Clerk should take out a warrant for the apprehension of W. J. Kirk- ham on a charge of desertion of his children. RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 543 inmates this week, 534 last week, and 508 in the corresponding week last year; 39 vagrants had been relieved, against 57 last year OFFICIAL VISIT.—The Local Government Board forwarded a copy of the report made by Dr. Southey and Mr. Philips to the Commissioners in Lunacy, after their visit to the Prescot Workhouse on the 27th ult. It ' stated that on their visit they found 30 males, and 28 females upon the list of lunatics. They were satisfied with the dress and personal cleanliness of the lunatics, who appeared well nourished and properly attended to. —Several of the Guardians expressed their satisfaction at the report. WIDNES MEDICAL Oretcnn.--frhe Local Government I Board wrote sanctioning the 'lre-appointment of Dr. I Cooper as the medical officer -for the Widnes (lower) division, at a salary of £7O per annum. THE rRESCOT AND WARRINGTON UNIONS.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board with reference to the family named Ward, who it was alleged, had been discharged from the vagrant wards of the Warrington Union whilst suffering from itch. The Board did not think it necessary to institute a formal inquiry, but had instructed their Inspector to visit the two Workhouses and make a report.—The Clerk said the inquiry had been held, and they would, no doubt, hear the result in due course.—The matter then dropped. ST. HELENS DEPUTY MEDICAL OFFICER.—Dr. McNicoll, the Union Medical Officer at St. Helens, wrote that he had entered into partnership with Dr. Challoner, of Abingdon, and he asked that he be appointed deputy medical officer.—The application was granted. ELECTION AT HALEWOOD.—The Clerk reported that Mr. James Mercer, farmer, Halebahk, had been elected Guardian for Halewood in the room of the late Rev. Thomas Chambers. DEATH OF A SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFCER.—The Clerk said he was sorry to have to report the death of Mr. Kay, School attendance officer for Woolton.—lnstructions were given that a successor should be advertised for. A NEW NURSE.—Miss M. B. Palmer, wrote resigning her appointment as nurse, owing to ill-health, and the Board appointed Mrs. B. Priestley-, of Bradford, as her successor. This was all the business.

div.head: GRAND CATHOLIC BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.
div.p: GRAND CATHOLIC BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.

MR. BRUNNER ON RELIGIOUS TOLERATION. A grand " fairy " bazaar in aid of the funds of St. Edwards' Catholic Church was opened in Runcorn Public Hall on Wednesday afternoon. During the past few months the Catholics of the town have completed one important undertaking; and they have now a second in active progress; and the object of the bazaar was to clear off as far as possible the liabilities thus incurred. Upon the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi taking charge of th e parish nearly a year ago, he at once concluded that the accom- modation provided for his flock was insufficient and inconvenient. The chapel on . Mill Brow had served its day and generation, and the Reverend Doctor, whose efforts were ably seconded by the prominent members of his congregation, at once set on foot a scheme for securing a new place of worship, with the satisfactory result that an iron church, handsome in design, commodious ii proportions, and convenient of access, was constructed in Irwelltlane. The edifice was opened for divine wor- ship a few weeks ago. This project brought to a consum- mation, Dr. Gastaldi turned his attention to the Weston end of his extensive parish, determined to put an end to a long-standing grievance there by the erection of a suitable building for educational purposes. A school is now in course of construction by Messrs. T. Kirkham and Co., and is expected to be finished within a brief period. Not numbering within their ranks many upon whom fortune's favours have been gene- rously showered in the shape of Wealth, the Catholics determined to appeal to outside sym- pathy and help by means of a bazaar, and the popularity of the genial and energetic pastor of St. Edwards was testified to in numerous ways. The appearance of the Public Hall on Wednesday afternoon when Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., performed the opening ceremony, Was extremely bright and gay. Stalls laden with valuable and useful articles were ar- ranged round the spacious room, which had been decorated in a fanciful and artistic fashion by Messrs. Hitchen Sr Squire. of Liverpool. Mr. Brunner, who was accompanied by Mrs. Brunner, drove over from North- wich in his carriage, and was received and entertained by Dr. Gastaldi, at the Presbytery. On entering the bazaar, the visitors were received by a body of fair damsels, and Mrs. Brunner was presented with a charm- ing bouquet of flowers by Miss Hughes, of Liverpool. A capital audience had assembled, and besides the stall- holders there were present the Revs. Dr. Gastaldi ; Father O'Connor, Ditton ; Father Chapman, Widnes; Father Comber, and Father O'Donnell, Liverpool; Dr. Mangan, Messrs. R. H. Smith, Preston; J. W. Lightburn, J. Smith, Appleton; Bowen, Ditton ; B. Birchall, F. Murphy, Liverpool; J. Burgess, P. Quinn, T. Wilrnson, J. Mutch, T. Nickson, and others. Dr. Gastaldi in opening the proceedings, said he had great pleasure and the greatest satisfaction in presenting to that assembly their friend Mr. Brunner; and at the same time they had to congratulate themselves upon the great condescension on his part in coming amongst them to help in the great work upon which they had entered. He had no doubt whatever, that his presence would be the harbinger of most certain success, and when the con- cluding day of the bazaar was at hand there would be a happy record of good substantial work done in the cause for which they laboured. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner said it gave him great pleasure to be present to help those who differed so widely from him in aith, and in methods of work, for the reason that he believed that it was one amongst very many signs which we saw amongst us to-day of the nearer approach of all sects, and members of all faiths, than had hitherto been the case. Some .300 years ago they might have given him a very much warmer greeting than that they had given him that day. They might, perhaps, have brought him into the market place and have put him upon a pile of wood, saturated with tar, and put a light to him. That would have been a much warmer recep- tion than they had given him; but where they had put him would be much greater entertainment to him than the fashion of thebad old days. (Laughter.) He believed that the reason why they were met togethtr helping each other at bazaars, instead of frying each other into steaks, was that we were very much freer than we were in the old days, for he found that wherever he went in the world—and his wife and he were considerable travellers— that wherever people were free they were friendly, and the more free the more friendly they were. He had lately been in Switzerland, and they would be surprised to hear that in a good many places, the Catholics and Protestants had but one church between them. The Catholics worshipped at one hour on the Sunday and the Protestants at another, and the only change made in the building was that those insignia which were peculiar to the Catholic faith were reverentially hidden by a curtain when the Protestants went to worship. He mentioned this because it was an illustration of that which seemed to be universally true—that wherever people were free they were none the less religious but they were far mons friendly. (Hear, hear.) He had had in Switzerland lately a con- siderable amount of conversation with the British Consul and he heard from him—he trusted none of his ultra-Protestant friends would be vexed with him—we heard from him with warm pleasure that in the part of Switzerland where the population was almost entirely Catholic, the standard of education was the highest in the whole of Switzerland. (Applause.) This gave him very warm pleasure for the reason that a good many of his friends were rather afraid of putting the managernent of education into the hands of such as Dr. Gastaldi. He (Mr. Brunner) described a 'scene he had witnessed at a
LOCAL CASES AT THE QUARTER SESSIONS. • ,

The following cases of local interest have this week been. heard at the County Quarter Sessions held at Liverpool. WIDNES. Catherine katthews, 36, was sentenced to twelve months' hard labour for having stolen; at Widnes, on thel'Ath of September, a basket and other articles, the property of Annie Jamieson. There were previous con- victions. John Hayes, 21, labourer, for stealing a shirt, the pro- perty of Wm. Calvert, at Widnes, on the 25th of August. There were previous convictions, and prisoner was now sent to gaol for six months with hard labour. Martin Mulvey, 18, labourer, was sentenced to six months' imprisonment, with hard labour, for having, at Widnes, on the 25th of September, stolen a coat and pair of trousers, the property of James MulVey. Three Poles, named respectively Maggie Lizdas (38), no occupation; Frank Ucas (27), labourer: and William Danvilatis (40), labourer, were found guilty of having, , at Widnes, on the 2nd August, stolen bed-clothing and cutlery, Szc., the property of Alexander Lizdas, a quantity of miscellaneous articles belonging to William Vosinitis, and two handkerchiefs, the property of Sam Cut, and were each sentenced to two months' hard labour.

harvest, festival in Switzerland, aid mentioned that amongst the offerings were a considerable number of bottles of wine. He understood that Dr. Gastalcli was a very ardent and very successful worker An the cause of temperance in the neighbourhood, and they had discussed that matter together that morn- ing and had come to a pretty unanimous agree- ment upon the subject. It was, that the fact ' that the wines in Italy were so pure was the cause of the very great sobriety of the people, and they both wished that the liquors people drunk in England were of very much better quality. They were satisfied that if the liquors consumed in England were better, there wOuld be very much more sobriety amongst us than there was. (Hear, hear.) Alluding to the bazaar, the speaker said they were gathered together to promote the work of the rev Doctor. He had two objects in view— one was to pay for the church which was now finished, and for schools which were not yet finished. There were two pieces of work in which he had great sympathy with him, and he could with all his heart recommend them to aid in the work. He thanked them very much for the warmth of their welcome and declaring that bazaar open, ha did so with the heartiest of good wishes for their cause and for their pastor. (Applause.) Mr. J. W. Lightburn said he had been requested by the Committee to thank Mr. Brunner for his presence amongst them, and he had great pleasure in doing so, because this was a work purely of a religious and chari- table character—entirely non-political—and he was glad Indeed to see such good feeling exhibited in helping to produce what Dr. Gastaldi and his church required very much. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The ladies then commenced the sale of their wares. Mr. and Mrs. Brunner manifested considerable interest in each stall and made extensive purchases. Afterwards they drcve to ti 3 Presbytery, where they remained for some time and then drove on to Winningtork, Hall. The stalls were presided over by the folloVring ladies: Nos. 1 and 2, Mrs. Hickson. Mrs. Byrne, Mrs. Burgess, Mrs. Keogh ; No. 3, Mrs. T. Willidmson, Mrs. Massey, and Miss Ellis; 4, Miss Fairclough, and Miss Burke • 5, Mrs. Done and Miss Done ;6, Mrs. Ball and Mrs. Red- man. There was also Dr. Gastaldi's stall, upon which were displayed ecclesiastical vestments &c., and a num- ber of volumes entitled " The duties and the rights of man," by J. B. Austin. Rumour had it, however, that the author ivas no other than the learned doctor and the books found a ready sale. This stall was attended to by Miss Hughes, Miss Dutton, Miss Cullen Miss Smith and Miss Henry. A pretty rustic stall, also denominated the doctor's was under the control of Miss Connor of Warrington. The small hall was devoted to refreshments, for here Mrs. Mutch, Mrs. Birchall, Mrs. Green, and Miss Watkinson dispensed the good things to the hungry and thirsty mortals, who entered. During the early part of the evening the band of the Runcorn 14olunteers played selections of music, and afterwards concerts arranged by Mr. Morrison of Widnes,were given for the delectation of those present, and proved highly successful. Thevocalists were Miss Nellie Handley, Miss C. Taylor, Dr. McCambridge, Messrs. Morrison and Cald- well. Mr. P. Speakman undertook the duties of chair- . man.

There were also other amusements provided, including a shooting saloon, and a" Fine art gallery. The receipts of the first day, including a donation of £lO from Messrs. cireenall and Co., of Wilderspool Brewery, amounted to upwards of £lOO. The bazaar was con- tinued on Thursday when the attendance of the public was highly satisfactory. In the course of the evening Mr. Murphy, of Liverpool, gave a magic lantern exhibi- tion. A dance, arranged towards the conclusion of the day's proceedings, proved a very popular break from the customary rounds of the bazaar. The Weston Brass Band performed selections of music during the evening. The receipts of this day also nearly totalled £lOO. Mr. Smith, of the firm of Messrs. Elwood, Smith, and Co., gave a sovereign to each stall—£9 in all.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

A strong gale blew off the Tyne on Thursday night, with a heavy sea, and navigation was seriously impeded. A reward of £250 has been offered by Lord Sheffield for the detection of the writer of an anonymous letter threatening him with assassination:

The noMination for Edinburgh and St. Andrews University haX..lseen fixed for Tuesday next, when it is expected Mr.'•Ettrling will be returned unopposed. At a Conference of Nonconformist Ministers held at Leeds, on Friday, resolutions were passed strongly pro- testing against the 'reactionary proposals contained in report of Royal Commission on Educatieh. ILLNESS OF CARDINAL NEWMAN. —Cardinal Newman, who has been severely indisposed for the past few days, waS reported on Friday morning to have passed a better night. His health, however, is critical, and causes much anxiety as to his recovery. In &letter to a correspondent, Sir Wm. Harcourt says that when the proper time arrives, which he fears may be at a distant period, he shall feel it necessary to con- tradict Captain O'Shea's evidence in material particulars, some of them, indeed, being pure fictions. SERIOUS RIOT AT CORR.—A serious riot occurred at Middleton, Cork, on Thursday night. A mob rescued a prisoner from the police, who had to take refuge in a shop. Here they were besieged by an angry crowd. but were ultimately rescued byarmed constables. A civilian was dangerously stabbed by a person at present unknown.

WOMEN'S SUFFIIAGES. —At the annual meeting of the Women's Suffrage Society, held at Manchester yester- day, the report stated that th 4 prospects of the Female Suffrage Bill were more hopeful'. The total number of members of House of Commons who had voted ode- dared themselves in favour of franchise for women was 359, being majority of 48 in the whole House. ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A WITNESS.—At Pow-st. Police Court on Friday, Joseph Cavanah, a witness in the Parnell Commission, was charged with attempting to murder Patrick Lane. another witness, by firing at him. —The accused was defended by Mr. Langham, represent- ing the "Times" solicitor. Prisoner and prosecutor met on Thursday evening in the George public-house, Strand, when the prosecutor taunted prisoner with being a scoundrel who would swear his countrymen away. A quarrel ensued, and the accused knocked the prosecutor down. The prosecutor then went outside the house. Cavana.h followed and fired a revolver, but witness stooped , and escaped the shot. Prisoner was remanded.

LORD GRANVILLE AT MANCHESTER. Addresses were presented to Lord Granville, at Manchester Reform Club, yesterday afternoon, by deputations representing thirty-three local and dis- trict Liberal Associations. His Lordship briefly returned thanks, and expressed satisfaction that in the great fight which Liberals had before them, the Lords would receive the vigorous support promised by the addresses just read. ADDRESS FROM WARRINGTON. , Dr. Gornall and Councillor H. Fleming attended as a deputation from the Warrington Liberal Association and presented the following address to his lordship : To the Right Honourable the Earl of Granville, K.G. My Lord,—Your lordship's visit to Manchester has afforded to the Liberals of Warrington art opportunity of which they have most willingly availed themselves to express their sincere admiration of the uniformly consistent manner in which you have, during a most important public career extending over upwards of half a century, supported those great measures of reform which have so largely added to the good government and material prosperity of the people of these realms. As leader of the Liberal party in the House of Lords, the strict integrity of your character maintained so unimpeachably in an atmosphere by no means congenial to robust political progress, has been a standing rebuke to such as have allowed the seductive influences of the gilded chaynber to sap the very foundations of the faith of their earlier days. The cause of the Sister Isle, which we know must certainly and at no very distant period prevail, has been materially advanced by the invaluable service which you have rendered to it both by speech and action,

We fervently trust that for many years yet to come you may remain as an honoured and tru.ted adviser and leader of our party, and that, associated as you are so intimately with the greatest and noblest statesman of our age, you may together witness the speedy fruit- tion of your hopes and efforts for down trodden Ireland. —Signed on behalf of the Warrington Liberal Associa- tion.
J. G. McMnims, President,
ACCIDENT ON THE PANAMA RAILWAY.

According to a cable message from Lloyd's agent at Panama, there 'has been a railway accident on the Panama Railway, but particulars are not furnished. Various packages for Panama and elsewhere were smashed, and the packages on the train were plundered.

• RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. Ta' OWD FOOAK. In a bit ov a plain whiteweshed cottage, As stood up some steps, just off t' rooad, Wi' a garden i' th' front on't, wi' fleawrs in, Wheer th' hummabees geet a rare looad ; Th' owd fooak lived, so humble an' hearty, They wur poor, but content as cud be; They'd a chear an' a gradely warm greetin', An' pleasant smiles allus for me. As far back as mi memory con tek me; (An' long years, aw'in towd, afooar thad), They'd lived snug i' thad cottage o' comfort, Th' fost time aw went to't, aw're a lad, Hey ! an' dudn'd aw glory i' th' garden, Wi' th' honey blooms sprodden o'er t' wo : ThPr wur rooases on t' bush up i' th' corner; An' marigowds too, a rare show. Th' heawse wur cleyn, fro'4' tiled floor up to t' ceilin', 0 th' little square windo's shooan breet, An' wur clear as t' brook watter as rindled th' loyne, babblin' music to th' leet. An' they'd neat scarlet dimity curtains, As med th' windo's bonnier still, An' some Ileawr pfats,—an' when t' plants wur bloomin', They'd clusters o' blossoms on t' sill. 0 ther goods wur so plain an' owd-fashioned, But everything looked gradely nice; A good bacon flitch hung as a pictur', To mek hungry een long for a slice, They'd an oil paint or two, crackt an' faded, Th' ooak kist wooar a face smooth an' streyt An' th' case-clock into th' nook clooase bi thi chimbley, Wi' clickin' voice chirruped "O's reight !" An' owd couple mooar kindly an' daycent Than they wor, aw'm sure, wur ne'er known; They'd never 'bin blessed wi' no ehilder, But used me as tho' aw'r ther own. Ther wur nowt as so suited th' owd fella , Like tekkin' me on to his knee; An' nowt med Owd Molly, when bakin', Forged to mek summat for,4pe ! To ther nebburs, they allus wur jannock, An' allus wur kindly to fooak; Ther cheeks glowed i' booath Winter an' Summer, As red as ml gronny's owd clooak. Nooan e'er heearrl'em harrin' an' jarrtre, Together they lived a snug life, An' clung clooase ther luv. tooan to t' other— Thad honest owd mon an' his wife. When aw grew up, aw oft used to camp 'em, An' cheer ther owd hearts ov a neet, While th' fire-flashes danced keen on t' fender; Like silver, if glittered so bract. Aw'd sometimes tek 'ern pappers an"bacco, An' then we'd o smook, an we'd chat, While MC smiled at thad cap o' owd Molly's, Her fleawrd printed frock, an' check brat. Hoo wur t' bonniest o' Lankysher witches, When hoe linked hersel to th' owd chap, An' hoo carried age wed, aw con tell yo', For young boo looked yet i' thad cap. An' her husband he fair gloried in her, Hoe wur sweet as a appo 'at's ripe; Wod a plain hooamly couple they wor, too, Booath puffin' eawt ov a long pipe. Th' only record at's left neaw's—a gravestooan, - An' th' memories as lurk i' ml mind; • But grim Deoth cuddn'd tear 'em asunder, They booath wur ta'en poorly, an' pined, 'Cause they cuddn'd assist one another; But Luv wur th' last words they spooak, An' th' fleawrs as they liked bloom an' breeten On th' grave mowd as lies o'er th' owd fooak. JACK .0' ANN'S.
